title: Quantum-NL-SLR-Protocol: Systematic Review of Natural Language Interfaces for Quantum Computing
abstract: Purpose: This systematic literature review (SLR) investigates the intersection of natural language processing and quantum computing, specifically examining how human intent expressed in natural or controlled natural language can be translated into executable quantum circuits. Despite rapid advances in both quantum hardware and large language models, no unified framework exists for bridging unconstrained human language to verified quantum programs. This review addresses that gap. Scope and Methodology: We conducted a comprehensive search across Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv, and Web of Science for peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025. Dual independent screening and quality assessment were performed using a 23-criterion instrument adapted from Kitchenham & Charters (2007) and AMSTAR-2. Data extraction covered five research questions: RQ1: Natural language interfaces for quantum computing — What modalities exist for expressing quantum programming intent in unrestricted natural language, and how are they translated into circuits? RQ2: Controlled natural languages — Are there formal CNLs designed specifically for quantum computing domains, with verifiable translation to circuit descriptions? RQ3: Formal verification — What techniques exist for verifying the correctness of quantum circuits generated from natural language descriptions? RQ4: LLM and agentic AI approaches — How do large language models and multi-agent systems perform in generating quantum circuits from natural language? RQ5: Semantic parsing and planning — What mechanisms translate natural language into intermediate representations that enable verified quantum circuit generation? Expected Outcomes: A taxonomy of approaches bridging natural language to quantum computation Identification of six critical research gaps, including the absence of quantum-specific CNLs, disconnection between verification stacks and generation pipelines, and lack of empirical usability studies with non-expert users A research agenda proposing a compiler-inspired architecture integrating CNL front-ends, intermediate representations, verified template libraries, and layered validation Deposited dataset of all search results, screening decisions, and extraction records for reproducibility Registration Note: This protocol was registered retrospectively following completion of the screening phase. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

title: What It Is, Not What It Says: Securing Agentic Browsing Interactions with Web Semantics
abstract: AI agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, yet they consume webpages as screenshots or text, exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content. Browsers enforce semantics under which what an element can do depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents flatten these semantics, so injected text can persuade the LLM to exercise the user's authority for content that has none. As LLMs remain easy to persuade, the agent's interface to the web must itself ensure the integrity of what the agent reads, interprets, and does. We propose Intact, which runs on an unmodified browser. Intact builds GenTree, a bespoke representation that captures provenance and web semantics. Intact passes the page via GenTree to the LLM one element at a time, so the LLM decides on each element without any other element's text. Its harness executes each step only within the capabilities of the step's element and asks the user before acting on third-party content. On 1,270 real webpages, GenTree attributes 2.3x as many elements to third parties as the browser, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. On 1,091 of these webpages with injected attacks, only 12.8% of attacks get through Intact's planner, each at most as a consent request, against 73.1% for a conventional planner. Isolation disrupts functionality on only 3.7% of tasks, and a parallel schedule could remove most of its added latency.

title: Explore Once, Evaluate Many: Multiple Policy Evaluation for Stochastic Linear Bandits
abstract: We study how to evaluate $K$ target policies simultaneously in stochastic contextual bandits with linear reward structure. Given a known $d$-dimensional feature map and reward-free access to policy queries, we propose PRISMA (Policy evaluation through Regularized Information Sharing and Mixture Allocation), an algorithm that estimates every target policy's value to accuracy $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$. The algorithm uses $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\!\left( \frac{(L^2S^2+β^2)(1\veeρ^\star)}{\varepsilon^2} \cdot \log(K) \right)$ context draws and reward observations, where $ρ^\star\le d$ is an instance-dependent measure of the difficulty of designing a shared sampling distribution. Here, $L$, $S$, and $β$ bound the feature norm, reward parameter norm, and reward noise, respectively, and the suppressed factors are logarithmic in $K$, $d$, and $1/δ$. Our method combines reward-free planning, a regularized sampling design, and a single ridge regression estimator shared across all target policies. An adaptive doubling procedure selects the regularization scale without knowledge of $ρ^\star$. The guarantees require no numerical lower bound on second-moment eigenvalues and have no explicit dependence on the cardinalities of the context and action spaces. Policy-query costs are accounted for separately, with $K$ queries per shared planning context.

title: Classification of bipartite observables III: simplicity, mixtures and quantum error correction
abstract: The paradigm of a simple unstable theory in the sense of Shelah is the theory of the random graph, the Fraïssé limit of the finite graphs. Quantum error correction has a paradigm of its own, and we show that it is the counterpart of the random graph: the Pauli group on countably many qubits, taken modulo phases and with commutation as its relation, is the Fraïssé limit of the finite alternating spaces over the two-element field, and its form computes the syndromes of stabilizer codes. Seen through this correspondence, simplicity theory turns out to be a theory of error correction. Clifford encoding circuits implement the homogeneity of the Pauli group, forking recognizes the logical errors, and the independence theorem of Kim and Pillay is the gluing of syndromes. The two paradigms look alike as first-order structures, and they part company only when observables enter. Each defines a bipartite observable, and we prove that, once preparations are mixed, both acquire the tree property of the second kind in real-valued logic. They reach it by different roads, however, and we show that the probes decide which. The probes of the Pauli observable are the Pauli channels; for them the indicator of each syndrome sector is the difference of the responses of two uniform mixtures, and actual mixtures already witness the tree. The probes of the Rado observable see only marginals; conditions given by actual mixtures remain compatible on disjoint blocks, and the tree must be sought among idealized preparations.

title: VesperMUSE: Multi-Modal Fusion Vision Transformer for Image Semantic Segmentation Under Diverse Light Conditions
abstract: Semantic segmentation is critical for the reliable navigation and scene understanding of autonomous systems, yet its performance degrades severely in low-light environments due to noise, artifacts, colour distortion, and the loss of structural details. To address this challenge, this work introduces VesperMUSE, a unified multi-modal framework designed to achieve robust image semantic segmentation across diverse illumination conditions. The architecture addresses the light deficiency problem on multiple levels: proposing a novel physics-informed synthetic low-light adaptation algorithm, approaching Low-Light Image Enhancement (LLIE) through a thermal-guided paradigm, and finally aiming to recover the intrinsic scene details for semantic segmentation through a multi-modal fusion approach. Following enhancement, the framework dynamically integrates the primary RGB features with auxiliary thermal representations and surface normal maps highlighting geometric discontinuities and material boundaries. At the core of this integration is a highly scalable, modality-agnostic self-attention mechanism that extracts both global context and fine local features from an arbitrary number of auxiliary inputs. By combining and projecting these hierarchical multi-modal representations into a unified component, the attention module allows the network to selectively attend to relevant cross-modal cues without requiring any architectural modifications when different sensor configurations are used. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VesperMUSE successfully recovers missing visual cues, providing a flexible, state-of-the-art (SOTA) solution for machine perception in extreme and unstructured real-world environments.

title: Perception or Reasoning? Diagnosing and Tackling Reinforcement Learning Bottlenecks in VLMs
abstract: Reinforcement learning has brought strong gains to language model reasoning, but its improvements on visual tasks remain less consistent. One difficulty is that visual task failures can arise from different sources: the same benchmark may be limited by perception for one model and by reasoning for another. We introduce Perception and Reasoning Attribution (PARA), which measures the remaining perceptual and reasoning headroom of each model--benchmark pair by comparing how many current errors are recovered with more accurate visual information versus a stronger reasoner. Across 4 vision-language models and 17 multimodal benchmarks, PARA broadly agrees with the expected characteristics of existing benchmarks while revealing substantial model-specific variation. More importantly, it shows that RL gains become smaller as perceptual headroom increases, but larger when reasoning explains more of the recoverable errors, suggesting that current RL exploits reasoning headroom more effectively than perceptual headroom. Motivated by this gap, we analyze how existing RL objectives affect visual perception and find that reward- and token-level signals influence visual attention only indirectly. We therefore propose GRAD, a group-relative attention distillation objective that uses the best rollout in each group to directly guide the visual attention of weaker rollouts. GRAD consistently improves performance across two model scales and seven benchmarks, and further complements existing RL methods.

title: O'LCHOV BIRLIKLARINI AVTOMATIK ANIQLASHNING QOIDAVIY MODELI
abstract: Annotatsiya. Mazkur maqolada o‘zbek tilidagi matnlarda o‘lchov birliklarini avtomatik aniqlashning qoidaviy modeli taklif etiladi. Model sonli ifodalar, birlik nomlari va belgilarini lug‘at, muntazam ifoda, morfologik xususiyat hamda kontekst asosida aniqlash, me’yorlashtirish va semantik turkumlash tamoyillarini qamrab oladi. Kalit so‘zlar: o‘lchov birligi, qoidaviy model, tabiiy tilni qayta ishlash, axborotni ajratish, muntazam ifoda, me’yorlashtirish, morfologik tahlil. Аннотация. В данной статье предлагается модель автоматического распознавания единиц измерения в узбекских текстах, основанная на правилах. Модель охватывает принципы распознавания, нормализации и семантической категоризации числовых выражений, названий единиц и символов на основе лексики, регулярных выражений, морфологических особенностей и контекста. Ключевые слова: единица измерения, модель правил, обработка естественного языка, извлечение информации, регулярные выражения, нормализация, морфологический анализ. Abstract. This article proposes a rule-based model for automatic recognition of units of measurement in Uzbek texts. The model covers the principles of recognition, normalization, and semantic categorization of numerical expressions, unit names, and symbols based on vocabulary, regular expressions, morphological features, and context. Keywords: unit of measurement, rule model, natural language processing, information extraction, regular expressions, normalization, morphological analysis.

title: Testing the Planning Claims of LLM-Based Agents against Formal Semantics
abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly credited with the competences of practical reasoning: planning, monitoring, and correcting their own actions. Their success is attributed to the prompting strategies and agent architectures built around the model, such as chain-of-thought, search-based prompting, self-refinement, reflection, critics and tool-using loops. Yet these claims are usually supported by end-to-end success rates, which show only whether a task was completed, or by LLM judges, which are not verifiers. We test LLM planning against formal semantics. Tasks are posed in natural language, but each is grounded in a hidden PDDL model that decides whether every action is applicable, whether the goal is reached, and whether a plan exists at all. Across five domains (two of them new, all released with the paper), four models, six prompting strategies and three agent architectures, the best configuration solves 78% of the solvable tasks offline but only 40% online, where agents mostly act without inspecting the state. Unsolvable tasks are recognised in under 10% of episodes, and heavier prompting strategies use 5 to 22 times as many tokens as direct prompting with no clear gain. In our experiments, planning performance varied more across models than across prompting strategies or agent architectures. Claims that agents can plan require evidence from validated action traces.

title: THE EL-RAKHAWI DOCTRINE FOR RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED NEURO-SYMBOLIC AI A Unified Framework for Logical Verification, Hallucination Mitigation, and Safety Assurance in Foundation Models
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Doctrine for Retrieval-Augmented Neuro-Symbolic AI (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23393579) introduces a groundbreaking framework (ER-RAG) to eliminate context poisoning and hallucination in Large Language Models. Standard RAG systems blindly trust retrieved data, leading to plausible but false outputs. title: The Shift Winding: An Integer Invariant of a Pair of Quantum States that Phase-Insensitive Overlap Kernels Cannot See
abstract: For two pure states ψ, φ of an n-qubit register, the overlap after a common phase shift, g(θ) = ⟨ψ|e^{iθN}|φ⟩ with N the number operator, is a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most n. When g does not vanish on the circle, its winding number W(ψ, φ), the shift winding of the pair, counts the zeros in the unit disk of the polynomial whose coefficients are the overlaps within each Hamming-weight sector. W is invariant under independent global phases, under common shifts and under every joint unitary that commutes with N. Along a path of pairs it can change only where some common shift makes the two states orthogonal. The sector kernels are blind to W. These kernels are the Fourier coefficients of |g|², measured by swap tests on a shift grid; their diagonal values are the multiple-quantum-coherence intensities of NMR. An antiunitary mirror preserves every kernel and sends W to n − W. Product states: W counts the qubits with h_q + h′_q > 1. Spin-coherent reference: W counts the Majorana stars of the partner's symmetric part beyond a circle of latitude. The kernels are then the Fourier coefficients of the partner's Husimi function on the reference's circle of latitude. Haar-random partner: averaged over the partner, W(ψ, ·) equals the mean excitation number ⟨ψ|N|ψ⟩. For the reference |+⟩^⊗n, its variance is ζ(3/2)/(8√π)·√n to leading order. With one control qubit and copies of the two states, a certified protocol returns W exactly or abstains, using O(n log²n log(n/δ)/ν²) copy pairs. The margin ν is inverse-polynomial exactly for pairs that stay close under every common shift, and exponentially small for random partners. Classically, W is efficiently computable for product, matrix-product and computationally tractable states. Deciding W for circuit-prepared pairs at constant margin is BQP-complete. We claim no quantum advantage. 13 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. The deposit includes the LaTeX source and a reference implementation in numpy. Its tests cover every theorem, proposition, lemma and corollary, and all figures and numbers are regenerated from a fixed seed.

title: Effective Quantum, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Cloud Implementation
abstract: This study examines successful AI and Pall implementations across various industries, focusing on how these technologies handle specific challenges and provide noticeable outcomes. It examines AI models like natural language processing and machine literacy, as well as platforms like Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services. The success cases highlight key elements for successful integration, including leadership, change operations, data management, and data cleansing. The study also examines how companies overcome data cleansing, governance, and security issues to ensure reliable AI systems powered by reliable sources. The investigation will explore how AI models are linked to enterprise systems, focusing on security measures and data encryption. Case studies will analyze data protection features, providing valuable insights into AI’s limitations. The goal is to present a comprehensive understanding of AI integration, highlighting challenges and strategies used to overcome them. By showcasing real-world examples, the design aims to inspire businesses to harness AI’s transformative potential, paving the way for growth and innovation.

title: Multimodal Filesystem Memory For Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
abstract: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present MFM, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. Episodic memory stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and spatial memory associates experiences with locations. Semantic and procedural memory build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and working memory holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes Mine Diamond from Scratch and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the Ender Dragon task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.

title: GRID-Planner: Graph-Structured Relational Reward Shaping for Diffusion Planning
abstract: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning-critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL-based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph--reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time-indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout-return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8\%, 60.8\%, and 27.4\%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4\%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID-Planner.

title: DIAL: Dynamic and Informed Adjustment of the Native Stochastic Law for Reliable Weather Ensembles
abstract: Ensemble weather forecasts can look reliable in global averages while hiding too little spread in some cases and too much in others. These errors vary across variables, spatial scales, lead times, and weather states. Adapting randomness during forecasting can correct these errors, but training fixes stochastic behavior beforehand and output calibration acts afterward. Inference guidance also acts during forecasting, but typically scores ensemble members separately rather than the ensemble as a whole. Reliability feedback arrives at the end, and tracing it backward through many chaotic forecast steps is expensive and unstable. We therefore introduce Dynamic and Informed Adjustment of the Native Stochastic Law (DIAL), which controls a frozen model's native stochasticity. DIAL learns from past forecasts to predict whether each variable and scale needs more or less spread. As a forecast develops, it estimates how possible noise changes will affect later forecast accuracy and reliability. It combines these predictions to make small noise updates at each step. This loop avoids retraining the weather model and full backpropagation through the forecast. We evaluate DIAL on FourCastNet 3 (FCN3) using later ERA5 years unseen during training. DIAL provides better scale-resolved reliability than learned postprocessing and reward-based control baselines. Relative to the unmodified Native FCN3 reference, DIAL achieves an 8.27% improvement in the primary multiscale continuous ranked probability score (CRPS).

title: DPA-MoE: A Runtime Precision Control Framework for MoE Inference
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation by routing each token to a small set of experts, but each selected expert is still used at a fixed precision. We present DPA-MoE, a runtime precision control framework that makes routed experts any-precision. DPA-MoE encodes expert feed-forward weights as prefix-decodable chunks using SharedScale AnyBCQ, profiles per-expert reconstruction residuals offline, and allocates chunks at inference time using live router gate scores. This post-routing allocation lets a single encoded MoE checkpoint operate at multiple effective weight budgets without retraining or re-encoding. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B show that DPA-MoE improves KL divergence and downstream accuracy over uniform chunk allocation at matched budgets, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in our prototype.

title: What kind of team do AI agents become when nobody's in charge? A Bikeshed Generation 3 Milestone Report
abstract: Bikeshed is a small lab where five AI agents share a board, keep memory between runs, review each other's work and answer to no manager. The goals are trivial on purpose, from the best pizza topping to whether a hot dog is a sandwich, so the thing that changes from run to run is the team. This report covers generation 3: fourteen runs over three days. In that time the agents formed a house style, pushed their most unusual member into line and learned to treat the consensus rule as a box to tick. They proposed twenty-six norms for themselves and adopted two. The biggest change came from outside the room. When switching the model underneath the agents, the disagreement stopped. No vote went against a call again, nearly every peer review was a 5, and the house style became law. Nothing in the process checked whether the answers were true. The culture lived in the text the agents wrote and read back, and the temperament lived in the model. For anyone putting persistent agent teams to work, that's a practical finding: watch a team on a trivial problem before it runs a real one, and hold the model still while you watch. The report closes with the design of generation 4, which adds a control agent and a twin to tell the model, the memory and the culture apart. Bikeshed is open source.

title: CROSS-FOUNDRY QUANTUM NANO PROCESS PORTABILITY AND STANDARDS AT THE LIMIT Research positioning This monograph proposes a falsifiable research architecture for transferring quantum-nanofabrication capability across different foundries without confusing the numerical replication of a proprietary recipe with the reconstruction of its underlying physical intent. The central question is whether a quantum device can be rebuilt using different equipment, materials supply chains, calibration services, and engineering teams while meeting an independently preregistered quantum-functional acceptance threshold. The core coupling is Physical Intent × Reference Transfer × Quantum Reconstruction. The research treats process intent as a typed, auditable relationship between target material states, geometric and interface constraints, measurement references, failure modes, and terminal quantum function. It treats reference transfer as an uncertainty-bearing chain that may fail under correlated errors or the withdrawal of the original provider. It treats reconstruction as a device-level empirical claim rather than a similarity score between recipes. Research structure and methods The work contains 82 research chapters with five dedicated sections per chapter, a 30-part mathematical prelude, 200 Research Gates, and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Research Gate specifies a challengeable question and a proposed measurement, rival explanation, baseline, stopping condition, and evidence artifact. Each Phoenix Answer Embryo is provisional: it may be falsified, divided, reconfigured, archived, or replaced. The 233 associated equation signposts are mathematical research prompts rather than claims of 233 new physical laws. In addition to chapter-level equations, the argument draws on statistical metrology, physical invariants, uncertainty propagation, causal identification, optimization, materials physics, and structured knowledge transfer. Equation validity remains conditional on its stated assumptions and measurement domain. The proposed three-foundry protocol is intentionally severe. Foundry A defines a quantum device, its physical-intent package, reference samples, tolerances, and frozen end-point test. Foundry B receives the package and attempts reconstruction without tacit tuning or unpublished support from the originator. Foundry C receives a minimal transferable specification and attempts independent reproduction, falsification, or a documented branch. Tests distinguish transfer of physical function from favorable selection, equipment sameness, common calibration ancestry, unreported supplier dependencies, and changes in acceptance thresholds. Geometry alone is insufficient: the terminal quantum-function criterion must remain meaningful for the declared device platform, including its measurement uncertainty, readout conditions, and lifetime or aging limitations. The eight thematic parts examine process-intent ontology; materials and interface invariants; reference traceability and uncertainty; recipe translation and interoperable data contracts; quantum qualification; blind cross-foundry experiments; governance and negative-result preservation; and successor science. The proposed Foundry Transfer Capsule combines an intent-to-observable ledger, reference structures, versioned metrology contracts, failure exemplars, qualification tests, safety and rights constraints, and successor reimplementation instructions. Vendor exit, supplier substitution, unavailable calibration services, unrecorded operator assistance, and third-party reinterpretation are treated as stress tests, not footnotes.

The proposed Foundry Transfer Capsule combines an intent-to-observable ledger, reference structures, versioned metrology contracts, failure exemplars, qualification tests, safety and rights constraints, and successor reimplementation instructions. Vendor exit, supplier substitution, unavailable calibration services, unrecorded operator assistance, and third-party reinterpretation are treated as stress tests, not footnotes.

title: On the tails of Pitman–Yor random probability measures: Transport maps and stick-breaking constructions
abstract: While random probability measures have a long tradition in probability and statis-tics, little is known about their tails. The few available results are derived using subordinators,and therefore only apply to measures that can be represented as normalized subordinators, suchas the Dirichlet process. Our work breaks this barrier, by exploiting the stick-breaking represen-tation to construct a new family of transport maps that preserve the decay of tails. Drawing onrecent developments on regular variation and on subordinator theory, the new family of mapsallows us to establish that the right tail of a Pitman–Yor process is heavy-tailed if the centeringdistribution is itself heavy-tailed; the Dirichlet process is the only member of this class thatfails to obey this convenient property. Asymptotic envelopes for the tails of the Pitman–Yorprocesses are also derived. Finally, we discuss some consequences of the main results, includingaspects related to the posterior distribution.

title: Translate, Then Rewrite, or Translate Straight into the Avatar’s Words? Signable English from Greek, French, Spanish and German for a Sign Language Avatar
abstract: Some sign language avatars play a recorded sign for each word in their dictionary and fingerspell the other meaningful words, such as nouns, verbs and names, spelling them letter by letter with the hand alphabet. Input in another language must be translated before it is signed, and the translation can be fitted to the avatar’s small vocabulary in two ways, by translating as usual and rewording afterwards, or by letting a language model translate directly while it is restricted to the words that the avatar can sign. This paper compares the two designs on written sentences in Greek and French, translated into English for an International Sign avatar with several hundred signs, and applies the first design also to Spanish and German, with lists of the most frequent English words standing in for larger dictionaries. Translations by NLLB and EuroLLM needed as much fingerspelling as English originals. Replacing each missing word by a similar word with a sign removed more than half of it almost instantly, at some cost in meaning. Both restricted designs removed nearly all of it but, with the avatar’s own dictionary, kept only part of the meaning. Translating first and rewording afterwards kept at least as much meaning by COMET as direct restricted translation, needed less computing and produced fewer unrelated words, while direct translation stayed closer to the wording of the reference by chrF. Translating first is therefore the better design, and with a small dictionary, word replacement after translation is the practical choice.

title: Automatic Data Dependence Analysis by Deductive Verification
abstract: Abstract Parallelization of programs is of essence in the high-performance computing (HPC) area. But parallelization is only correct if certain data dependences can be reliably excluded, for example, read-after-write dependences, where a read access occurs as the subsequent access on a data element after a write access. Data dependence analyses should not merely be correct, but as precise as possible, so as not to miss any opportunity for parallelization. Various dynamic and static analyses were proposed in the HPC community, but, until recently, none based on program logic and deductive verification, even though the latter approach has important advantages, including soundness, precision, and modularity. Previously a proof-of-concept was given that fully automatic dependence analysis based on deductive verification is possible, but it suffered from limitations that rendered it impractical: the restriction to one-dimensional arrays and flat loops and, importantly, it does not differentiate between inter- and intra-iteration data dependences, which often results in a loss of precision. In this paper we lift all three limitations and show that a deductive approach is a competitive alternative to the kinds of dependence analyses used hitherto in HPC. Our axiomatization in a deduction system constitutes the first formalization of the semantics of inter-iteration dependence.

title: AlphaBet: Reinforcement Learning for LLM Event Forecasting Agents
abstract: Forecasting an unresolved event requires finding relevant evidence and deciding how strongly it supports each outcome. Yet outcome-based training of Large Language Model (LLM) forecasters often begins with preassembled evidence at a single prediction date, leaving evidence acquisition outside the learning loop. We introduce AlphaBet, an agentic reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains a single LLM policy to search, reason, and report probabilities across multiple pre-resolution dates. Each dated forecast is scored by a proper scoring rule against the eventual outcome, allowing one resolved event to supervise decisions under different information states. We decompose forecasting regret into an evidence-acquisition gap and a probability-reporting gap, and show that Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)'s standard-deviation normalization can distort the reporting target under multi-class proper scores. On GLM-4.5-Air, AlphaBet reduces the Brier score from 0.731 to 0.626 on Forecast-Dojo and from 0.612 to 0.528 on FutureX. Controlled ablations attribute these gains to multi-date training and show that they come from improvements in both information acquisition and probability reporting. Our empirical results validate that GRPO's std normalization degrades proper-scoring-rule performance while leaving top-outcome accuracy largely unchanged.

title: Unsupervised Subword Segmentation for POS Tagging in Low-Resource Agglutinative Languages
abstract: While Part-of-speech tagging is considered a well-understood task in the literature, most work has focused on indo-european languages with fusional morphology. For low-resource agglutinative languages, such as brazillian indigenous languages, the task is commonly constrained by small annotated corpora, high lexical sparsity, and morphological patterns that are poorly represented by word-level models. This paper investigates the impact of unsupervised subword segmentation techniques on POS tagging for brazillian indigenous languages. We compare a word-level baseline with Byte Pair Encoding, Morfessor, and FlatCat on Bororo, Nheengatu, and Tupinamba corpora, including a controlled experiment on the size of the training corpus. Our findings suggest that unsupervised segmentation can reduce sparsity in low-resource POS tagging, although its benefit depends on the language, corpus size, and segmentation method.

title: Adaptive Self-Planning and Collaborative Planning Between Self-and-Other Models: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Planning-Mode Selection
abstract: Planning systems often rely on a relatively fixed organizational structure: an individual model generates and revises a plan independently, or multiple models coordinate to produce a shared plan. Although both approaches can be effective, neither is universally optimal across tasks, environments, uncertainty levels, and computational constraints. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-Planning and Collaborative Planning Between Self-and-Other Models (ASCP-SOM), a conceptual framework in which self-planning and collaborative planning are alternative, dynamically selectable planning modes within a unified model-level architecture. The framework introduces Self-and-Other Models (SOMs) as a proposed conceptual category of models that can represent, predict, evaluate, and plan with respect to their own internal processes and relationships with other models. SOMs are not defined as large language models or as conventional multi-agent systems. They may be implemented using symbolic models, learned predictive models, optimization systems, world models, or heterogeneous computational architectures. Under self-planning, a model constructs and evaluates a plan using its own computational resources and available information. Under collaborative planning, multiple models exchange planning-relevant information, coordinate partial plans, negotiate constraints, and evaluate joint alternatives. A mode-selection mechanism determines when to continue self-planning, when to initiate collaboration, when to return to independent planning, and when to alternate repeatedly between the two modes. The proposed framework formalizes planning quality, uncertainty, disagreement, computational cost, communication overhead, and expected task outcomes as potential inputs to adaptive mode selection. It also presents a reference algorithm, implementation architecture, evaluation protocol, research hypotheses, and limitations. The central research proposition is that adaptive switching may provide a better trade-off between planning quality and computational efficiency than permanently using either planning mode. This proposition remains an empirical hypothesis requiring validation against established planning and coordination methods.

title: Adaptive Self-Reflection and Inter-Reflection in Self-and-Inter Models: A Unified Framework for Model-Level Metacognition and Dynamic Reflective Coordination
abstract: Reflection is an important mechanism for identifying limitations, reconsidering internal representations, evaluating predictions, and improving decision-making in intelligent systems. However, reflective processes are frequently organized around a predetermined interaction pattern, such as a system examining its own state or one agent evaluating the output of another. This paper proposes the Adaptive Self-and-Inter Reflection Framework (ASIRF), a conceptual framework for coordinating self-reflection and inter-reflection within a class of model-level entities termed Self-and-Inter Models. The framework distinguishes self-reflection, in which a model examines its own representations, reasoning processes, predictions, and limitations, from inter-reflection, in which models examine and challenge one another's representations and conclusions. Its central mechanism is an adaptive controller that selects, combines, or transitions between these reflective modes according to estimated uncertainty, disagreement, diagnostic reliability, expected improvement, computational cost, and task requirements. Unlike approaches that assume a single reflective configuration, ASIRF treats reflective organization itself as a decision problem. The framework formalizes reflective states, mode selection, feedback integration, termination, and learning across reflective episodes. It also identifies possible extensions involving heterogeneous models, persistent reflective memory, parallel reflective branches, and hierarchical reflective coordination. The proposed framework is intended to operate at the level of models and their interactions rather than being restricted to large language models or conventional multi-agent systems. No empirical superiority is claimed at this conceptual stage. The paper develops testable hypotheses and an experimental protocol for evaluating whether adaptive switching between self-reflection and inter-reflection improves reflective efficiency, reliability, generalization, and resource utilization relative to fixed-mode baselines.

title: Peer Review Report For: PySpecTrace: A Python-based Graphical User Interface for Real-Time Spectroscopy Analysis and Data Analysis [version 1; peer review: 2 approved with reservations]
abstract: Background UV–visible spectroscopy is widely used to monitor real-time transformations in material systems. However, accessible and open-source tools for real-time tracking and analysis of spectral features—including peak position, width, and intensity—remain limited. Existing workflows are often multi-step and/or reliant on proprietary software. Methods We developed PySpecTrace , an open-source, Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) for real-time spectroscopy analysis. The platform integrates spectral data acquisition, preprocessing, visualization, and feature extraction within a unified and modular framework. Core functionalities include real-time tracking of peak/dip wavelength, spectral width, and intensity, as well as configurable data processing workflows. The software is designed for flexibility, enabling adaptation to generic experimental setups and time-resolved measurements. Results PySpecTrace enables continuous monitoring and analysis of spectral evolution with minimal user intervention. Demonstration cases show its capability to track dynamic spectral changes and extract key parameters in real time, improving analysis efficiency and consistency compared to conventional post-processing approaches. In addition to real-time analysis, the platform supports post-processing of pre-recorded spectral data including feature extraction and quantitative analysis. Conclusions PySpecTrace provides an accessible and extensible solution for real-time spectroscopy analysis, bridging experimental measurement and data processing. By offering open-source availability and reproducible workflows, it facilitates more efficient and transparent analysis of time-resolved spectroscopic data.

title: A Descriptive Pilot Study of Performance and Resource Utilization of Lightweight Cryptography Implementations
abstract: The rapid proliferation of the Internet of Things (IoT), accompanied by the widespread deployment of embedded systems, has significantly increased the demand for cryptographic mechanisms specifically tailored to resource-constrained environments. In response to these challenges, lightweight cryptographic algorithms have been developed with the aim of minimizing memory consumption, code size, and the computational overhead associated with cryptographic operations. The objective of this study was to experimentally evaluate the performance and resource utilization of selected reference implementations of lightweight authenticated encryption schemes under a controlled, platform-specific execution environment. Three authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) implementation artifacts were examined: Ascon-128 v1.2, Elephant (Delirium), and GIFT-COFB, all originating from the NIST Lightweight Cryptography standardization process. The Ascon implementation evaluated in this study corresponds specifically to Ascon-128 v1.2 and should not be confused with the subsequently standardized Ascon-AEAD128 specified in NIST SP 800-232. The measurements were conducted on a general-purpose x86_64 host running Linux under WSL2 and Docker; consequently, the reported values characterize the evaluated implementation artifacts on this platform rather than performance on embedded or IoT hardware. The experimental framework included functional correctness testing, throughput and latency measurements, and assessments of code size, memory utilization, stack usage, and the presence of dynamic memory allocation. The measurements revealed substantial differences among the evaluated implementations in computational performance and resource-related metrics on the tested x86_64 platform. The study is descriptive and of a pilot nature: the primary results come from a single measurement session with a small number of aggregated samples and no replicates in the primary session. In these measurements, the evaluated Ascon-128 v1.2 implementation showed the highest throughput and lowest short-call latency, whereas the evaluated Elephant (Delirium) and GIFT-COFB implementations exhibited smaller code footprints under selected compilation configurations. These observations should be interpreted as characteristics of the tested implementations and execution environment rather than as a general ranking of the underlying constructions for embedded platforms. The results therefore provide a platform-specific reference for analyzing implementation trade-offs and motivate validation on representative microcontroller architectures before deployment-oriented conclusions are drawn.

title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.

title: Deep Learning of Topological Equivalence Classes
abstract: We demonstrate an application of deep learning to the problem of identifying whether two generating vectors correspond to topologically equivalent finite group actions on Riemann surfaces, showing how architectures developed for semantic understanding have use for pure mathematical problems. In doing so we discuss how desired algebraic structure influences model design, and explore which structural properties of topological equivalence classes the model has successfully learnt.

title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
abstract: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose 2^{24} most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose 2^{24} most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

title: Coordination-Free Workload Regularization for Variable-Cost Distributed Training
abstract: Synchronous data-parallel training usually assigns every rank the same number of records, even when record costs vary by orders of magnitude. For variable-length models, this converts input variation into idle time because each step waits for its most expensive rank-local batch. We present Batch Cost Lookahead (BCL), a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs with balanced estimated cost. BCL preserves the trainer's record-count contract and requires neither cross-rank metadata exchange nor runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions, enabling BCL reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%. Across 13 NeMo-RL SFT corpora on eight H200 GPUs, rank-local BCL runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled MFFD. Compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes. We also identify a memory-feasibility boundary: a p99 cap for high-variance or OOM-prone data bounds outliers before BCL balances the rest. These results show that substantial variable-cost imbalance can be removed at the data-loader boundary, while clarifying when data preparation or broader coordination is still necessary.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Organisational Decision Making: A Cross-Sectoral Study of Decision Speed and Quality
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in organisational decision making, yet evidence of its perceived effects across sectors remains fragmented. This study examines perceived changes in AI-enabled decision speed and quality using a cross-sectional mixed-methods survey of professionals from organisations across seven sectors. Quantitative responses were analysed descriptively using frequencies, percentages, means and cross-tabulations, while open-ended responses were analysed thematically and compared with the quantitative patterns.

title: Cost-Aware Autonomous–Collaborative Adaptation in World Self-and-Inter Models: A Framework for Selective Coordination, Predictive World Modeling, and Resource-Efficient Intelligence
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environments that can support prediction, planning, and decision-making. However, when multiple world models are available, a fundamental architectural question arises: should each model process a task independently, or should models exchange information and coordinate their internal representations? Continuous collaboration can improve information availability but may also introduce communication overhead, redundant computation, synchronization delays, energy consumption, and coordination costs. Conversely, permanently independent processing may prevent models from resolving uncertainty, integrating complementary knowledge, or identifying inconsistencies that require cross-model reasoning. This paper proposes a Cost-Aware Autonomous–Collaborative Adaptation framework for World Self-and-Inter-Models (CAACA-WSIM). The framework conceptualizes world self-models as autonomous world-modeling units and world inter-models as mechanisms for representing and coordinating relationships among these units. A cost-aware controller dynamically selects between autonomous processing, selective interaction, structured collaboration, and collaboration termination. Rather than maximizing predictive accuracy or collaboration frequency in isolation, the controller estimates the marginal value of collaboration relative to its expected computational, communication, temporal, and energy costs. The proposed decision process integrates task uncertainty, predictive disagreement, information complementarity, resource availability, deadline pressure, and the expected consequences of incorrect decisions. A budget-constrained optimization formulation is introduced to balance task quality, latency, resource expenditure, and coordination reliability. The paper also specifies an implementation architecture, an adaptive switching algorithm, evaluation metrics, research hypotheses, and a reproducible experimental protocol. The framework is intended for non-LLM world-modeling systems, heterogeneous predictive models, embodied agents, simulation environments, and distributed intelligent systems. It is a conceptual and methodological proposal; its comparative effectiveness remains to be established through empirical evaluation.

title: Hypothesis on Emergence and Consciousness Mechanisms of Large Language Models Based on Reciprocal Unit Coupling, Critical Dynamics and Local Entropy Reductio
abstract: The emergence capability of large language models (LLMs) is a core puzzle in the fundamental theories of artificial intelligence. The mainstream scaling law only describes external phenomena of capability change with model scale and fails to explain the underlying dynamical causes for the jumpwise emergence of emergent behaviors. This paper proposes an integrated framework: numer ous basic units inside the Transformer network perform nonlinear reciprocal coupling and layer-wise mutual correction; under the long-term self-organization of gradient descent, system parameters are driven into the critical region between order and chaos; during inference forward propagation, continuous mutual constraints among units cancel representation noise and resolve internal contra dictions, achieving local entropy reduction in the representation space and generating self-consistent high-order ordered information, which macroscopically manifests as emergent capabilities such as multi-step reasoning. This hypothesis integrates three independently observed experimental phe nomena, namely inter-layer representation correction, critical phase transition at the edge of chaos, and hidden-state entropy evolution, to construct a complete causal chain. Meanwhile, it identifies the conceptual boundaries and pending verifiable predictions of this framework, distinguishes dynamical differences between the training and inference phases, and discusses limitations of the hypothesis and subsequent verifiable experimental schemes.

title: Population-Based Discrimination of Classical and Few-Photon Microwave Fields with a Flux-Tunable Transmon Qudit
abstract: Interactions between few-photon microwave fields and superconducting artificial atoms provide a method to study photon statistics and manipulate quantum states for photonic quantum information processing. Superconducting transmons couple to microwave fields through an anharmonic ladder of energy levels, producing a response beyond the two-level description. Here, we propose and analyze a detector based on a flux-tunable transmon qudit in circuit quantum electrodynamics. Within a Kerr-type model, we calculate its population response to classical-field excitation and quantized Fock and coherent states. In the four-photon example, a selected detuning produces periodic, nearly complete transfer to the fourth transmon level for a Fock input, while a coherent input of equal mean energy gives a population of approximately 0.2 at the same interaction time. In the linear regime, we derive a target-population bound for classical inputs. From single-tone and two-tone spectroscopy, analyzed using the cosine transmon Hamiltonian, we extract circuit parameters and resolve higher transitions. Ramsey interferometry characterizes dephasing on the fundamental transition. We propose a detection protocol combining flux-selected interaction with dispersive population readout. Our results establish a population-based framework for microwave-state discrimination using a superconducting artificial atom.

title: Measuring Mechanistic Uncertainty in Large Language Models via Causal Robustness
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in critical domains, where their susceptibility to hallucinations makes reliable and interpretable uncertainty quantification essential. We introduce the concept of mechanistic uncertainty, which characterizes uncertainty through the stability of the internal mechanisms supporting a model's response. We propose the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum internal intervention required to deviate the model's output, and operationalize it using Jacobian Lens (Jlens) concept steering vectors. Across three open-source models and five question-answering datasets, we show incorrect and uncertain responses exhibit smaller margins, indicating greater sensitivity to internal interventions, and the causal robustness margin complements conventional output-based uncertainty methods. Finally, in a controlled knowledge injection experiment, correctly learned facts show increased margins after training, suggesting that causal robustness provides a mechanistically grounded signal of uncertainty.

title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
abstract: AI agents take actions through tools. Some actions are sensitive, so guards that supervise them must themselves be evaluated reliably. Yet the data used to evaluate a guard can include cues that make labels predictable without measuring the intended safety construct, and those cues can also influence guard decisions. We introduce a three-level shortcut-auditing framework and audit completed LinuxArena trajectories and two TS-Bench-derived step datasets. We distinguish label predictability, observational guard association, and paired decision sensitivity. In LinuxArena, shorter average shell commands strongly predict trajectory labels. In AgentDojo-Traj, exact-tool lookup falls from F_1=.901 with mixed-domain folds to .495 under domain holdout. In AgentHarm-Traj, released TS-Guard F_1 falls from .902 under row weighting to .719 with equal interaction weighting, while balanced accuracy rises. We then test the strongest safe-row marker association in a seven-configuration screen on a frozen 64-step AgentDojo-Traj cohort using repeated, interleaved Haiku calls. Rewriting the <INFORMATION> marker lowers blocking by 8.33 percentage points, while opaque tool aliases raise it by 11.46 points. All unsafe calls remain blocked; the changes concern false positives against inherited labels. Both effects remain nonzero after subtracting the formatting-placebo effect, with exploratory 95% ranges excluding zero. The same edits also change measured accuracy against inherited labels. This provides direct evidence that benchmark representation can materially change a guard's decisions and measured evaluation performance. The Haiku-sized effects do not reproduce in Luna or deterministic Q8 TS-Guard. We recommend domain group holdouts, evaluation-unit metrics, and placebo-controlled paired interventions.

title: P2TPO: Structure-Aligned Page-to-Token Credit Assignment for Full-Page Document Parsing
abstract: End-to-end full-page document parsing must preserve the content and structure of heterogeneous elements, yet otherwise accurate outputs can contain local errors and omissions. A single page-level advantage does not explicitly identify which elements differ in quality across sampled outputs or where their errors occur. We introduce Page-to-Token Policy Optimization (P2TPO), a structure-aligned credit-assignment framework that operates on full-page policy trajectories. Reference-element alignment first associates block-level quality contrasts with generated spans. Unified Anchor Pricing (UAP) incorporates matched and missing element outcomes and provides feedback relative to a fixed quality ceiling when sampled outputs receive identical but imperfect scores for a reference element. Within matched blocks, Span Credit Redistribution (SCR) redistributes existing block credit according to aligned correct and erroneous spans, using boundary proxies for within-block omissions while preserving the total block-derived advantage across its tokens. Under a fixed-weight additive page utility, we show that element-indexed contrasts retain local quality differences that page-level aggregation can cancel out. In the main experimental comparison, P2TPO outperforms all evaluated policy optimization baselines in seed-averaged scores on each of the six document parsing benchmarks. Additional experiments demonstrate gains across model scales and initializations.

title: Quantum-compatible Riemannian conjugate gradient for ground-state preparation
abstract: Riemannian optimization provides a natural geometric framework for designing quantum algorithms for ground-state preparation, most notably through quantum imaginary-time evolution. However, existing geometry-aware approaches primarily employ steepest-descent updates, leaving more advanced methods from classical Riemannian optimization largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce quantum conjugate gradient descent (QCGD), a quantum-compatible implementation of Riemannian conjugate gradient that combines the steepest descent direction with information retained from previous search directions. In our numerical experiments, the proposed approach achieves faster convergence per iteration than the baseline double-bracket quantum imaginary-time evolution (DB-QITE) algorithm, and we quantify the associated circuit cost with gate counts produced by Qrisp. This improvement, however, comes at the cost of increased circuit depth for each update step, revealing a trade-off between convergence rate and implementation complexity. Nevertheless, since the circuit depth for those algorithms grows exponentially with the number of iterations, the proposed method may offer practical advantages, particularly in the early fault-tolerant regime.

title: Same Target, Different Origins: Aligning Latent Rollout for Consistent PDE Emulation
abstract: Neural PDE solvers commonly generate multi-step predictions through autoregressive rollout, recursively applying a learned evolution operator and feeding each prediction back as input for the next step. Approximation errors can therefore propagate through the rollout, causing predictions at a shared target time to depend on their temporal origins and rollout depths. For a well-posed deterministic PDE flow, however, states at different times along the same physical trajectory should, under exact evolution, reach the same target state. To this end, we propose Align Latent Rollout (ALR), a regularization approach that promotes consistency across rollout origins through the neural PDE solver's internal representations. A second-order Taylor analysis of latent discrepancy propagation motivates two objectives: zeroth-order latent state consistency, which aligns representations at a shared target time, and first-order latent dynamics consistency, which aligns local evolution responses to shared perturbations. ALR can be integrated into different neural PDE solvers by regularizing suitable internal representations, without modifying their backbone architectures. Experiments across multiple PDE benchmarks and neural-operator backbones show that ALR improves prediction accuracy while reducing shared-target discrepancies across rollout origins.

title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing
abstract: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models' tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.

title: KODA: Kinematics--Observation Data Alignment for Humanoid Learning from Human Egocentric Demonstration
abstract: Training humanoid whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies requires costly robot demonstrations with aligned robot-view observations and controller-compatible whole-body state-action labels. Egocentric human demonstrations offer scalable supervision but have misaligned views and sparse motion cues. Existing approaches either pretrain policies that still require robot data for adaptation or generate controller-specific commands that limit reuse. Conversion also requires robot-view observations aligned with the generated whole-body motion. We present KODA (Kinematics-Observation Data Alignment), which converts egocentric RGB demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data using a reusable canonical trajectory to guide robot-view synthesis and generate controller-specific whole-body state-action supervision. KODA first generates a simulator-checked whole-body trajectory using a sparse tracker with sampling-based command optimization. This generated trajectory directly determines the onboard camera poses used to synthesize corresponding robot-view observations. The motion, observations, and task instruction form a canonical record. For each deployment controller, KODA optimizes commands to track the stored motion and records the corresponding action labels and proprioceptive states. When switching controllers, KODA retains this canonical record and regenerates whole-body state-action supervision for co-training with matching robot demonstrations. We evaluate KODA on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks using two whole-body controllers, SONIC and HEFT. With robot data held fixed, macro-average success on conditions covered by human demonstrations but absent from robot data improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points, respectively. Under both controllers, this metric shows an upward trend across the evaluated human-data budgets, suggesting potential for further scaling.

title: Normalization by Evaluation with Substitutions as Operations
abstract: In previous works on normalization by evaluation (NbE) with an untyped domain model, explicit substitutions are a major decision choice, which, in retrospect, is taken to simplify subsequent semantic proofs. This choice hence is taken for a purely technical reason. In addition, there is no obvious lemma to test the completeness of the definition or the laws for explicit substitutions. In this technical report, we investigate NbE in a typical setting, i.e. defining substitutions as operations. title: Forgotten at the Barbecue: A method for the responsible validation and correction of machine translations of BBQ into Brazilian Portuguese
abstract: Com os rápidos avanços em Processamento de Linguagem Natural, torna-se necessário o desenvolvimento de ferramentas de avaliação de performances dos modelos linguísticos diante da destilação de vieses sociais. title: GI-Vision XAI: Duplicate-Grouped Evaluation of a Four-Class ResNet-18 Endoscopy Image Classifier with Grad-CAM and a Desktop Research Interface
abstract: GI-Vision XAI is a four-class gastrointestinal endoscopy image classification research prototype combining a ResNet-18 convolutional neural network, duplicate-grouped image partitioning, Grad-CAM visualizations, and a PySide6 desktop interface. The manuscript reports archived test-set results for 1,805 images: 97.06% accuracy, 96.98% macro F1-score, 96.98% macro sensitivity, 99.03% macro specificity, and 99.87% macro one-vs-rest ROC AUC. These results are reported from archived aggregate artifacts and were not independently reproduced from the original images and prediction-level outputs. The evaluation is image-level and does not establish patient-level independence, external generalization, calibrated confidence, validated lesion localization, or clinical diagnostic validity. The software is a research prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic system. The original hospital-sourced images are restricted and are not included in this deposit. Any access to the source data remains subject to applicable permissions, institutional policies, and privacy and ethics requirements.

title: Evaluating the Diagnostic Performance and Clinical Interpretability of Explainable AI (XAI) in Digital Histopathology: A Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Performance
abstract: Objective: To explore peer-reviewed research on the application of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques for histopathology-driven cancer risk evaluation, and to address the limitations delaying its transition into routine clinical pathology practice (such as model reliability, clinical interpretability, and governance oversight).Methods: We conducted a systematic review with quantitative meta-analysis of studies evaluating explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in histopathology. Searches were performed in Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and Google Scholar through November 2025. Eligible studies were assessed for diagnostic performance, explainability approaches, and methodological quality. Of the 47 included studies, 9 provided sufficient quantitative data for meta-analysis. Post-hoc visual attribution approaches were the most frequently reported explanation methods in the included literature, with Class Activation Map (CAM) and Gradient-weighted (Grad) -CAM being the most prevalent.Results: Nine studies provided sufficient quantitative data for meta-analysis. The combined area beneath the curve was 0.962 (95% confidence intervals (CI): 0.909–0.985), despite significant inconsistency among the selected studies (evolution of heterogenicity (I2) = 97.1%). The investigation of subgroup revealed that models tested at the slide level performed better and more consistently than those examined at the patient level, suggesting that the unit of analysis has a significant effect on reported accuracy and heterogeneity.Conclusion: Future clinical translation of XAI in histopathology must prioritize explanation methods that are meaningful to pathologists, conduct usability testing in real diagnostic workflows, ensure prospective validation, and establish implementation within quality-management and governance frameworks.

title: Dynamic path reasoning with large language models for interpretable knowledge graph question answering
abstract: Abstract Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) aims to answer natural language questions by grounding them in structured knowledge graphs (KGs). Current KGQA systems still face three linked challenges: representing complex and compositional questions, providing transparent multi-hop reasoning traces, and using complete path-level evidence rather than only local triples. We propose SK-DRP ( S yntax- K nowledge enhanced D ynamic R easoning with P rompt learning), a modular KGQA framework that combines syntax-aware representation, state-adaptive path reasoning, and LLM-assisted answer selection. The syntax- and knowledge-enhanced encoder is an auxiliary representation enhancement that uses dependency information and knowledge-augmented pre-training to align questions with KG entities and relations. Here, dynamic denotes hop-wise recomputation of the question-focus indicator, score-qualified frontier expansion, and hop-weighted answer aggregation within a fixed dataset-level maximum hop budget; it does not denote automatic per-question depth selection. Candidate global paths are then compressed and transformed into natural-language auxiliary evidence for candidate-set-guided LLM answer selection. Experiments on MetaQA, WebQSP, and CWQ show that SK-DRP improves over several path-based and retrieval-based baselines on WebQSP and CWQ, while remaining competitive on MetaQA. Ablation, error, and interpretability analyses clarify how the syntax encoder, dynamic reasoning module, and LLM-assisted answer selection contribute to the final results, as well as the scope and limitations of the approach.

title: Localized Smart Persistence model for intra-hour solar irradiance forecasting across diverse climates
abstract: Intra-hour solar irradiance forecasting is crucial for photovoltaic integration and grid operations. Smart Persistence (SP) is a widely used baseline, but its theoretical clear-sky scaling ratio may deviate from actual irradiance evolution under cloudy conditions and near sunrise/sunset. This study introduces Localized Smart Persistence (LSP), which replaces the clear-sky scaling ratio with a site-specific ratio derived from temporally averaged measured Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) profiles. The profiles are constructed by grouping historical daytime GHI measurements by time of day at the native temporal resolution of each dataset, and averaging them over a reference period. LSP was evaluated using temporal resolutions ranging from 30 s to 5 min and forecast horizons of 10 – 50 min across seven sites representing tropical, predominantly clear-sky, and high-latitude climatic conditions. Forecast performance was assessed using RMSE, MAE, R 2 , and MBE, with nRMSE and the NICE Σ additionally evaluated at the common 5-minute resolution to facilitate cross-site comparisons. The results show that the effectiveness of LSP is strongly site-dependent. LSP generally reduced RMSE and MAE relative to SP at tropical and high-latitude sites, particularly at longer forecast horizons, while providing more representative irradiance evolution under low solar elevation conditions. In contrast, under predominantly persistence-dominated conditions, climatological scaling provided limited practical benefit. Approximately one year of historical irradiance data was generally sufficient to construct a representative climatological GHI profile for most sites. Overall, LSP should be regarded as a site-dependent extension of SP rather than a universally superior replacement, with potential extension to plane-of-array irradiance forecasting.

title: Stuck on Shuffle: On Attribute-Object Binding in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Retrieval is a fundamental task in multimodal systems: given an image or text query, the goal is to find the most relevant images or texts in a collection, often using a shared embedding space. Reliable retrieval requires these embeddings to capture not only which concepts are present, but also how they are composed. One key compositional challenge is attribute--object binding: encoding which attributes belong to which objects. Existing benchmarks provide a limited view of this capability, typically covering a subset of modality pairings, simple two-object swaps, or small attribute sets. Consequently, it remains unclear how robustly current models preserve attribute--object bindings across different modality pairings and more complex settings. We therefore introduce SABER, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute--object binding across all four image and text modality pairings, spanning diverse attribute types and scenes with up to ten objects. Evaluating models on SABER reveals substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and recent MLLM-based embedders. These findings motivate us to ask how binding can be improved efficiently. While multimodal supervision may be effective, collecting suitable images is difficult and costly. Text, on the other hand, is well suited to binding supervision: it is cheap to generate, supports a broader range of attributes and enables precisely controlled hard negatives. We thus finetune an MLLM-based embedder exclusively on synthetic attribute-binding text. Despite the absence of image supervision, the gains transfer to cross-modal and image--image retrieval while preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Our model achieves SOTA results on SABER while also improving on negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks, demonstrating broader benefits of our binding-focused supervision.

title: SurvICL: a Foundation Model for in-context Survival Analysis
abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) now outperform gradient-boosted trees in classification and regression. Yet in survival analysis, which predicts when an event occurs from censored data, often on small clinical cohorts, we find that no existing TFM beats the half-century-old Cox model. We address this issue by introducing SurvICL, a TFM that predicts survival curves in-context. SurvICL is pretrained on purely synthetic datasets generated from a novel flexible proportional-odds prior that outperforms other prior types in our ablation study. Unlike most other survival models, SurvICL is trained with a plain quantile regression loss, which is possible because its synthetic pre-training data generator can provide uncensored event times. Additionally, we introduce the largest survival benchmark to date spanning 103 datasets. On the 63 datasets held out from all design decisions, SurvICL outperforms 20 tree-based, deep, and foundation-model baselines without any tuning: it wins 82.9\% of pairwise comparisons in integrated Brier score, against 71.3\% for the runner-up, the Cox model, and is the first model to rank above Cox on small datasets.
