title: Local Temporal Contrasts on Human Motion Data Induce a Latent Geometry
abstract: Time series such as recordings of human motion data often encode structure across multiple temporal scales, and when a latent state determining this sequence evolves, this structure needs to survive in the representation space for downstream use. Yet the currently prevalent attention-based encoders paired with sequence-level pooling have made single-vector, pointwise comparison the default mode of inference, discarding the trajectory a sequence traces through the representation space. We propose recovering this geometric structure directly, without relying on forecasting-based objectives, by training an encoder model (SemTAC) with a temporal-neighborhood contrastive loss: representations that satisfy local consistency everywhere must give rise to a coherent global structure, letting inference happen at temporal scales beyond those seen during training. We evaluate SemTAC against four baselines on a five-step motion sequence discrimination task: the same architecture trained with a classification or a standard contrastive objective, and two established self-supervised time-series methods, TS-TCC and TS2Vec. At the full sequence length all five are broadly competitive, but on incomplete, truncated sequences SemTAC holds a large advantage: a median F1 of 0.77 one step before the sequence completes, against 0.27-0.70 for the four baselines. A hyperparameter-matched ablation attributes this effect specifically to the temporal-contrastive objective. SemTAC's representation trajectories are also the only ones among these five to exhibit interpretable geometric structures, exceeding a no-structure chance baseline on a displacement-smoothness metric which we introduce. This is evidence that its objective, not classification accuracy alone, produces genuinely temporally-ordered trajectories.

title: ESG-Kor: A Korean Dataset for ESG-related Information Extraction and Practical Use Cases
abstract: With the expansion of pre-trained language model usage in recent years, the importance of datasets for performing tasks in specialized domains has significantly increased. Therefore, we have built a Korean dataset called ESG-Kor to automatically extract Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) information, which has recently gained importance. ESG-Kor is a dataset consisting of a total of 118,946 sentences that extracted information on each ESG component from Korean companies' sustainability reports and manually labeled it according to objective rules provided by ESG evaluation agencies. To verify the effectiveness and applicability of the ESG-Kor dataset, classification performance was confirmed using several Korean pre-trained language models, and significant performance was obtained. Additionally, by extending the ESG classification model to documents of small and medium enterprises and extracting information based on ESG key issues and in-depth analysis, we demonstrated potential and practical use cases in the ESG field.

title: Expansão da Ferramenta Doccano para a Anotação de Análise de Sentimento Estruturada
abstract: Ferramentas de anotação são fundamentais para a construção de conjuntos de dados em Processamento de Linguagem Natural (PLN). Contudo, a versão do Doccano adaptada para Análise de Sentimento Baseada em Aspectos (ASBA) não representa explicitamente o autor de uma opinião. Este trabalho apresenta uma extensão dessa ferramenta que incorpora o opinion holder à estrutura de anotação, modificando o modelo de dados, os fluxos de importação e exportação e a interface. A avaliação preliminar anotou 30 avaliações de hotéis em ambas as versões: 10 continham um autor explicitamente identificável, casos em que a extensão permitiu registrar uma associação indisponível na versão base.

title: When Degree Anonymity Is Not Enough: Assessing Structural Re-identification Risk in Social Graphs
abstract: Removing identifiers and equalizing node degrees do not guarantee graph privacy, as network topology acts as a structural quasi-identifier. Evaluating rather than assuming privacy, this article frames structural re-identification risk assessment as a reproducible evaluation problem and presents a configuration-driven pipeline that anonymizes graphs, validates anonymity, and reports privacy-utility metrics. We adopt the structural k-anonymity paradigm as our core design choice, evaluating it on Facebook Ego-Nets and Email-Enron across k ∈ {2, 5, 10, 20}. Under a 1-hop subgraph adversary (d = 1), effective protection reduces to degree-based anonymity: the 1-hop re-identification rate exceeds the degree-based rate by approximately 6× on Facebook and 38× on Enron at k = 2, indicating that neighborhoods can remain structurally distinguishable. We position this assessment relative to differential privacy (a difference of premises: publishing the whole graph versus releasing queries) and to stronger learned de-anonymization adversaries. Furthermore, increasing k does not improve privacy monotonically, as aggressive anonymization distorts degree distributions and shifts vulnerability patterns. Since our scenarios model basic adversaries, these risk rates represent lower bounds, indicating that graphs anonymized by degree-based protection should undergo structural risk assessment before publication.

title: Replication Package for Proof-Producing Automated Reasoning for Social Welfare Eligibility and Service Referral
abstract: This repository contains the public replication data for the study “Proof-Producing Automated Reasoning for Social Welfare Eligibility and Service Referral: Formal Semantics of Defeasible Rules, Incremental SMT Solving, and System Implementation.” The package provides raw and aggregated benchmark data, statistical test outputs, experimental metadata, and documentation required to reproduce the reported analyses of full reconstruction, push/pop incrementality, and assumption-literal-based incremental SMT solving. All benchmark cases are deterministically generated and policy-realistic; no personal, confidential, or operational welfare data are included.

title: Beyond Short Names: Emoji Keyword Retrieval across Models and Bounded Causal Tests
abstract: Revised independent preprint, version 1.0.0. This preprint was revised in response to reviewer feedback from the NeurIPS 2026 workshop Interpretability as a Science (InterpScience). It is not an accepted workshop paper or a conference proceedings paper. We distinguish information readable from hidden states from its causal contribution to a specified computation. Using emoji as a controlled text-only case, we prospectively separate cross-model keyword retrieval, component-local mediation, and attention-path contributions after a readout reset. We compare raw, official-name, word-disjoint CLDR-keyword, and codepoint views of 55 emoji and 55 non-emoji Unicode symbols. title: HI-ALWPA: A Cooperative Island-Parallel Framework for Large-Scale UAV Reconnaissance Task Allocation
abstract: Large-scale multi-UAV reconnaissance task allocation requires efficient optimization of coupled vehicle assignments and target visit orders. This study presents HI-ALWPA, a cooperative island-parallel extension of the Adaptive Lévy Wolf Pack Algorithm. The framework distributes eight operator configurations across concurrent islands and coordinates their search through asynchronous ring migration, a passive elite archive, and contribution-based population transfer. In the tested synthetic scenarios with 60–200 UAVs, HI-ALWPA reduces the mean objective by 19.07–26.60% relative to serial ALWPA under the prescribed iteration schedules. Five-seed results on ten instances per scenario show reductions of 15.61% and 24.73% in the 60- and 100-UAV cases, respectively. Ablation results support the contribution of the combined island-coordination mechanisms. In exclusive 16-vCPU measurements, HI-ALWPA achieves an iso-iteration timing ratio of 2.69 relative to serial ALWPA on the 100-UAV/200-target scenario. These results support cooperative island parallelization as an effective extension of ALWPA for the tested large-scale static UAV allocation settings.

title: Short-Term Photovoltaic Power Forecasting under Extreme Weather Conditions Based on Feature Mode Decomposition and Adaptive Sparse Self-Attention
abstract: Abstract Aiming at the strong non-stationarity, pronounced abrupt changes, and error accumulation that characterize photovoltaic power series under extreme weather conditions, this paper proposes a shortterm photovoltaic power prediction model, FMD-LSTM-ASSA-Transformer. First, feature mode decomposition (FMD) is employed to perform multiscale decomposition of the original power sequence, and effective modes are selected by combining correlation kurtosis and correlation coefficient, thereby reducing the impact of trend, periodic, and disturbance component aliasing on prediction performance. Second, long short-term memory (LSTM) is used to extract local temporal features, and an adaptive sparse self-attention (ASSA) mechanism is introduced to improve the model's responsiveness to key abrupt segments such as power dips and rapid recovery. Finally, Transformer is used to model long-term dependencies and improve the stability of multi-step prediction. Based on measured power and meteorological data from a photovoltaic power station collected during 2020-2021, extreme-weather scenarios in four seasons are constructed for validation. The results show that the proposed model outperforms the comparison models in spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Taking spring as an example, the model achieves an RMSE of 1.725 and an MAE of 1.150, which are 39.13% and 43.49% lower than those of LSTM, respectively, while the R² reaches 0.963. Decomposition comparison and ablation experiments further demonstrate that FMD and ASSA can effectively improve prediction accuracy and stability.

title: Evolutionary Informed Translation from Protein to Nucleic Acid Sequence
abstract: The choice of nucleic acid sequence for a given protein strongly impacts function and is species-specific. Current protein-to-nucleic-acid translation models treat sequences in isolation, often over-favoring frequently used codons. To generate more natural nucleic acid sequences, we introduce PINATA (Phylogenetically Informed protein to Nucleic Acid Translation with sequence Alignment), a model that leverages sequences from related species encoded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to guide prediction. Our architecture leverages evolutionary context and learns species-and protein specific context to make biologically-informed predictions. Evaluated across 61,934 gene trees and 882 species, PINATA generates sequences that mirror the naturally-occurring sequence substantially better than existing language models. PINATA leverages MSA data to improve exact native codon recovery by 17.95 percentage points over existing language models, effectively preserves natural rare-codon nuances, and more closely matches native sequence properties. PINATA maintains strong predictive performance even with limited evolutionary data. While previous methods largely treated sequences from different species in isolation, our method leverages the evolutionary relationships between nucleic acids and proteins across species to create a more biologically-informed translation. We demonstrate that leveraging rich evolutionary data through an biologically-designed method strongly aids in translating protein sequences to nucleic acid sequences across species. We will make data and code publicly available upon publication.

title: Time to Fake It: Continual Machine Learning Intensifies Unfairness in Deepfake Detection
abstract: Deepfake detectors safeguard against misinformation, rendering their failures as much a societal as a technical concern. As generators constantly evolve, detectors trained on static datasets miss newly arising threats, while progressive training interferes catastrophically. Yet, mitigating forgetfulness in terms of accuracy, the prevalent focus of continual learning (CL), is insufficient to reflect real-world impact. We therefore scrutinize the effects of CL methods with respect to evolving fairness. To this end, we analyze four dimensions of fairness across diverse demographics for detectors trained progressively on a chronological sequence of 11 real-world deepfake generation methods. Tracking fairness metrics over time, we expose non-trivial interplays between performance and fairness that depend on both the choice of CL algorithm and demographic intersections. We find accuracy degradation to typically exacerbate unfairness and, conversely, fairness improvements to remain scarce over time. Dissecting the CL method families (rehearsal, prompts, regularization), we observe that inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone, but likely entangled with representation learning. We thus issue a call to action for CL methods to take social outcomes into account when balancing the stability-plasticity tradeoff.

title: EOS Banking AI Barometer. How Europe really feels about AI in banking.
abstract: For the EOS Banking AI Barometer study – How Europe really feels about AI in banking – 4,400 people in eleven European countries (Bulgaria, Croatia, France, Germany, Greece, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland, 400 respondents per country) were surveyed about their attitudes towards artificial intelligence in bank communications. The data was collected in July 2026, and the target group consisted of bank customers aged 18 to 65. The study was conducted online and was representative of the population. Find more information, infographics and downloads on the EOS Banking AI Barometer here.

title: StateDrift
abstract: A small benchmark on belief revision, built in Inspect. A model reads a workplace chat channel in which later messages correct earlier ones, then reports the current state of a purchase order. Every scenario exists as a matched pair with a length-matched control arm, so a gap between arms is attributable to having to revise. Scaffold verified against a mock model. No frontier-model results yet. Version 1.2.0. AUDIT.md records six defects found and fixed before release; RESTORED.md records how the code was rebuilt and verified. Licensing is split: the code under Apache-2.0, and the prose (README, AUDIT, RESTORED) under CC BY 4.0.

title: Reading a Drifting Machine: Fresh Characterization, a Corpus-Prior Receiver, and Symbol-Level Message Exchange on Three 156-Qubit IBM Heron Processors
abstract: We report a set of pre-registered experiments on the three 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors reachable on a single open-plan account (ibm_kingston, ibm_marrakesh, ibm_fez), carried out on 14–15 October 2026. The object of study is not computational speedup but channel reliability: whether fixed symbolic messages can be delivered intact through a present-day noisy processor when the processor's per-wire readout response is measured fresh in the same sitting, and whether two such processors can exchange messages with per-position verification. Messages are 17-symbol sequences drawn from a 13-symbol test alphabet whose preparations collapse to nine distinguishable readout classes. A receiver combining per-wire selection from a fresh characterization, grammar-constrained decoding, and a corpus-frequency tie-break delivered 36/36 messages on ibm_kingston in two independent campaigns, 36/36 on ibm_marrakesh, and 35/36 on ibm_fez, against stale-plan and uncharacterized controls ranging from 2/36 to 30/36 depending on backend and control type. The grammar-constrained receiver without the corpus prior scored 30/36, 30/36, and 29/36 on the three backends; its losses are a single systematic mechanism — a deterministic tie on one battery message — identified from saved counts and closed by the prior. In a separate experiment, ibm_kingston and ibm_marrakesh exchanged self-introduction streams authored by each backend from its own fresh characterization, through a six-stage symmetric relay, with 204/204 position-flights received exactly and zero substitutions. In a counts-only blind test, an independent decoder with no shared codebook recovered the discreteness and grouping structure of two authored streams (pooled pairwise grouping agreement 0.971 against a pre-registered 0.90 strong-pass bar) while overestimating the alphabet size (reported 8, true value 6). A census of repeated characterizations shows that the ranking of a device's clearest wires turns over within hours (same-day top-17 wire overlap of 1–2 of 17 on ibm_marrakesh), while per-wire response quality moves by only ~0.01, so characterizations are within-sitting instruments. No speedup, no machine networking, and no machine understanding is claimed. The full receiver implementation is withheld as a trade secret; verification is offered through the published job IDs, retained raw counts, and tiered third-party reproduction.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Learning and Collaborative Learning in Self-and-Mutual Models: A Unified Framework for Autonomous Knowledge Acquisition
abstract: Learning systems can acquire knowledge through independent learning or collaborative learning. Independent learning enables a system to explore its own experiences, develop specialized knowledge, and preserve autonomy, whereas collaborative learning enables multiple learning entities to exchange information, resolve knowledge gaps, and benefit from complementary capabilities. However, a system that consistently relies on only one learning mode may suffer from insufficient knowledge diversity, unnecessary communication costs, redundant learning, or limited adaptability to changing tasks. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-and-Mutual Learning Framework (ASMLF), a conceptual framework for dynamically switching between self-learning and collaborative learning within a proposed class of Self-and-Mutual Models. Unlike approaches that focus exclusively on individual learning, social learning, multi-agent coordination, or the collaboration of large language models, the proposed framework treats self-models and mutual models as distinct model-level structures that support autonomous and relational knowledge acquisition. A state-aware switching mechanism estimates learning uncertainty, knowledge deficiencies, expected collaborative gains, communication costs, and the reliability of shared knowledge to determine whether learning should proceed independently, collaboratively, or through a hybrid sequence. The framework also incorporates reciprocal knowledge transfer, collaboration-triggered self-learning, self-learning-triggered collaboration, and feedback-driven adaptation of switching policies. We formulate the framework mathematically, establish testable research propositions, and design an experimental protocol for evaluating learning performance, sample efficiency, knowledge retention, adaptability, and computational efficiency. The paper provides a conceptual foundation for investigating adaptive learning-mode selection in self-and-mutual model architectures without assuming that either learning mode is universally superior.

title: Adaptive Self-Interaction and Cross-Interaction in General Computational Systems: A Parallel-World Framework for Dynamic Switching Between Independent and Cooperative Computation
abstract: Computational systems are commonly designed around predefined execution strategies, fixed coordination structures, or predetermined optimization procedures. Although existing approaches support self-adaptation, distributed computation, cooperative optimization, parallel search, and dynamic algorithm selection, computational systems may still be restricted by rigid assumptions about when individual processes should operate independently and when they should exchange information or cooperate. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-Interaction and Cross-Interaction in General Computational Systems (ASIC-CG), a computation-agnostic framework that dynamically coordinates autonomous computation, interaction among computational processes, and the generation and evolution of parallel computational worlds. A computational process may independently inspect, optimize, verify, correct, reinforce, evaluate, or modify its own operation. Alternatively, it may interact with other processes through information exchange, cooperative optimization, cross-validation, mutual correction, resource sharing, or other applicable mechanisms. The framework adaptively selects among these modes according to computational progress, uncertainty, disagreement, historical performance, task requirements, and resource costs. A parallel computational world represents a branch of an existing computation that explores a different parameter configuration, assumption, constraint, initial condition, search direction, or execution strategy. Multiple branches may evolve independently, interact selectively, or merge information when beneficial. The framework also accommodates heterogeneous computational processes that do not originate from the same parent computation. This paper formalizes the proposed framework, introduces a mode-selection mechanism, presents an operational algorithm, identifies application domains, and establishes hypotheses and an experimental evaluation protocol. The contribution is a general research architecture for adaptive coordination of computational processes rather than a claim that its individual mechanisms are unprecedented. Its central research question is whether adaptive switching between self-directed computation, cross-process interaction, and parallel-world exploration can improve solution quality, robustness, and resource efficiency relative to appropriately matched fixed-mode and existing adaptive baselines.

title: The Self-and-Mutual Model: A General Computational Framework for Adaptive Switching Between Autonomous and Interactive Modes
abstract: Computational systems are commonly designed around particular organizational assumptions. Some systems emphasize independent computation within individual components, whereas others rely on interaction, coordination, information exchange, or collective decision-making among multiple components. Although both modes are well established across computer science, artificial intelligence, distributed computing, and complex systems research, a general framework for representing and adaptively switching between them remains an important research direction. This paper proposes the Self-and-Mutual Model (SMM), a general computational framework that treats autonomous operation and mutual interaction as two fundamental organizational modes of a system. The framework is not restricted to large language models, neural networks, intelligent agents, or any particular computational technology. Instead, it can be instantiated in systems whose components perform computation, maintain internal states, exchange information, modify behavior, or contribute to shared objectives. The central principle of SMM is adaptive organizational selection: a system should determine whether to operate independently, interact with other components, or combine both modes according to task requirements, uncertainty, expected interaction benefits, computational costs, and observed performance. This principle is formalized through a unified state representation, an interaction graph, a mode-selection policy, and a feedback-driven adaptation mechanism. The framework further distinguishes self-directed and mutual mechanisms across optimization, diagnosis, verification, learning, memory, planning, evaluation, and decision-making. The paper establishes a conceptual foundation, presents a reference algorithm, identifies theoretical properties and limitations, and proposes an experimental program for evaluating the framework against fixed autonomous, fixed interactive, and existing adaptive coordination baselines. The proposed framework is intended to provide a common organizational abstraction for studying when computational independence is sufficient, when interaction is beneficial, and how systems can learn to transition between the two.

This principle is formalized through a unified state representation, an interaction graph, a mode-selection policy, and a feedback-driven adaptation mechanism. The framework further distinguishes self-directed and mutual mechanisms across optimization, diagnosis, verification, learning, memory, planning, evaluation, and decision-making. The paper establishes a conceptual foundation, presents a reference algorithm, identifies theoretical properties and limitations, and proposes an experimental program for evaluating the framework against fixed autonomous, fixed interactive, and existing adaptive coordination baselines. The proposed framework is intended to provide a common organizational abstraction for studying when computational independence is sufficient, when interaction is beneficial, and how systems can learn to transition between the two.

title: CFC26: Building Evaluations for Deployment in Sonar-Based Fish Counting
abstract: Accurate counts of fish populations are essential for monitoring ecosystems and making decisions for conservation, harvest limits, and river management. In many field deployments, these counts are obtained from sonar videos that experts must inspect manually, making large-scale monitoring slow, expensive, and difficult. Automated counting systems have been proposed as a scalable alternative, but so far this promise has been difficult to realize in deployment. Developing evaluations that better reflect real-world deployment conditions will help close this gap and drive improvements in counting performance in practice. To achieve this, we propose Caltech Fish Counting 2026 (CFC26), a new dataset with improved evaluation protocols that simulate deployment to seen and novel rivers, testing in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance. We expand the CFC22 dataset to eleven deployment locations across nine Pacific salmon river systems from Alaska to Northern California, capturing a broader geographical and ecological range of data. We additionally introduce two new evaluation metrics for counting, nMNE and nMANE, that mirror the operational workflow that experts use and help surface errors that frame-level detection metrics do not capture. Using these metrics, we reveal previously-concealed directional bias in upstream vs downstream counts, which would have direct and significant ecological implications if undetected. The dataset and code are publicly available on CaltechDATA and GitHub.

title: Query-Efficient Rejection Sampling for Parallel Masked Diffusion
abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) accelerate generation by unmasking multiple tokens in parallel, but sampling these tokens independently ignores their correlations and biases the output. Anari et al. (2026) corrected this bias with rejection sampling, decomposing the log acceptance probability into a sum of token-level terms, but the evaluation requires one score query per unmasked token. We propose the Single-Increment Rejection Sampler (SIRS), which provides an estimate of the log acceptance probability from a single randomly sampled increment at the cost of one query. SIRS then converts a Poisson number of clipped estimates into accept/reject decisions through a Bernoulli factory adapted from Chen et al. (2026). Since each query returns the conditionals of all remaining tokens in the block, we further Rao-Blackwellize each increment by averaging over these tokens at no extra cost, thereby reducing clipping. We show that the KL-divergence between the data distribution and the SIRS output is bounded by a clipping term plus the model's training error. With exact scores, parallel decoding pays the full within-block dependence, whereas SIRS pays only the part beyond the clipping range.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Federated Learning for Joint Communication and Computation in XR Systems
abstract: The convergence of communication and computation, empowered by artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced capabilities, emerges as a key enabler for realizing the promising functionalities of the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G). To this end, this paper investigates an AI-native, robust network, where multiple base stations (BSs) simultaneously serve several extended reality (XR) devices. The paper then presents an innovative distributed deep learning-based approach to simultaneously manage the transmit and computing powers, and computation allocation, amidst uncertainties in both channel and computing states information. Under such an interference network scenario, the paper proposes a robust approach for minimizing the worst-case delay across the served XR devices, subject to computation and power constraints. The paper leverages a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained either centrally or in a federated manner to map estimated channels and computation requirements to optimized resource allocations per BS. During training, uncertainty samples, reflecting both channel and computing estimation errors, are injected after the DNN output to account for such joint uncertainties. Our results validate the enhanced robust delay performance and scalability of joint uncertainty injection as compared to uncertainty-agnostic methods and state-of-the-art benchmarks, with federated learning-based solutions achieving near-centralized performance while enhancing efficiency, privacy, and adaptability.

title: Training-Free Target-Aware Refinement of 3D Gaussian Language Map
abstract: Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals. Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/

title: RenoLayout: Unified Floorplan Renovation and Furniture Layout for Constraint-Aware Residential Design
abstract: Residential design aims to transform existing homes into functional living spaces while satisfying diverse design preferences and physical constraints. However, existing floorplan generation methods typically assume empty building boundaries as input, whereas renovation requires reasoning over existing floorplans. Furthermore, floorplan renovation and furniture layout are commonly addressed as separate tasks, overlooking their inherent spatial dependency. Consequently, practical residential design must preserve immutable structural components while transforming editable spatial elements. It must also optimize furniture placement under design objectives and physical constraints. To address these challenges, we formulate residential design as a design-point-guided conditional generation task and propose RenoLayout, a framework that translates a pre-design residential state together with a design-point set into an executable Geometry-as-Code program. To enable controllable supervision, we construct a Design Map comprising 123 fine-grained design points covering structural renovation and furniture layout. We further introduce Difference-Grounded Design-Point Annotation to derive design-point sets automatically from before--after design pairs with VLM-based consistency verification. RenoLayout is trained using a three-stage CPT--SFT--RL pipeline, progressively improving spatial reasoning, instruction following, and constraint compliance. We also introduce the RenoLayout Benchmark, a set of 200 real-world before--after renovation cases with complete furniture layouts. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first benchmark for unified residential design. These cases include design-critical structural and building-service constraints.

title: Multiplicative Semidefinite Programming Upper Bounds on Quantum No-Signalling-Assisted Zero-Error Capacity
abstract: We study zero-error communication and exact simulation of quantum channels assisted by quantum no-signalling correlations. For a channel with Kraus operator space $K$, we introduce a semidefinite programming parameter $Γ(K)$ that is exactly multiplicative under tensor products and upper-bounds $Θ_{\rm NS}(K)$, where $\log_2Θ_{\rm NS}(K)=C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ and $C_{0,\rm NS}(K)$ denotes the asymptotic quantum no-signalling-assisted zero-error capacity. Among known upper bounds on $Θ_{\rm NS}$ given by semidefinite programs, $Γ$ is the tightest. We also prove that the previously introduced simulation lower bound $Σ^{-}(K)$ is exactly multiplicative and satisfies $Θ_{\rm NS}(K)\leqΓ(K)\leqΣ^{-}(K)\leqΓ(K)^2$. Using this multiplicativity, we show that neither $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\log_2Σ^{-}(K)$ nor its regularized extension $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)=\lim\nolimits_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log_2Σ^{-}(K^{\otimes n})$ holds in general. This answers an open question about the asymptotic simulation cost $S_{0,\rm NS}(K)$. For classical-quantum channels, we obtain sharp bounds. If $r$ is the effective output dimension, then $Θ_{\rm NS}\leqΓ\leq(1+r^{1/2})Θ_{\rm NS}/2$ and $Γ\leqΣ^{-}\leq(1+r^{1/2})Γ/2$. If $k$ is the minimum rank of the output support projections, then $Σ^{-}/Θ_{\rm NS}\leq[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]^2$, and this bound is sharp for every $1\leq k\leq r$. Thus, we obtain the sharp bound $S_{0,\rm NS}-C_{0,\rm NS}\leq2\log_2[(1+r^{1/2})/(1+k^{1/2})]$.

title: Modified Brusentsov Entailment Logic and Four-Valued Verdict Calculus for External State-Control Systems
abstract: In standard generationand planning loops, machine learning models may fail to maintain a formal boundary between a plausible predictionand a certified state transition: an unverified hypothesis or intermediate reasoning step can enter the mutableworking context and influence subsequent tool calls, physical actions, and long-term memory writes [21-24]. Classicaltwo-valued Boolean algebra and material implication are unsuitable as a verification semantics for such transitionsbecause they conflate the non-applicability of a rule with its confirmation (vacuous truth) and fail to distinguishlogical incompatibility (exclusion) from incidental inessentiality [8, 10]. This document specifies a formal verificationcalculus extending N. P. Brusentsov’s three-valued algebra of contentful consequence [3-8] and Lewis Carroll’s methodof indices [2]. It separates pointwise transition assessment from ensemble-level law assessment and distinguishesfulfillment, neutral indifference, incompatibility, and epistemic uncertainty. It defines an operational verdict space,evidence certificates, metric and geometric instantiations, and hierarchical graph coarse-graining. Formal guaranteesare stated together with their operational assumptions: in particular, the pointwise cascade is the normative decisionprocedure, semilattice aggregation is proved equivalent to the cascade (Proposition 4.2), law statuses are computedon reliably grounded transitions only, and rollback guarantees apply to logged logical state unless external effects aretransactional or compensated

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement in Multi-Agent Systems: A Dynamic Framework for Individual and Collective Intelligence Optimization
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve their performance through individual learning and inter-agent cooperation. However, relying exclusively on individual reinforcement may limit the exploitation of complementary knowledge, whereas persistent mutual reinforcement may introduce communication overhead, correlated errors, excessive behavioral conformity, and dependence on potentially unreliable agents. These limitations motivate a dynamic framework in which agents adaptively switch between self-reinforcement and mutual reinforcement according to task conditions, learning progress, uncertainty, interaction quality, and resource constraints. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Reinforcement and Mutual Reinforcement (AS-SMR), a general framework for multi-agent systems. Self-reinforcement enables an agent to improve its policy through individual experience, self-evaluation, and locally available feedback. Mutual reinforcement enables agents to improve their policies through reciprocal feedback, cross-agent evaluation, experience exchange, and mutually informative learning signals. A context-sensitive controller estimates the relative utility of these mechanisms and selects individual reinforcement, mutual reinforcement, or a hybrid mode. The framework further incorporates reinforcement credibility, interaction costs, diversity preservation, and feedback-based switching to prevent unnecessary collaboration and unproductive isolation. The proposed framework is applicable to heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning systems and can potentially be adapted to language-model agents, robotic teams, distributed optimization systems, and other intelligent systems. We formulate the problem mathematically, describe an implementable algorithm, and establish research hypotheses and an experimental protocol for evaluating learning efficiency, collective performance, robustness, diversity, and communication costs. The framework is presented as a research proposal requiring empirical and, where applicable, theoretical validation rather than as an experimentally established superior method.

title: Application of Sentinel-2 Multispectral Satellite Imagery in Lithological Mapping: A Case Study of Meda Kebele and Its Surroundings, Ethiopia
abstract: Lithological identification and mapping are crucial in understanding geological processes, mineral exploration, natural resource management, land-use planning, and other applications. Conventional field-focused mapping of geology is often requiring a lot of time and expensive, particularly in remote and rugged terrains, like in our area. Recent advances in satellite remote sensing provide efficient tools for lithological discrimination. This study explores the application of Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery to develop a lithological map in a case of Meda kebele. The Sentinel-2 satellite image was classified by using support vector machine (SVM) classification system to prepare a excellent geological map, which was validated by previous geological maps and field surveys For this purpose, several band combinations, spectral indices, and image processing methods, including OIF, ICA and PCA, were used in order to enhance the contrast among different rocks. Following that, a supervised classification supported by field survey and previous lithological maps of the area was carried out to create a lithological map. The results show that Sentinel-2 imagery can distinguish between the common geological units found in the area, which include metavolcanics, basalt, dolomite, limestone, marble, slate and sandstone, due to it has good spatial resolution of 10- 60 m and vast spectral extent from VNIR-SWIR. This paper highlights the significance of Sentinel-2 data for regional geological mapping, giving baseline information for mineral prospecting and resource management in Meda kebele.

title: SIEVE: A Parameterized GitHub Corpus Builder for Software Engineering Research
abstract: Software engineering research increasingly relies on large, richly annotated corpora of real-world code. Still, researchers typically assemble these with ad-hoc scripts or static, pre-built datasets that offer no control over corpus composition. This leaves a gap for a reusable tool that goes below the repository level and builds annotated, function- and class-level code corpora under researcher-specified criteria. We present SIEVE (Software Ingestion & Extraction for Verifiable Evaluation), an open-source, parameterized GitHub corpus builder that, unlike repository-level mining tools, works at code granularity: it locates individual functions, methods, and classes in repositories and extracts them as records, giving direct control over corpus construction based on several criteria, including widely used programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C++), repository quality, and creation date. To support software engineering research and LLM evaluation on real-world code, SIEVE extracts CodeSearchNet- and OpenClassGen-compatible records, each annotated with 22 structural metrics and AST-derived features, and optionally with a CodeBERT-based P(AI-generated) score (F1=0.9478, AUROC=0.9902), alongside the third-party dependencies declared in each repository's package manifest. These annotations enable researchers to conduct structural analyses, investigate code dependencies, assess AI-generated code, and construct customized benchmarks for evaluating LLMs, including under temporal constraints. A manual validation of 400 records in four languages and two granularities shows 100% accuracy in code metrics and import detection, 99.0% in source completeness, and 99.5% in metadata accuracy. SIEVE is publicly available with a live demo at https://mrahman2025-sieve.hf.space.

These annotations enable researchers to conduct structural analyses, investigate code dependencies, assess AI-generated code, and construct customized benchmarks for evaluating LLMs, including under temporal constraints. A manual validation of 400 records in four languages and two granularities shows 100% accuracy in code metrics and import detection, 99.0% in source completeness, and 99.5% in metadata accuracy. SIEVE is publicly available with a live demo at https://mrahman2025-sieve.hf.space.

title: MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models
abstract: Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.

title: A Decision-Aware Evaluation Protocol for Uncertainty in Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Medical segmentation uncertainty is often evaluated with calibration error or pixel-level error-detection scores, but these metrics do not show whether uncertainty improves downstream review decisions. We propose a decision-aware evaluation protocol that separates uncertainty estimation from deferral policy and evaluates their combination under fixed review budgets: which pixels, regions, or images should be accepted, and which should be reviewed. The protocol reports fixed-budget error reduction, risk-coverage behaviour, region-level review proxies, structural failure modes, probability-derived baselines, and sensitivity to review assumptions. We instantiate it across retinal vessel, skin lesion, and polyp segmentation with multiple backbones and uncertainty estimators. Under matched inference budgets and canonical multi-layer MC Dropout, test-time augmentation (TTA) gives a stronger error-detection signal across matched MC--TTA comparisons, including architecture and dropout-placement checks. However, estimator rankings are not universal. For example, probability-derived scores remain competitive, deep ensembles can outperform TTA, learned deferral helps mainly when the base estimator is weak, and rankings can change with review unit, uncertainty target, correction assumptions, and cost model. Structural and second-observer analyses further show that boundary and thin-structure failures are partly tied to annotation ambiguity. These findings support evaluating uncertainty as an estimator-policy-review configuration, not as a standalone score map. title: CoDeFont: One-Shot Font Generation via Multi-Scale Factor-Specific Representation Learning
abstract: One-shot Font Generation (OFG) aims to synthesize a target glyph by transferring the stylistic characteristics of a single reference glyph while preserving the structure of the target character. However, accurately capturing font style from a single reference image remains challenging due to the limited stylistic information available in a single glyph, and this challenge is further amplified for complex scripts. We propose CoDeFont, a script-agnostic OFG framework that addresses this challenge through multi-level style-content factorization and progressive style-content reconciliation. CoDeFont independently aggregates complementary style and structural information across multiple spatial levels to obtain factor-specific representations, while a contrastive objective explicitly encourages separation between style and content embeddings. During reconstruction, the disentangled representations are progressively injected through multi-level style conditioning, enabling stylistic information to be incorporated at different decoding resolutions while preserving the underlying glyph structure. We evaluate CoDeFont on structurally distinct Bengali and Latin scripts across seen and unseen font styles. Extensive quantitative and qualitative analyses demonstrate consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed framework for OFG across diverse writing systems.

title: Análise de comportamento do modelo NotebookLM em transcrição automática
abstract: Esta pesquisa analisa o comportamento do modelo NotebookLM na transcrição automática da fala, tomando como corpus a transcrição de 55 entrevistas de economia do programa Roda Viva. O estudo parte da hipótese de que as escolhas de registro textual do modelo revelam tanto suas capacidades quanto suas limitações diante da fala espontânea. Com a identificação e organização de padrões de comportamento, construiu-se uma tipologia que representa as particularidades de comportamento do modelo para compor uma diretriz de anotação. Os resultados obtidos até o momento demonstram que o modelo alterna entre sensibilidade às disfluências da fala e limitações na organização textual.

title: TME LLM OS: A Closed-Loop Systems Engineering Architecture for Epistemic Correction in AI Agent Systems
abstract: Abstract. Current AI systems can combine foundation models, retrieval, tools, agents, and execution controls, yet still amplify an unsupported premise or require repeated user correction because generation, review, and release are not organized as one bounded epistemic episode. This systems-engineering proposal translates selected functions from the human Theoretical-Mechanistic-Experiential (TME) framework into a generic artificial architecture. The source framework distinguishes the real-time experiential field from cognition, memory, and action, and orders correction through salience, attention, ordinary awareness, functional self-awareness, reflective delay, secondary segmentation, discriminative comparison, and renewed orientation. The proposed TME LLM OS retains the Transformer-foundation-model core while adding episode continuity, source provenance, role-specific agents, structured correction, residual-mismatch assessment, and gated execution. Runtime correction returns unresolved mismatch to the current episode until provisional convergence reaches a task-dependent tolerance |Δ| ≤ ε; validated corrections can enter a separate, governed, auditable, versioned, and reversible refinement path across episodes. The proposal does not equate functional implementation with lived experience. It yields testable predictions concerning grounding, recovery from false premises, safe release, recurrence of corrected errors, user burden, total task cost, and time-to-acceptable-result. Keywords: TME Framework; TME LLM OS; Epistemic Correction; Reflective Delay; Secondary Segmentation; Discriminative Intelligence; Episode Context Controller; Overthinking Drift; Residual Mismatch; AI Agent Systems.

title: Report and Representation in a Second Model: A Registered Replication of Meaning Reorganization in Qwen3.8-27B
abstract: When a story’s ending shows the narrator’s belief was wrong, does the meaning of the belief’s own words move inside the model, and does its judgment go with that movement? This registered replication asks it of a differently built model, Qwen3.8-27B. Across the same ten stories, each ending came twice, once from outside the narrator and once from within; after each, the belief was judged true, false, or unknown, and the movement of its hidden-state representation was measured across 64 layers. The representation moved beyond wording after a revising ending, in every story and in both studies, in a single band of layers 18– 64 (p = 2/59,049 for endings from outside, p = 1/59,049 for endings from within), as in Gemma (Bruyn, 2026d). The one-word judgment followed the revising endings, FALSE in 20 of 20 versions in each study, but not the confirming ones, TRUE in only 4 of 20, leaning FALSE while uncertain. The registered rank correlation across stories was not significant in either study. H1 is split: supported for the revising endings, not for the judgment after the confirming ones. The design exists to find where the report and the representation part, and here that place is the confirmation, not the revision; an exploratory comparison found the movement larger after endings from within than from outside, layers 44–57, p = .033. Correction: in the reference list, the DOI of Bruyn (2026), “What next-token surprisal can and cannot see”, should read 10.5281/zenodo.23340596.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Language Models: A Systematic Survey of Mechanisms, Detection Paradigms, and Architectural Defenses
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on the autoregressive Transformer architecture have achieved remarkable empirical capabilities across open-domain dialogue, reasoning, code synthesis, and analytical tasks. Despite these milestones, their operational deployment in high-stakes settings—such as clinical informatics, jurisprudence, and autonomous systems—remains bottlenecked by hallucination: the generation of fluent, syntactically coherent text that is factually erroneous, unfaithful to provided source material, or entirely fabricated. This survey provides a comprehensive, rigorous synthesis of the LLM hallucination phenomenon. We formalize the taxonomy of hallucinations, distinguishing between factuality violations and context-faithfulness discrepancies. We investigate the underlying computational and statistical etiology of hallucinations across data pipelines, objective functions, representational bottlenecks, and decoding dynamics. Furthermore, we systematically categorize contemporary detection paradigms—ranging from internal activation probing and semantic entropy estimation to external verification networks—and examine defense strategies spanning Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), internal representation steering, contrastive decoding, and alignment algorithms. Finally, we highlight unresolved challenges across multimodal models and propose actionable frontiers for achieving epistemically grounded artificial intelligence.

title: An Investigation of Functional Size Measurement of Error Correction Overhead in Quantum Software
abstract: As quantum computing has progressed toward fault-tolerant implementations, quantum error correction (QEC) for quantum hardware and software has become a dominant concern. While conventional QEC measurements, such as qubit overhead, code distance, and error thresholds, quantify physical resource costs, they do not capture the software-level functionality introduced by error detection, correction, and fault-tolerant gate protocols. This study investigated the QEC contribution to the functional size of quantum software and demonstrated that this contribution can be systematically measured using the COSMIC Functional Size Measurement method. A gate-level sizing approach, known as Gates’ Occurrences, was used to quantify functional user requirements (FUR) associated with QEC processes, including logical encoding, syndrome extraction, and recovery operations. A prototype measurement tool, implemented in Qiskit (Version 0.7.2), enables the automated calculation of COSMIC Function Points (CFP) from annotated circuit representations. Case studies involving Bell state preparation, Grover’s search algorithm, and 15-to-1 magic state distillation revealed that QEC-related functionality can account for 70–85% of the total functional size, even under simplified encoding assumptions. The results underscore the importance of QEC for the functional size of quantum software. These findings offer a reproducible foundation for functional sizing and future fault-tolerant quantum applications.

title: Evaluating enterprise AI assistants on everyday business tasks
abstract: Enterprise AI procurement often combines a choice of application bundle with a choice of language model. This exploratory study examined three model selections available through enterprise interfaces: Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol in the installed Microsoft 365 Copilot desktop application, and Gemini 4 Argon in the Gemini Enterprise web application. Six fictional English business scenarios addressed source authority, invoice arithmetic, customer communication, meeting actions, vendor eligibility and policy application. Each identical prompt was submitted three times in fresh chats for each selection, producing 54 retained responses and 18 responses per selection. Five binary checks were specified locally for each scenario before collection. All selections passed all 90 check opportunities and all 18 responses per selection passed five of five checks. However, supplementary inspection identified an unsupported procurement approval rule, an unstated assumption about missing revenue and a sentence-count deviation in Opus responses. These observations were outside, or not enforced by, the original operational scoring and were not used to revise the scores. Customer email lengths also differed descriptively while remaining within the requested range. The shared maximum score therefore indicates a ceiling of this small rubric; it does not establish model equivalence or error-free performance. The study used one unblinded AI assistant as operator and evaluator, lacked independent human ratings and did not control backend configuration. Its contribution is a transparent pilot dataset and an account of how narrow business checklists can conceal relevant differences. Enterprise purchasing decisions require further evaluation of actual workflows, review effort and application governance.

title: Literal Lock-In: How Test Language Shifts Literal Attraction in Typed Decision Models on Bengali Idioms
abstract: Decision models, non-generative scorers that report a probability over caller-supplied options and emit no text, are increasingly deployed as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they generate nothing, rationales and chain-of-thought do not apply. We audit three: an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API, entirely through interventions on their input, using expert-annotated Bengali idioms carrying a gold figurative and a gold literal gloss. Dropping an idiom's own literal gloss into the option list draws every arm toward it, taking 65% to 96% of each arm's remaining Bengali errors. A model-by-language matrix over one shared item set shows how far this depends on the test language: every arm is 1.9 to 6.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries, the commercial model's apparent resistance is a property of its test language, and capability does not order the failure. Calibration degrades in all three arms, and on the open arms confidence inverts, so gating on it is worse than gating at random. On a semantics-free option list, where accuracy is at chance, the best-calibrated arm still reports mean confidence 0.82. Code and data: https://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-in.

title: Dimension reduction of compositional data through mixtures of latent source compositions
abstract: Understanding the distribution of mineral compositions is an important challenge in geology. This motivates new variations on dimension reduction for compositional data, lying on a simplex, that approximate observations with lower-dimensional subsimplices. This representation interprets compositions as convex combinations of fewer number of latent source compositions, providing unique insight into the underlying data-generating processes. We develop this approach within the framework of backwards principal component analysis, which constructs nested approximating structures by successive dimension reduction by rank one. We introduce a class of subsimplices, termed proper subsimplices, and provide a formal definition together with a systematic study of their geometric properties. Proper subsimplices admit effective parametrization via hyperplanes, while providing a more flexible approximation than subsimplices obtained by amalgamation. We characterize simple conditions under which hyperplanes generate proper subsimplices. Based on these conditions, we propose both an exact algorithm and a computationally efficient approximate algorithm for estimating proper subsimplex representations. The usefulness of this method is demonstrated on two geochemical datasets where it gives improved insights compared to the conventional PCA approach. Main ideas are further illustrated in a toy example and a simulation study.

title: When to Ask for Help: A Decision-Theoretic Account and Measurement Standard for Slow-Module Scheduling in Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $ρ$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $ρ$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$ρ$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($ρ=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.

Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($ρ=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Evaluation and Cross-Agent Evaluation in Multi-Agent Systems: A Reliability-Aware Framework for Dynamic Evaluation Selection
abstract: Multi-agent systems frequently rely on evaluation mechanisms to assess the correctness, quality, reliability, and task relevance of intermediate outputs and final decisions. Two fundamental evaluation modes are self-evaluation, in which an agent assesses its own outputs, and cross-agent evaluation, in which one or more other agents independently assess those outputs. Self-evaluation can reduce communication overhead and preserve autonomy, but it may be affected by shared assumptions, incomplete self-knowledge, and systematic estimation errors. Cross-agent evaluation can introduce complementary perspectives and expose errors that an agent fails to recognize, but it incurs additional computational and communication costs and may introduce correlated judgments or unreliable feedback. Consequently, neither evaluation mode is universally optimal. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Cross Evaluation Switching (ASCES), a reliability-aware framework that dynamically selects between self-evaluation and cross-agent evaluation according to the estimated uncertainty, historical calibration, task difficulty, disagreement signals, evaluation cost, and expected value of additional assessment. Rather than requiring all agents to follow a fixed evaluation pathway, ASCES treats evaluation-mode selection as a sequential decision problem. An agent initially evaluates its own output when this is sufficiently reliable and economical, requests cross-agent evaluation when the expected benefit justifies the additional cost, and may return to self-evaluation after incorporating external evidence. The framework also supports repeated switching when new evidence changes the preferred evaluation mode. This paper formalizes the evaluation process, defines a switching policy, presents an implementable algorithm, and develops an experimental methodology for assessing accuracy, calibration, robustness, latency, and resource efficiency. The proposed framework is a research design requiring empirical validation, rather than a report of completed experiments.

title: REPTILE
abstract: We present an automated Machine Learning (ML) tool designed as a continual learning pipeline to adapt to evolving data streams in the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). This tool creates ML experiences, starting with training a neural network model. It then iteratively refines this model using fresh data while judiciously replaying pertinent historical data segments. When applied to IIoT sensor data, our tool ensures sustained ML performance amid evolving data dynamics while preventing the undue accumulation of obsolete sensor data. We have successfully assessed our tool across three industrial datasets and affirm its efficacy in dynamic knowledge retention and adaptation.

abstract: A specification document package, distributed free of charge. title: Probing, Not Tutoring: Design of a Conversational AI Agent for Introductory Mechanics and a Definition of "Cave Detection"
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents built for teaching tend to leak evaluation: they praise right answers, hint after wrong ones, and drift toward explaining. This note records the design of Talk It Through: Newton's Laws, a prompt-engineered agent for introductory mechanics that probes understanding instead of tutoring. In a short conversation, a student commits to a prediction about each of Newton's three laws, explains it in everyday words, and defends it against a changed case built from the student's own words that alters exactly one variable of the original scene. The agent never confirms, corrects, or hints during the conversation and scores only at the end. Each law receives one of four outcome codes: held, caved, self-corrected, or misconception survived. We define cave detection, the identification of a correct initial idea that is abandoned under a single changed case, as a measure of robustness that right/wrong item scoring cannot see. We summarize design rules found through more than 40 scripted simulation runs. All results reported here come from simulated prototype testing; no real-student data have yet been collected. A full design paper and an IRB-approved classroom study are in preparation. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

title: Trustworthy Cloud Infrastructure for Secure and Privacy-Aware Artificial Intelligence Processing
authors: Jesika P. Chourpagar Kashish J. Panjwani
abstract: The exponential growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cloud computing technologies has revolutionized data processing and intelligent service delivery at scale. Organizations across virtually every sector now rely on cloud-hosted machine learning pipelines to extract value from data that is collected continuously, at volumes and velocities that on-premises infrastructure struggles to match. However, this technological advancement comes with significant challenges, particularly concerning privacy and security of sensitive data transmitted to cloud environments. This research paper addresses the critical intersection of trustworthy cloud infrastructure and privacy-preserving artificial intelligence processing. Our work explores a comprehensive framework that integrates privacy protection mechanisms, secure computation techniques, and confidence assessment measures to establish reliable and trustworthy AI services in cloud environments. We propose that by combining differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, and confidence-aware prediction mechanisms, organizations can maintain data confidentiality while leveraging the computational power of cloud-based AI systems. Rather than treating privacy, security, and reliability as separate concerns to be bolted onto a finished system, the framework proposed here treats them as first-class design requirements that shape every layer of the processing pipeline, from data ingestion through model inference to the communication of results back to end users. This study examines existing privacy-preserving techniques applicable to cloud AI, analyzes their performance trade-offs, and evaluates the reliability of AI predictions through confidence scoring. Our findings demonstrate that it is possible to achieve a balanced approach where sensitive data remains protected, AI model performance remains acceptable, and computational overhead is manageable. The research contributes to the development of secure, trustworthy AI solutions suitable for healthcare, financial services, educational institutions, and other sectors requiring stringent privacy compliance. We further situate our contribution within the broader movement toward trustworthy and responsible AI, arguing that privacy-preservation is not merely a compliance checkbox but a foundational property that determines whether AI systems can be adopted at scale in sensitive domains.

title: 3L-GBC: structure-aware granular-ball clustering for layered structure discovery
abstract: Many synthetic and real-world datasets contain clusters with heterogeneous internal densities, where dense central regions gradually transition to sparse boundaries. However, most current clustering methods rely on single-layer modeling or rigid partitioning criteria, which limits their ability to capture complex cluster shapes and heterogeneous density distributions. To address these limitations, a density-gradient-guided three-layer granular ball clustering method (3L-GBC) is proposed. The method adopts a three-layer granular-ball representation to model dense, transitional, and sparse regions within clusters. Within this framework, candidate centers are efficiently identified using a lightweight density peak–inspired strategy, followed by the construction and adaptive expansion of density-gradient-guided granular balls. A curvature-based mechanism is further introduced to reveal an explicit three-layer internal structure. Finally, granular balls are merged into complete clusters through adaptive density propagation driven by multi-regional structural consistency. Experimental results on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that 3L-GBC achieves competitive clustering performance on complex structures.

title: Learning the Shared Latent Structure of Cryo-EM Inverse Problems
abstract: Understanding biomolecular function requires characterizing three-dimensional structure and conformational variability, for which cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a powerful tool. Cryo-EM produces noisy two-dimensional particle images in which molecular structure, particle pose, and imaging conditions are jointly encoded. Recovering biological information from these observations spans inverse problems including pose estimation, heterogeneity analysis, and reconstruction. These tasks are usually addressed independently despite shared protein structure and image formation, motivating a common representation across inverse problems. Since biologically meaningful differences may be spatially localized, we study self-distillation with complementary global and masked patch objectives. Because experimental dataset discrimination can reflect acquisition-specific cues, we develop controlled synthetic and experimental evaluations and find that structural discrimination benefits from dense spatial features. We introduce the EMber family of vision transformers, pre-trained on >50 million experimental particle images from 214 EMPIAR datasets together with simulated projections from 268,000 molecular assemblies. EMber improves upon existing methods at conformational and compositional discrimination by 14.85 and 14.26 percentage points, estimates conformational populations to within 1.59pp error with a linear probe, and produces particle assignments yielding reference-quality reconstructions in fewer epochs. We demonstrate how to learn representations that capture biological information for use across multiple cryo-EM inverse problems.

title: WaveLLM: Wavelet-Domain LLM Entropy Modeling for Lossless Image Compression
abstract: Lossless image compression fundamentally relies on accurate entropy modeling, driving a recent shift toward large language model (LLM)-based methods. However, existing approaches mainly emphasize the modeling capacity of LLMs while directly serializing images into pixel or residual sequences, leaving heterogeneous signal patterns entangled within a single prediction stream. In this paper, we argue that effective entropy modeling depends not only on model capacity, but also on the predictability of the input representation. Motivated by this insight, we propose WaveLLM, a wavelet-domain LLM-based entropy model for lossless image compression. By decomposing an image into multi-level wavelet subbands, WaveLLM converts a heterogeneous prediction problem into a set of more structured and statistically homogeneous subproblems that are more amenable to autoregressive probability estimation. To bridge numerical coding symbols with the LLM's native text token space, we introduce a dedicated numerical interface featuring value embeddings and a coefficient prediction head. Furthermore, a task-adaptive prompting strategy is designed to enable a single shared model to adapt to diverse subbands within a unified framework. Built on Llama-3.2-3B with LoRA adaptation, WaveLLM achieves 2.51, 2.24, and 2.27 bpsp on Kodak, CLIC.pro, and DIV2K, respectively, outperforming the PixelCNN-based codec using the same wavelet transform by 0.43, 0.36, and 0.46 bpsp, and surpassing recent LLM-based lossless compressors on all three benchmarks.

title: SelectPFN: Amortized Bayesian Variable Selection for Sparse Nonlinear Regression with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
abstract: Tabular foundation models based on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) predict on a new data set in a single forward pass, but they cannot report which inputs their predictions depend on. We propose SelectPFN, a PFN that performs Bayesian variable selection and prediction jointly for sparse nonlinear regression. In one forward pass it returns posterior inclusion probabilities for every variable, and its predictions are computed from sampled subsets only, so excluded variables provably cannot affect them; we show this is exactly what the Bayesian model prescribes. The network is pretrained once on synthetic tasks from a meta-prior built around a group spike-and-slab sparse-input neural network. Column-permutation equivariance combined with random interleaving of original and knockoff columns yields knockoff statistics with exact finite-sample false discovery rate control, even when the meta-prior is wrong. We develop theory for amortized selection: a Bayes-regret bound for the amortized median probability model, a characterization showing that the information needed to detect a variable grows like $(2/λ)\log(1/ω)$ in the prior weight $ω$ of structures that can use it, where $λ\le1$ is an efficiency, and a negative result showing that average-case training does not transfer to frequentist guarantees at a fixed truth. On out-of-prior nonlinear designs with p up to 500, SelectPFN improves the area under the precision-recall curve by 0.23-0.28 over the lasso, BART, DART, LassoNet and a group-penalized sparse neural network, at a false discovery proportion of about 0.07 and 0.04 seconds per data set. The advantage persists on real covariate matrices, and, as the theory predicts, detection of interaction-only variables rises monotonically with their prior weight.

title: Agent-assisted experimental strategy transfer across quantum processors
abstract: Progress in quantum hardware requires a growing volume of experiments across diverse devices, straining the capacity of human experts. Automation remains challenging because device differences and drift can render workflows developed on one processor unsuitable for another. Here we present an agent-assisted experimental strategy for conducting experiments across three-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance processors. Developed on one processor and applied sequentially to four others, the strategy uses an agent to assess experimental evidence, select subsequent measurements and adapt procedures, with operators providing instrument preparation and physical intervention. Using three-qubit Grover state preparation as a common task, each deployment combined device-specific calibration, control-pulse optimization and measurement. The experimental strategy was refined through sequential deployment, and all four processors ultimately produced outputs dominated by their respective marked states. The marked-state populations of the reconstructed dominant eigenstates ranged from \(0.910\) to \(0.959\), with relative deviations below \(3.8\%\) from the ideal value of 0.945. These results demonstrate that an agent-assisted experimental strategy can be reused and refined across processors to realize a common quantum task, providing a basis for scaling experimental practice beyond individual devices.

title: Text segmentation with mixed data: evaluating symbolic and neural approaches
abstract: A segmentação de texto vem sendo amplamente difundida e utilizada para extrair informação relevante de documentos. Essas informações estão distribuídas em diversos tipos de estruturas, que incluem dados heterogêneos. A extração desses dados tem sido ultimamente, utilizada por LLMs (Large Language Models). Porém, os treinamentos dos modelos de linguagem não detém características peculiares de dados mistos, tais como dados lexicais e dados fonéticos. Assim, torna-se um desafio analisar a corretude das transcrições de maneira automatizada por LLMs. Neste estudo, a segmentação textual e extração de informação foi paralelizada em duas principais abordagens com o intuito de avaliar a comparação de uma abordagem simbólica e uma abordagem neural. Os resultados demonstram as vantagens e desvantagens em ambas as abordagens para os tipos de dados mistos.
