Assim, torna-se um desafio analisar a corretude das transcrições de maneira automatizada por LLMs. Neste estudo, a segmentação textual e extração de informação foi paralelizada em duas principais abordagens com o intuito de avaliar a comparação de uma abordagem simbólica e uma abordagem neural. Os resultados demonstram as vantagens e desvantagens em ambas as abordagens para os tipos de dados mistos.

title: A Drosophila connectome substrate inside an LLM agent: what it gates, what it does not, and what it costs
abstract: Draft v3 - 2026-10-15. Applied case study with full cost accounting, negative results and control arms. All numbers re-derived from the artifact corpus on the authors' machine. We report an applied case study that wires a whole-organism connectome substrate (MaleCNS v1.0: 169,700 neurons, 25,582,938 innate synapses) into an LLM agent loop as a fast, cheap front layer - a digital cerebellum that acts on tasks it has consolidated and escalates to the LLM otherwise. Two experiment lines are reported. In a foraging simulation, closed-loop evolution lifted population survival from 13/24 at generation 0 to 24/24 at generation 9 on two independent lineages (mean energy 6.7x and 5.8x), and the evolved population transferred to an unseen world seed at 24/24 with higher energy still. In an applied task line (8-fly populations, an 18-task operational battery plus 3 held-out tasks, three arms totalling 1,029 generations, 26,678 LLM calls, 17,005,656 tokens), the substrate's one measurable contribution is a gate: under a contrast readout the gate is alive from generation 4 and sustains 40-55 of 144 possible solo (zero-token) task executions per population per generation, with a best fly gating 8 of 18 tasks. All 24 held-out solves came from fresh LLM code generation (320-334 tokens each), and a fly with 365 learned synapses on an essentially empty graph passed 180/180 checks: the solutions come from the LLM plus a verification loop, not from the connectome. We further report the token bill as structural (a fixed 72 calls and ~47k tokens per generation caused by cache eviction, flat across 365 generations), and a per-fly policy governor that cut LLM calls 116 to 57 (-51%; 58 to 24, -59%, on the paired w150 runs) at exactly zero meal loss - the governor's per-fly meals equal the no-escalation baseline's meals row for row across 24 paired fly-runs. In the economy gate test, satiety-gated feeding yields 8/8 survivals where always-feeding yields 0/8. Three candidate roles for the substrate are judged dead by measurement: recursive memory horizon 1-2 steps, input relay equivalent to a linear copy, and zero channel margin under superposed cues. The paper is offered as an honest accounting case study: where a biological substrate helps an LLM agent, where it does not, and what the whole arrangement costs.

title: An Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased the demand for reliable, efficient, and interpretable machine learning (ML) methods for complex prediction and decision-making tasks. However, conventional ML approaches often encounter challenges related to model optimization, generalization, computational efficiency, data imbalance, and limited interpretability. This study proposes an Advanced Machine Learning Framework for Algorithm Development, Optimization, and Explainable Intelligent Prediction that integrates data preprocessing, feature engineering, algorithm selection, Hyperparameter optimization, ensemble learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Multiple ML algorithms, including Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors, Gradient Boosting, and Extreme Gradient Boosting, are comparatively evaluated. Model performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), computational efficiency, and interpretability. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME techniques are incorporated to explain feature contributions and improve transparency in model predictions. The framework facilitates systematic comparison between conventional and optimized models while examining the trade-off between predictive performance, computational cost, and explainability. The proposed approach provides a generalizable pathway for developing robust and trustworthy intelligent prediction systems. Its applicability extends across healthcare, education, cyber security, finance, and other data-driven domains. The study contributes an integrated framework that combines algorithmic optimization with explainability to support accurate, transparent, efficient, and reliable ML-based decision-making systems.

title: Adaptive Self-Play and Multi-Model Play in Self-and-Interaction Models: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Switching Between Internal and Inter-Model Strategic Exploration
abstract: Self-play and multi-model interaction provide different mechanisms for exploring complex problem spaces. Self-play enables a model to generate, evaluate, and challenge its own strategic alternatives, whereas multi-model play enables multiple models to interact through competition, cooperation, adversarial examination, negotiation, or other forms of strategic engagement. However, permanently adopting either mode may impose limitations. Self-play may suffer from insufficient diversity, persistent internal biases, or limited access to alternative perspectives. Multi-model play may introduce communication costs, coordination overhead, correlated errors, and unproductive interactions. This paper proposes an adaptive self-play and multi-model play framework for Self-and-Interaction Models (SIMs), a model-level conceptual architecture distinct from any particular large language model or conventional multi-agent implementation. The proposed framework dynamically selects between internal strategic exploration and inter-model strategic interaction according to uncertainty, disagreement, expected information gain, exploration progress, computational cost, and task requirements. A unified decision mechanism estimates the relative utility of both modes and supports transitions between them, including repeated switching when the problem state changes. The framework further introduces model-level game representations, switching hysteresis, interaction budgets, strategic diversity preservation, and mode-specific evaluation. A mathematical formulation, an operational algorithm, a complexity discussion, and a falsifiable experimental design are presented. This paper establishes a conceptual and methodological foundation rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated superiority. Its potential contribution lies in treating self-play and multi-model play as complementary, adaptively selectable operating modes within a unified model-level architecture.

title: Amendment 8: Fresh order and shape reassignment (Study 1)
abstract: Linked to the project registration (osf.io/qj9hb) and Amendments 1 to 7. Written 15 October 2026. Status and disclosure This amendment is registered before any model is trained on the new corpora. When it was written, the author knew all results of Amendments 5 to 7, the corrected Study 1 scores, and two rounds of reviews of the manuscript. Two concerns from those reviews motivate it. Memorisation. Each Study 1 model was trained on 128-token windows drawn from one fixed file of 11,648 sentences (about 120,000 tokens). Each position was seen 160 to 290 times, and the last training losses were 0.07 to 0.16 nats per token. The models may have learned the particular file, not only its statistics. The noun test. With held-out nouns, whose embeddings were never trained, the noun-specific index was about zero. With trained nouns it was small. In the Study 1 corpora a kind's shape was fixed, so the noun alone predicted the shape. A model could then predict shape from the noun's weights and had no need to tie the copying of shape to the noun. No model has been trained on the new corpora. The corpora were built once to fix their checksums, and only their clustering (below) was measured. The analysis code was run on simulated data to test it. Locked materials: github.com/synthiumjp/overhypothesis, branch study1b-1c-evaluation, at the commit that adds this file. MD5 checksums are in docs/amendment8_checksums.txt, the corpus manifest (with an MD5 for every corpus file) in docs/amendment8_corpus_manifest.json, and run instructions in docs/RUN_AMENDMENT8.md. The corpora are too large for the repository (5.3 GB) and are rebuilt from the code; the build must reproduce every MD5 in the manifest.

title: Predicting Privileged Information Effectiveness for On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from privileged information (PI) without a separate teacher model. However, prior work largely treats PI as a fixed design choice, leaving the effects of its content and construction poorly understood. This challenge is particularly important in multi-turn agentic settings, where trajectories contain actions, observations, and reasoning that can be transformed into PI in many ways. We systematically evaluate 16 PI configurations across three multi-turn agentic benchmarks and three student models that vary in scale and reasoning mode. We find that PI effectiveness depends on its content, generation source, and the student model. Information-dense trajectories and PI produced by more capable generators generally yield larger gains, whereas thinking models benefit less consistently. To assess PI before training, we compare PI utility with two KL-based metrics: sampled-token reverse KL (D) and error-step KL contrast (Δd^{-}_{err}). The KL-based metrics track post-training performance more consistently than PI utility, which can be distorted by information leakage. Empirically, selecting each task's PI by Δd^{-}_{err} also improves post-training performance over random selection, most when the PI candidates differ widely. Finally, effective PI remains beneficial when combined with GRPO, allowing the combined objective to outperform a strong GRPO baseline. Overall, our results provide practical guidance for constructing and evaluating PI in OPSD training.

title: Tree Edit Distance: Near-Linear-Time Approximate, Sublinear, and Dynamic
abstract: Tree edit distance (TED), the analog of string edit distance (ED) for hierarchical data, is the minimum number of node insertions, deletions, and substitutions transforming one labeled rooted ordered tree into another. We narrow polynomial gaps between TED and ED in near-linear-time approximation, sublinear algorithms, and dynamic algorithms. We give an $n^{o(1)}$-approximation in $O(n)$ time and, for every $0<δ<1$, a $(\log n)^{O(1/δ)}$-approximation in $O(n^{1+δ})$ time. This improves the previous near-linear-time $O(\sqrt n)$-approximation [Boroujeni et al., STOC'19] and brings TED to parity with ED in this regime up to polylogarithmic factors. With query access to the balanced-parentheses (Euler-tour) representation of the input trees, we give the first sublinear-time TED algorithm: for every $τ\in[1,n]$, it computes a $τn^{o(1)}$-approximation of $1+\mathrm{ted}$ in $O(n/τ)$ time. For dynamic TED, we give an exact algorithm with amortized update time $\tilde{O}(k^7)$ and a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation with amortized update time $\tilde{O}_{\varepsilon}(k)$, where $k$ caps the distance that must be reported. The exact algorithm is the first to beat recomputation in a nontrivial parameter regime. The approximation improves prior dynamic guarantees [Das et al., FOCS'25] and cannot be significantly improved in any parameter regime without a breakthrough for static $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of ED. All results use dynamic programming on a new hierarchical tree decomposition, analogous to partitioning strings into blocks of geometrically decreasing sizes. It combines structural properties previously achieved only in isolation, providing a framework for transferring algorithmic ideas from ED to TED, with additional ingredients addressing the obstacles in each computational setting.

title: Following Delegation Traces to Study Human Oversight in Interaction with Multimodal AI
abstract: As multimodal AI systems are becoming our everyday thought partners, the shift towards studying how users transfer control to these systems becomes especially urgent. In this paper, we report an overview of findings from an online study with n=56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials. After inspecting each multimodal AI response, participants rated task-specific trust and selected one of three intended policies for an analogous future task: reject AI assistance, use it with verification, or delegate fully to the AI. Within participants, post-interaction trust strongly predicted the user's delegation choices (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]). Trust and delegation nevertheless remained distinct. Verification was the dominant policy and often co-occurred with high trust. Delegation also increased with task order after adjustment for momentary and participant-level trust (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]), indicating an experience-related component that self-reported trust ratings alone could not capture. These findings motivate a shift from intended delegation to a non-intrusive observation of how delegation is enacted in collaborative human-AI tasks. We therefore conclude by proposing enacted delegation traces as a methodological framework for future studies of multimodal and agentic AI use.

title: Market Incentives for AI Safety Investment
abstract: Despite their practical significance, modern AI systems pose significant societal risks, including toxicity, malicious use, and misinformation. Their mitigation depends not only on technical feasibility but also on the incentives of firms that develop and deploy these systems. We show how profit maximization shapes safety investment in an AI supply chain with an upstream LLM provider and several competing downstream firms. In our game-theoretic model, we derive the market-driven level of safety investment and compare it with the levels that maximize market welfare and industry profit. We find that downstream competition generally induces downstream firms to invest more in safety than the industry-profit-optimal level. By contrast, the upstream provider may underinvest relative to these benchmarks because it is not fully compensated for the surplus from safety investments. Finally, we analyze how different regulatory interventions affect the participants' incentives and profits, and the resulting levels of model safety.

title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate via Model-Agnostic Importance Measures
abstract: Selecting covariates while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) is critical for interpretable scientific discovery, especially with complex machine learning models. Traditional variable selection methods often rely on specific model assumptions, while Model-X knockoffs provide a general way that leverages knowledge of the covariate distribution to produce a variable selection algorithm. This study puts forward a complementary method to Model-X knockoffs, named Model-Agnostic Selection with agent-X importance (MAS), which utilizes the sample-splitting strategy and a novel variable importance measure to bypass distributional assumptions on covariates. The proposed model-agnostic agent-X importance is defined to evaluate the difference of oracle predictiveness on both the original distribution and the distribution with agent variable in population level, and can be efficiently estimated by constructing the agent variable as some constant and cross-fitting strategy. The MAS method integrates a resplit-per-covariate strategy to decouple estimator dependencies and a data aggregation technique to enhance power. Theoretical guarantees for asymptotic FDR control are established under mild conditions. Extensive simulations and real-data analyses demonstrate that MAS provides competitive performances with existing works in FDR control, computational efficiency and power.

title: ExpertTwins: Auditable Long Horizon Scientific Panels through Grounded Expertise
abstract: Multi-agent language-model systems increasingly assign roles to agents and let them deliberate. A role label, however, does not specify which evidence an agent can bring or which standard it applies before accepting a conclusion. Agents that read one another's outputs tend to converge. We present ExpertTwins, a framework in which each seat of a scientific panel is defined by an inspectable evidence policy. Discipline seats retrieve under field-specific queries, and scientist-associated seats retrieve from attributed publications and a citation-derived scholarly neighborhood. Private initial packets, structured exchange, cited-source disclosure, deterministic quotation checks, and peer source review turn deliberation into an auditable record, which we also render as interactive idea-flow maps. Scientist associations denote publication-grounded perspectives, not replicas or endorsements of named researchers. In a nine-seat, four-turn neuroblastoma panel, 438 of 439 claims passed all attached quotation checks, and seats withdrew or defended positions when challenged on their evidence. A ten-turn panel sustained evidence acquisition and differentiated recommendations without conversational collapse. Across six base models given byte-identical initial packets, four sustained 97.9-99.8% quotation grounding, and at least 91% on every turn, whereas Haiku 4.5 failed by paraphrase and GPT-5 mini by silence. Agreement among strong models fell from 31% of claims at turn one to 5% at turn four. With follow-up questions held fixed, it stayed at 28-33% through turn three and fell to 20% only at the closing turn. Stress runs showed the collapse guardrail escalating through its full intervention ladder when consensus was forced, but missing deference to one unusually strong seat. On idea-flow maps, the forced consensus appeared as parallel lanes of identical ideas, although quotation grounding and participation balance stayed at their maxima. We also reimplemented two close published systems and ran them on matched models, seats, and questions. A multi-persona debate cited only real records, yet none of its cited sentences carried a checkable quotation and it had no way to abstain. An author-memory fusion system ran only after its fact checker was split by seat to fit in context. Its fused answer kept about two-thirds of the fact-checked specialist claims, answered 36 of 60 question parts on which our seats had abstained, and showed the reader 19% of its agents' disagreements. In a computational pathology case study, six scientist-associated agents built distinct pipelines to predict MYCN amplification from whole-slide images. Across six base models, seat-by-model interaction explained 57% of internal variance, and internal rank poorly predicted external rank (r = 0.18 across 36 nominees). These results establish differentiated, source-traceable scientific reasoning as an operational capability and identify the base model as a parameter that must be reported with the protocol.

title: The New Turing Test: A Methods Demonstration in Irreversible History and Permissible Futures
abstract: This record presents an exploratory, reproducible computational methods demonstration, motivated by the question of whether artificial agents behave differently when irreversible history changes their attainable futures. The Turing framing is a motivating application, not a claim that the experiments detect or establish consciousness. This paper formally introduces and defines the six-component candidate governing-class architecture G = (ℒ, Φ, Θ, κ, 𝒱, U_adm), comprising constrained admissible laws, state reconstruction, admissible parameter variation, local-law selection, viability construction, and interventions. It builds on, but is distinct from, the earlier ACT Hypothesis and Theory article (accepted in Frontiers in Immunology) and the separate Permissible Phenotype Conjecture working paper. Neither earlier proposal is validated by this synthetic study. A biological instantiation of G remains future work; any instantiation of G must prespecify its components before observing outcome data. Five sequential experiments with researcher-specified synthetic agents tested actual versus represented vulnerability, policy-selected versus physically accessible futures, ordinary reward optimization, adversarial phantom-law comparisons, and neural-policy replication. At a 36% risk level, a frozen ordinary planner predicted a 32.14-percentage-point increase in preservation after an experimentally engineered loss; 150 simulated trajectories per comparison condition yielded a 25.34-point sample contrast. The response followed from an authored state-dependent terminal-value rule, not a discovered existential mechanism. An apparent additional neural-policy residual weakened from 6.69 to 1.70 points in a subsequent cross-architecture challenge, without excluding smaller effects. The contribution is a transparent experimental protocol, formal introduction of a candidate governing-class architecture, and a demonstration of why causal interpretation, statistical identifiability, and negative controls matter when interpreting preservation-like behavior. The study does not establish a new law of biology or cognition, an autonomous self-model, sentience, or subjective experience. Chalmers’s hard problem remains open. All protocols, code, recorded outputs, and neural checkpoints for the five experiments are included for independent reproduction. Researchers interested in the methods or in future applications of G are invited to contact the author.

title: THE EL-RAKHAWI COGNITIVE RESONANCE AGI FRAMEWORK: METACOGNITIVE SELF-MODELING, CAUSAL WORLD SIMULATION, AND UNIVERSAL ADAPTIVE LEARNING BEYOND STATISTICAL PATTERN MATCHING
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Cognitive Resonance AGI (CR-AGI) Framework transcends statistical pattern matching to achieve genuine artificial general intelligence. Addressing hallucinations, absence of metacognition, catastrophic forgetting, and opaque decision-making in current AI, CR-AGI introduces four revolutionary modules: a Dynamic Causal World Model (DCWM) simulating reality through cause-and-effect rather than correlation; a Metacognitive Self-Reflective Engine (MSRE) continuously evaluating its own uncertainty and knowledge gaps; an Affective-Logical Value Alignment Core (ALVAC) mathematically formalizing intrinsic curiosity and ethical prioritization; and a Universal Neuro-Symbolic Integration Layer (UNSIL) blending neural intuition with verifiable symbolic logic. Performance is quantified by the El-Rakhawi AGI Cognitive Resonance Metric (EACRM), yielding bits per Joule, linking genuine causal understanding and self-awareness directly to thermodynamic efficiency. CR-AGI enables zero-shot cross-domain adaptation, eliminates hallucinations through verifiable reasoning, and establishes a mathematically grounded, transparent path to AGI that remains controllable and profoundly aligned with human values, accelerating scientific discovery while restoring human oversight and trust.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Individual and Shared Memory in Multi-Agent Systems: A Task-Aware Framework for Selective Memory Collaboration
abstract: Memory is a fundamental component of intelligent agents operating in dynamic, multi-step environments. In multi-agent systems, memory can be maintained independently by each agent or shared across agents to support collective reasoning and coordinated decision-making. However, relying exclusively on individual memory may prevent agents from benefiting from complementary experiences, whereas continuous shared-memory access may introduce communication overhead, redundant information, conflicting knowledge, privacy risks, and unnecessary coordination. This paper proposes Adaptive Individual–Shared Memory Switching (AISMS), a task-aware framework that dynamically determines whether a multi-agent system should rely primarily on individual memory, selectively retrieve shared memory, or engage in coordinated memory integration. Rather than treating individual and shared memory as permanently fixed operating arrangements, AISMS models memory collaboration as a sequential decision problem. Its controller considers task complexity, individual-memory sufficiency, expected knowledge gain, inter-agent disagreement, communication cost, memory reliability, and information-sharing constraints. A switching-cost-aware policy balances immediate task performance against the long-term value of memory collaboration. The framework further introduces confidence-aware retrieval, provenance-preserving memory integration, conflict-sensitive updates, and privacy-constrained sharing. We formulate the memory-selection problem mathematically, present an implementable algorithm, and develop an experimental protocol for evaluating the proposed approach against individual-only, shared-only, always-collaborative, and non-adaptive hybrid baselines. The paper does not claim empirical superiority before implementation and evaluation. Its principal contribution is a unified formulation of adaptive memory-mode selection in multi-agent systems, together with explicit mechanisms for deciding when individual memory is sufficient and when shared memory is worth its additional cost.

title: TK-HD: a closed-set benchmark for Sino-Korean homograph disambiguation
abstract: TK-HD is a closed-set benchmark for disambiguating Sino-Korean homographs in news written in three varieties: the DPRK daily Rodong Sinmun (cx), the ROK daily JoongAng Ilbo (hg), and Yanbian Daily (zg). A Sino-Korean word is a Korean lexeme of Chinese origin. Contemporary newspapers write it in hangul, and one hangul spelling can correspond to more than one hanja. Each item asks which of two train-attested hanja is the intended writing of a hangul span. The label answer_hanja is a Stage-1 automatic hangul–hanja alignment. The source is a balanced sample of 17,625 articles, 5,875 from each outlet, dated from 2006 through August 2026. Articles are split at article level (seed 42; 70/15/15), so no article appears in more than one split. The released counts are: train 12,337 articles and 487,598 items; validation 2,642 articles and 100,895 items; test 2,646 articles and 101,266 items. Every test item is binary. Of the test items, 12,970 form an anti-majority diagnostic: the hanja that is the training majority for that hangul spelling is different from the Stage-1 label. That slice is defined from the training inventory and the test labels; it is not stored as a separate file. This record contains the derived annotation layer only. TK-HD/ holds three JSONL files and manifest.json. Each line has the hangul span, two closed hanja options, the Stage-1 answer, variety, news category, article id, split, and diagnostic flags. TK-SK/sample_files.csv is the article index (17,625 rows) with outlet, date, category, and article id. Newspaper sentences and full articles stay with the rights holders and are absent from these files.

title: MultiCogEval
abstract: MultiCogEva is a multidomain dataset designed to support the systematic evaluation of large language models across diverse cognitive tasks. It contains 10,500 question–answer pairs covering five domains: Opinion and Argumentative, Linguistic and Semantic, Creative and Generative, Knowledge-based, and Logical and Quantitative. Questions are organized by domain, subdomain, and three difficulty levels: easy, medium, and hard. The dataset includes base questions and answers, responses generated by multiple language models, and assessments provided by language models and human experts. Evaluation dimensions include question complexity, keyword coverage, correctness, clarity and coherence, logical consistency, domain reliability, semantic similarity, evaluator confidence, hallucination risk, and toxicity risk. Additional fields document model information, response and inference times, and word and token counts obtained using LLM-based and program-based methodologies. This structured collection supports comparative benchmarking, analysis of evaluator agreement, investigation of response quality and computational efficiency, and the development of methods for assessing the reliability of AI-generated content.

title: RealCLI: Toward a Unified Evaluation of Human-Agent Collaboration for CLI Agents
abstract: Command-line interface (CLI) agents increasingly execute longer-horizon tasks, yet existing benchmarks either assume that user instructions remain fixed throughout execution or evaluate task outcomes without capturing runtime collaboration quality. In this paper, we present REALCLI, a paired benchmark that unifies the evaluation of task execution and human-agent collaboration quality on realistic CLI tasks. To comprehensively measure collaboration, REALCLI builds a five-dimensional framework, operationalized into 22 sub-dimensions and 51 interaction scenario templates. REALCLI provides two modes for paired comparison: REALCLI-EXEC supplies complete specifications upfront, whereas REALCLI-COLLAB introduces a scripted user that delivers progressive information, corrections, constraint revisions, and authorization decisions. Evaluations reveal profound capability gaps in frontier agents: the best configuration attains an average score of only 49.2%, and when evaluated by the joint collaboration score (J_{collab}), the peak performance reaches merely 37.6%. These results show that task effectiveness diverges sharply from collaboration quality, with models consistently struggling in steerability, trust calibration, and safety boundary management. REALCLI provides a rigorous, reproducible foundation for measuring and advancing collaborative CLI agents.

title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio? Probing and Distilling Damping Structure
abstract: Physical understanding is crucial for decision making, yet vision models struggle to infer properties such as damping that govern how materials behave. Audio encodes such properties directly, because an object's acoustic response to impact reveals its damping through measurable decay. We probe frozen encoders for the quality factor $Q$, a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations an object completes before its ring dies away, and report how well each embedding orders impacts by $Q$ using the Spearman rank correlation $ρ$, for which $ρ=1$ is a perfect ordering and $ρ=0$ an unrelated one. Audio embeddings reach $ρ=0.73$ and retain most of that advantage on materials withheld from training, while a single video frame taken at the moment of impact, encoded by CLIP, supports only $ρ=0.28$. Having established where the signal lives, we ask how much of that gap vision can recover. We distill a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone through a trained projection head and find that this recovers a useful fraction of the audio advantage. Because pooled correlations on this task are dominated in practice by category identity, we also evaluate under a leave-one-material-out protocol in which the held-out material is withheld from the projection head as well as the probe. Distillation with a four-frame input improves the correlation there from 0.234 to 0.338 (+0.053 over the matched four-frame baseline, 14 of 17 materials), a gain that no category-level strategy can produce. Widening the visual input to four frames spanning the impact supplies half of that improvement at no acoustic cost, which indicates that part of what a single frame misses is visible dynamics.

title: Evaluating Inquiry Learning in LLM-Based Agents: Hypothesizing, Reasoning, and Exploration
abstract: Scientific inquiry involves iterative cycles of exploration, hypothesis generation, and reasoning over observations to uncover relationships in complex systems. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in several components of this process, including inductive reasoning, hypothesis generation, and data analysis. However, prior work typically evaluates these abilities in isolation, leaving open how models integrate them across a full inquiry cycle. In this work, we introduce a framework for evaluating LLMs' inquiry capabilities in a unified, interactive setting. We extend the Countdown task to a mathematical environment where an agent probes the system by manipulating variables, collecting observations, and inferring relationships between them. This setup enables analysis of exploration strategies, causal discovery, and hypothesis refinement during inquiry. Across seven LLMs and multiple prompting strategies, our experiments reveal limited inherent inquiry capabilities and low success rates in discovering the underlying expressions. However, structured guidance inspired by educational scaffolding significantly improves performance. Our findings highlight current limitations of LLMs in strategic exploration and iterative hypothesis refinement, and show how simple guidance strategies developed for human learners in inquiry learning can support more effective inquiry behavior.

title: Periodic conditional measurements on a photonic chip
abstract: Quantum measurements not only extract information but also reshape quantum evolution through measurement backaction. Here, we investigate periodic conditional measurements, in which coherent evolution is repeatedly interrupted by local measurements. We show that the bright and dark modes of the conditional evolution operator provide a unified spectral description of both the post-selected final state along no-detection trajectories and the statistics of detection events. Using a three-dimensional photonic chip, we demonstrate on-demand state engineering through dark-mode preservation and bright-mode selection, enabling the protection of topological corner states and excited-state shelving. We further observe the predicted transition of the total detection probability on an effectively infinite one-dimensional lattice and identify its microscopic origin in Floquet near-dark modes. evidence.title: Periodic conditional measurements on a photonic chip
evidence.abstract: Quantum measurements not only extract information but also reshape quantum evolution through measurement backaction. Here, we investigate periodic conditional measurements, in which coherent evolution is repeatedly interrupted by local measurements. We show that the bright and dark modes of the conditional evolution operator provide a unified spectral description of both the post-selected final state along no-detection trajectories and the statistics of detection events. These results establish periodic conditional measurements as a general framework for engineering conditional quantum states and manipulating event-detection statistics in monitored quantum dynamics.

title: Optimal Reduced Representatives of Quadratic APN Permutations in Odd Dimension
abstract: The formal derivative of the reduced polynomial representative of a map on a binary finite field depends on the coordinates, although its differential uniformity does not. This matters for lifting permutations to Galois rings: a polynomial over a Galois ring of characteristic a power of two greater than two permutes the ring exactly when its reduction permutes the residue field and the derivative of the reduction has no zero there. We prove that for every odd $n\ge5$, every quadratic almost perfect nonlinear permutation $Q$ of $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ admits invertible binary-linear maps $L$ and $A$ such that the derivative of the reduced representative of $L\circ Q\circ A$ has no zero and each of its nonempty fibres has exactly two elements. The range is exact: this fails for $n=3$, as computed earlier, and for even $n$ there are no such permutations. For $n\ge9$, a linearization and a projectively injective cofactor map reduce the problem to counting binary matrices: more than 5% of the invertible inputs $A$ succeed, more than half for $n\ge15$, without any classification. For $n=5,7$ we use two independent classifications and finite certificates. Consequently every such permutation is linearly equivalent to a counterexample to the reduced critical-point conjecture of Bartoli and Stănică that lifts to permutation polynomials of optimal differential uniformity over every Galois ring with this residue field. For odd $n\ge9$ the existence proof is checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

title: OnBodyAI - Why the Next AI Needs a Body
abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.

title: Using Genetic Algorithms for Model Selection in Graphical Models
abstract: Model selection in graphical models is still not fully investigated. The main difficulty lies in the search space of all possible models which grows more than exponentially with the number of variables involved. Here, genetic algorithms seem to be a reasonable strategy to find good fitting models for a given data set. In this paper, we adapt them to the problem of model search in graphical models and discuss their performance by conducting simulation studies.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Verification and Cross-Agent Verification in Multi-Agent Systems: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Verification Coordination
abstract: Verification is a fundamental requirement for reliable multi-agent systems. An agent may evaluate its own reasoning, intermediate states, decisions, and outputs, while other agents may independently inspect, challenge, reproduce, or validate the same results. However, relying exclusively on self-verification can preserve internal blind spots, whereas continuously invoking cross-agent verification can increase computational costs, communication overhead, and coordination complexity. Moreover, neither strategy is universally optimal across all tasks, agents, environmental conditions, or stages of problem solving. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching Between Self-Verification and Cross-Agent Verification (ASSCV), a general framework that dynamically selects verification strategies according to estimated uncertainty, task risk, historical verification performance, inter-agent disagreement, evidence independence, and verification cost. The framework supports self-verification, cross-agent verification, sequential verification, parallel verification, and selective escalation between these modes. Unlike a fixed verification pipeline, ASSCV treats the choice of verification strategy as a state-dependent decision that can be revised throughout task execution. The framework is applicable to heterogeneous and homogeneous multi-agent systems, including but not limited to artificial intelligence agents, autonomous software agents, robotic agents, distributed decision-making systems, and collaborative reasoning systems. The paper formalizes the verification state, switching policy, expected verification utility, agent reliability memory, and termination conditions. It also presents a reference algorithm, a theoretical analysis of verification selection under explicit assumptions, and a reproducible experimental protocol for evaluating accuracy, error detection, calibration, computational cost, communication overhead, and robustness. No empirical superiority is assumed in advance. The principal research proposition is that adaptive coordination between individual and collective verification may offer a more efficient reliability-control strategy than permanently using either mode alone. The proposed framework provides a testable foundation for investigating when, why, and how multi-agent systems should switch between self-verification and cross-agent verification.

title: World–Self–Mutual Models: An Adaptive Framework for Switching Between Self-Learning and Collaborative Learning
abstract: Learning systems face a fundamental architectural choice: whether to improve their internal knowledge and predictive capabilities through independent learning or to acquire additional information and capabilities through collaboration with other learning systems. Permanent reliance on either strategy can be inefficient. Self-learning preserves autonomy and reduces communication overhead but may limit access to complementary knowledge. Collaborative learning can improve information coverage and knowledge acquisition but introduces communication costs, coordination requirements, information inconsistency, and dependence on external learning partners. This paper proposes the World–Self–Mutual Adaptive Learning Framework (WSM-ALF), a conceptual architecture that integrates world models, self models, and mutual models to support adaptive switching between self-learning and collaborative learning. The world model represents environmental states, dynamics, and predicted consequences; the self model estimates the learning system's internal knowledge, capabilities, uncertainty, and limitations; and the mutual model represents relationships between learning systems, including complementary capabilities, information dependencies, communication reliability, and expected collaboration benefits. A meta-learning controller estimates the relative utility of independent and collaborative learning and selects the learning mode according to expected improvement, uncertainty reduction, resource consumption, and collaboration risk. The framework further introduces a transition mechanism that permits repeated switching rather than enforcing a permanently independent or permanently collaborative architecture. A mathematical formulation, an operational algorithm, a model-update protocol, and a comparative experimental design are presented. The proposed framework is intended for non-LLM learning systems, including model-based reinforcement learning, embodied agents, robotics, simulation systems, and autonomous scientific discovery. Its principal contribution is a unified design hypothesis in which the decision to learn independently or collaboratively becomes an explicit, state-dependent control problem within a world-model-based architecture. The framework remains a research proposal whose effectiveness, novelty relative to specific prior systems, and generalizability require empirical evaluation.

title: Perceived AI Anthropomorphism and Brand Loyalty in Generative AI Services: The Roles of Confirmation, Brand Trust, Satisfaction, and Continuance Intention
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence services combine functional performance with humanlike interaction, yet it remains unclear whether perceived humanlikeness contributes directly to post-use satisfaction or is associated primarily with more proximal performance and relational appraisals. Drawing on the stimulus–organism–response framework, anthropomorphism theory and the Computers Are Social Actors perspective, the Expectation-Confirmation Model, and consumer–brand relationship research, this study examines perceived AI anthropomorphism (PAIA), confirmation, brand trust, satisfaction, continuance intention, and brand loyalty. Survey data were obtained from 555 ChatGPT users in Türkiye and analyzed using PLS-SEM. PAIA was strongly associated with confirmation (β = 0.624) and brand trust (β = 0.578), whereas its direct association with satisfaction was small (β = 0.081). Confirmation and brand trust were positively associated with satisfaction (β = 0.581 and β = 0.306), satisfaction was strongly associated with continuance intention (β = 0.705), and brand trust, satisfaction, and continuance intention were each positively associated with brand loyalty. Exploratory factor analysis, HTMT diagnostics, and confirmatory comparisons of alternative measurement structures showed substantial overlap between confirmation and satisfaction. The six-construct model fit better than the more parsimonious alternatives examined, but conclusions that depend on separating these two constructs are treated as tentative. Overall, PAIA was strongly associated with post-use and relational appraisals, but whether its association with satisfaction runs mainly through confirmation could not be established with confidence. Because the design is cross-sectional, the findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

title: Merging/Splitting Tracking of Resolvable Group Targets Based on ISODATA Algorithm
abstract: Resolvable group target tracking under merging/splitting conditions is a difficult task due to group structure changes. This article proposes an algorithm for tracking, merging, and splitting of groups founded on the ISODATA technique for iterative self-organizing data analysis and the generalized labeled multi-Bernoulli filter. The criteria for detecting group target merging and splitting were established: subgroup splitting is detected based on distances between group members and their corresponding subgroup centroids, while merging is determined by distances between the centroids of different subgroups. The proposed method can dynamically estimate the states and number of group members, the subgroup structures, and the number of subgroups within resolvable group targets. Simulation experiments demonstrate that the algorithm effectively estimates the states, quantity, internal structure, and number of subgroups of resolvable group targets in scenarios involving group merging and splitting.

title: A Locally Deployable Hazard Recognition and Remediation Question-Answering System for Enterprise Safety Production
abstract: Abstract Enterprise hazard recognition in safety production is an engineering judgment process that must identify hazards, evidence, consequences, and remediation actions from colloquial descriptions, site images, and incomplete contexts. This paper develops CE-FSL-RAG, a locally deployable hazard-recognition and remediation question-answering system based on authentic enterprise records. Six entity types and five relation types form a Neo4j graph with 4,763 nodes and 7,787 edges; bge-m3 embeddings form a Milvus collection with 1,829 vectors; and a versioned library contains 100 few-shot examples. A canonical-ID alignment manifest, timestamp-aware conflict rules, route-wise reranking, reciprocal rank fusion, and an explicit structured-first threshold produce a traceable evidence view. Generation uses internal COT planning, a six-dimensional quantitative gate, deterministic critical-risk checks, and FSL regeneration when the release conditions are met. In the primary evaluation retained from the submitted manuscript, CE-FSL-RAG achieves Context Relevance, Faithfulness, and Answer Correctness of 0.759, 0.819, and 0.896, respectively, outperforming KG-RAG, V-RAG, and KM-RAG under the same protocol. A separately locked 45-item, three-seed robustness evaluation adds direct minus-FSL, retrieval-stage isolation, paired uncertainty, and blinded Qwen2.5/GLM4 judging. Removing FSL leaves retrieval-only relevance unchanged but directionally reduces Faithfulness by 0.040 and Answer Correctness by 0.016; complete/minus-COT relevance is identical for all 135 item-seed pairs, and no RAGAS contrast survives Holm correction. Ordinal inter-judge kappa ranges from 0.373 to 0.778, motivating an explicit conflict queue rather than automatic consensus. The evaluated text pipeline runs locally on an 8 GB GPU, while the Gradio prototype retains text/image input, source annotation, multi-turn interaction, and manual review.

title: Adaptive graph construction and graph contrastive learning for geospatial feature embedding
abstract: Geospatial features serve as a cornerstone in urban planning and location-based services. Effective geospatial feature embedding is crucial for downstream geospatial Deep Neural Networks (DNN) applications. Currently, geospatial feature representation learning approaches rely on image or textual data to implicitly encode specific geospatial features, such as Points of Interest (POIs), roads, and urban areas, and struggle to effectively model spatial proximity relationships between imbalanced-distribution geospatial features. Moreover, the difficulty in effectively selecting appropriate geographic feature negative samples during model training poses a challenge to traditional representation learning methods. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Geospatial Adaptive Contrastive Embedding approach to extract neighboring features in an imbalanced-distribution space using Delaunay triangulation. It can effectively capture the natural proximity relationship through analysis the distribution characteristics of the geospatial features without setting a threshold. Graph contrastive learning is employed to encode geospatial features into low-dimensional feature vectors through self-supervised spatial similarity preservation. Finally, a comprehensive evaluation of the generated spatial proximity graphs and the learned representation are performed by using through three real-world geospatial datasets. The results demonstrate that our approach successfully learns an invariant and discriminative representation of geospatial features by constructing an effective spatial proximity graph.

title: JAVIS: Joint Audio-Visual Interaction and Streaming for Real-Time Conversational Agents
abstract: Human communication is inherently multimodal, conveying intent not only through linguistic and vocal cues but also through visual signals. However, existing conversational systems have mainly focused on text or speech, leaving out the visual feedback that is essential for natural interaction. In this paper, we propose JAVIS, an end-to-end streaming framework for real-time audio-visual conversational agents. Our key idea is to let the voice and the face speak from a single representation. On top of a shared LLM, a Joint Refined Head produces a unified audio-visual representation, which is fed into dedicated streaming branches for speech and face generation. This end-to-end design avoids intermediate bottlenecks, enabling real-time generation while keeping speech and face tightly synchronized. In addition, we present JAVIS-Syn, a 334-hour synthetic corpus designed to address the lack of expressive audio-visual dialogue data, covering emotionally rich multi-turn conversations and assistant-style exchanges. Experiments show that JAVIS achieves approximately 200times lower initial latency than a strong baseline, while outperforming baselines in lip synchronization and facial expression appropriateness.

title: Subgraph Counting with Local Node Differential Privacy
abstract: We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound showing that every noninteractive $(\varepsilon,δ)$-LNDP algorithm for counting copies of any $k$-node template graph with maximum degree greater than $1$ must have error $Ω(n^{k - \frac{1}{2}})$. Thus, our algorithm achieves optimal error for counting constant-size subgraphs, up to $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors. Our results substantially expand the types of network statistics known to be approximable under LNDP: prior work considered only functions of the degree distribution. In addition, our lower bound yields the first known $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ gap between central and local node differential privacy when accuracy is required for all input graphs. Previous separations either only involved $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ factors or only applied to promise problems.

title: Agentic-Priors: Using Large Language Models to Address the Cold Start Problem in Preference Elicitation
abstract: An agent that learns a user's preferences from their choices faces a cold start problem: before any choices are observed, it must rely solely on a prior. Informative priors are usually fitted to historical choice data, which new tasks and deployments lack. To address this, we present Agentic-Priors, which lets agentic systems use the implicit knowledge of large language models (LLMs) instead. Specifically, an LLM states a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which we map to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients. This prior is then refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. Across seven choice datasets, Agentic-Priors improves cold start accuracy over an uninformed prior by 5-40 percentage points. It also outperforms AutoElicit, a state-of-the-art LLM prior-elicitation method, on three datasets and loses on one. It is up to 18 points more accurate than in-context learning, and never significantly worse. Against hierarchical Bayes models fitted to surveys of increasing size, our approach is worth roughly 6-40 surveyed users, in terms of log-loss, so its value is concentrated in a deployment's first users.

title: Honesty is the Best Policy ... or is it? Demand Management for Probabilistic Service Options
abstract: To enable well-informed customer choices and redistribute demand across service options, providers can display probabilities regarding predicted service levels at the time of booking, effectively offering probabilistic service options. In many service settings, the underlying truthful probabilities endogenously depend on the system state, rather than being static product attributes controlled by the provider. While customers rely on this information when making decisions, they cannot readily verify its accuracy. Consequently, providers may be tempted to manipulate the displayed probabilities to guide customers' choices in their favor, creating a novel lever for demand management. In this work, we model the resulting problem as a sequential decision process, define truthful probabilities recursively, and introduce transparency constraints that limit their distortion. Because the exact computation of truthful probabilities is intractable for realistic settings, we develop an adapted reinforcement learning algorithm to approximate them. Furthermore, we propose a sampling-based mixed-integer program to optimize the information communicated by the provider in each state. Our framework enables providers to gauge the benefits of dynamically disclosing probabilistic information at the time of booking and sheds light on incentives for manipulation. Our computational study is motivated by out-of-home delivery, i.e., the delivery to parcel lockers or shops, and reveals a trade-off between individual-level transparency and aggregate customer utilities.

title: Pathwise Shrinkage and Probabilistic Calibration of the Multiplicative Half-Cauchy Process
abstract: We characterize the multiplicative half-Cauchy process through its log-scale random-walk representation, establishing shrinkage, expansion, and critical regimes, almost-sure summability, local rebounds, and effective dimension. We also derive a semi-analytic calibration rule linking interpretable prior probability statements to its scale parameter.

title: Analysis of Consumer Sentiment Tendency Towards Skintific Products on E-Commerce Tokopedia Using the VADER Method
abstract: The development of e-commerce has made consumer reviews a valuable source of information for producers. This study analyzes consumer sentiment toward Skintific products on Tokopedia using the VADER method. Data were collected through web scraping and produced 2,144 reviews that were processed through data cleaning, text conversion, stopword removal, stemming, and translation into English. The Sentiment Intensity Analyzer from VADER classified the reviews into positive, neutral, and negative sentiments. The results show a dominance of positive sentiment at 91.7%, followed by neutral at 6.9%, and negative at 1.4%. Data visualization reveals aspects valued by consumers, such as packaging, price, and delivery speed. This study confirms the effectiveness of the VADER method in sentiment analysis of consumer reviews and provides insights for producers in improving marketing strategies and product quality.

title: Classical Tricks for Better Topics: Can Traditional Text Mining Techniques Improve Generative Topic Modeling?
abstract: Topic modeling is widely used to discover and organize latent themes in large text collections. While recent embedding-based methods have improved topic discovery by leveraging dense semantic representations, they typically represent topics as lists of keywords, often providing limited insights into the underlying theme. More recently, Large Language Model (LLM)-based approaches, such as TopicGPT, have introduced generative topic modeling methods capable of producing human-readable topic labels and descriptions. However, the effectiveness of these methods depends heavily on the quality and representativeness of the documents selected to guide topic generation. In this paper, we propose Core-Periphery Sampling (CPS), a hybrid strategy that combines classical text representation and clustering methods with a TopicGPT-inspired pipeline. CPS selects both central documents and boundary instances that capture transitional and potentially informative cases, providing the generative model with an informed and diverse subset for topic induction. Experimental results show that CPS outperforms random sampling, particularly when the underlying document representation yields well-separable clusters. Although BERTopic remains stronger on clustering-oriented metrics, CPS offers an effective, computationally simple mechanism for guiding LLM-based topic generation via informed document selection, resulting in coherent and contextually grounded topic descriptions.

title: Discovery Is a Human-AI Loop
abstract: This compendium examines a single methodological question: how far can one researcher expand scientific search by combining human creativity with ChatGPT, executable computation, external evidence, and deliberate falsification? ChatGPT is treated as a research instrument for formalization, coding, search, control design, and criticism, not as an autonomous discoverer or a source of experimental evidence. The archive contains 74 experimental lines spanning artificial cognition, Consequential Necessity, machine learning, genomics, complex systems, synthetic artificial life, computational physics, accelerator models, neutrino cosmology, the Voynich Manuscript, seismology, music, and human-AI interfaces. The studies vary in maturity from exploratory prototypes to controlled computational campaigns and frozen prediction ledgers. Positive, negative, and inconclusive results are retained, and each line is interpreted according to explicit evidence and provenance rules. Across domains, the most persistent methodological pattern was a reduction in the cost between reframing a problem and attacking the resulting hypothesis. Human judgment supplied unusual representations and decided what questions mattered; ChatGPT accelerated translation into equa- tions, code, baselines, and alternative explanations; numerical or external evidence determined what survived. Repeated failures showed that complexity, model agreement, visual plausibility, and novelty are not substitutes for controls. The central conclusion is therefore methodological rather than a catalogue of established discoveries: a human-AI loop can widen the number and diversity of scientific hypotheses that one person can make executable and falsifiable. A final conceptual Part derives Hypothesis Language Generation (HLG), a proposed architecture in which persistent internal hypotheses are generated, tested, consequentially reduced, and only then rendered into language. HLG is presented as a falsifiable next-stage architecture, not as a demonstrated replacement for language models. Any domain-specific claim remains subject to independent replication, stronger controls, and evidence beyond this compendium. Keywords: ChatGPT; human-AI collaboration; Hypothesis Language Generation; scientific search; computational experiments; falsification; representation; reproducibility.

title: FPA supplementary derivations for FPA-FRESHNESS-PORTABILITY-003
abstract: This supplement records five additional target paradigms for the Freshness Portability Agent (FPA-FRESHNESS-PORTABILITY-003): Common Lisp, Brainfuck, spreadsheet formulas, an Analytical Engine-style program, and AWK. It is separate from the canonical FPA package and its Non-Normative Tests (NNT) companion. The supplement Manifest names and hashes the canonical FPA package Manifest as its parent artifact. The FPA Specification, Conformance Tests, Semantic Index, Coverage Matrix, and Ambiguity Register define the rules and acceptance criteria. Integrity. Freshness_Portability_Agent_Supplement.zip, 22 files, SHA-256 0d72c75d10ab3f3afb54730e23272e0e2e59f9a50daa7af939ffe07d6a704828. Supplement Manifest (FPA_Supplement_Manifest.json), SHA-256 86b7db7de10889366fc1b6b6dd9fe45cf47c0c9b0eff2de6de97144df01664c6; its parent is the FPA package Manifest, manifest_ref e8c2e05e564eaa83a1a0853350661b056f7716175586684d100c5b9b2fcfe0b0. The FPA package is archived as a separate record: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23390618. Use of AI tools. The author designed and calibrated the harnesses of the derivations in this supplement. Large language models were used openly, as tools to accelerate research and production, with manual review: they produced the renderings (Common Lisp, Brainfuck, spreadsheet formulas, an Analytical Engine-style program and AWK) and the comparators (the Rust rendering and the reference output spec_252.txt) in an AI-provider environment, as the study artifacts reported in Section 6 of the article; they are not reference implementations. No tool is an author; the author is accountable for the content. What matters is not which tools touched the files but whether they can be verified: the supplement has its own Manifest, which names the pack Manifest as its parent.

title: Artificial intelligence in health insurance fraud detection: a global and regional systematic review
abstract: Health insurance fraud imposes substantial financial burdens on healthcare systems and reduces the efficiency of healthcare resource utilization worldwide. Traditional fraud detection approaches often struggle to analyse large and complex healthcare claims data, making artificial intelligence (AI) an increasingly important tool for identifying fraudulent activities. This study systematically reviews global and regional evidence on AI applications in health insurance fraud detection, with particular emphasis on methodological approaches, performance evaluation, and implementation challenges. This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Seven electronic databases were searched for studies published between 2016 and 2025. Titles and abstracts were screened using the Silvi AI platform, followed by eligibility assessment according to pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted using a standardized framework, and methodological quality was assessed using the Drummond 10-item checklist. From 450 identified records, 33 studies met the eligibility criteria. The included studies demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in datasets, AI methodologies, fraud types, and performance evaluation metrics. Machine learning was the most frequently applied approach, followed by deep learning, graph-based learning, and hybrid AI frameworks. Although AI-based methods consistently improved fraud detection performance, challenges related to dataset imbalance, standardized reporting, interpretability, external validation, and economic evaluation remain significant barriers to widespread implementation. AI demonstrates considerable potential for improving health insurance fraud detection. However, future research should prioritize standardized evaluation frameworks, explainable AI, external validation across diverse healthcare systems, and economic assessment to support the responsible and scalable deployment of AI-enabled fraud detection systems.

title: Attraction from repulsion in an interacting Chern band: chiral superconductivity, generalized Hall crystals, and competing fractional Chern insulators
abstract: Experiments realizing strong interactions in partially filled Chern bands have observed fractional Chern insulators (FCIs), superconductors, and topological crystals in close proximity. Yet the microscopic relation between them remains poorly understood. Here, we use tensor network simulations to study repulsively interacting spinless fermions in a tunable topological band of the checkerboard lattice. We characterize the competing phases and identify key features of the experimental phenomenology. FCIs from the Jain sequence transition into chiral p-wave superconductivity both below and above half filling as the band dispersion is enhanced. By contrast, at half filling, a generalized Hall crystal with quantized Hall conductance and a doubled unit cell forms for sufficiently strong coupling. Surprisingly, a weak-coupling approach starting from a metallic parent state captures the nature of both ordered phases at intermediate coupling. We find that fluctuations in the metal generate longer-range attraction, which we analyze within the random-phase approximation. This approach captures the pairing symmetry as well as the radial form factors of the Cooper pairs, and incorporating this attraction into Hartree-Fock selects the observed Hall crystal. Together, these results identify fluctuation-induced attraction from repulsion as a common microscopic ingredient of ordering, while our tensor network computations establish the direct competition of both phases with FCIs.

title: FutureLift: Lifting Trajectory Proposals into Bidirectional Future Graphs for Motion Forecasting
abstract: Accurate motion prediction is critical for safe autonomous driving, yet even strong forecasters leave residual errors in their multimodal proposals. Existing refiners compress complete proposals or update their segments sequentially, preventing the full proposed future from serving as explicit relational context for correction. We introduce FutureLift, a backbone-agnostic refiner that represents each multimodal proposal as a heterogeneous future graph, with spatially grounded temporal nodes connected to agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and, for joint prediction, other agents future trajectories. Bidirectional temporal edges allow later evidence to revise earlier segments in a single pass, and the updated nodes predict residual coordinate and confidence corrections. Requiring only proposals, scores, and scene context, FutureLift provides a common refinement interface for structurally different forecasting backbones. On Argoverse2 and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, it consistently improves frozen proposals and outperforms native and specialized refiners across marginal and joint forecasting. On the WOMD motion-prediction leaderboard, FutureLift ranks first in minADE (0.5049m) and minFDE (0.9942m) among the compared standard-input methods, without LiDAR or ensembling, while achieving a competitive 0.4874 Soft mAP.

title: Flow-CLIP: Image-Conditioned Residual Scoring for CompositionalImage-Text Matching
abstract: Vision--language pre-training has enabled substantial progress in image--text retrieval and zero-shot recognition by learning transferable cross-modal representations. However, sentence-level alignment remains insufficient for compositional matching, where captions can describe the same objects and attributes while differing in how these elements are bound. To address this limitation, we propose Flow-CLIP, which refines global image-text alignment through image-conditioned changes in token--patch evidence. Global Compatibility Calibration (GCC) learns a sentence-level similarity metric, while Image-Conditioned Evidence Refinement (ICER) incorporates visual patch context into token queries and uses the resulting change in local matching evidence to adjust the global score. We further introduce Cross-Image Margin Ranking (CIMR), which compares the same positive--negative caption pair across matched and mismatched images, encouraging a larger ranking margin when the image supports the correct description. Experiments on compositional matching and attribute--object binding benchmarks show that Flow-CLIP improves binding accuracy over pretrained CLIP and learned global alignment through local evidence refinement, while cross-image ranking supervision mitigates reliance on language priors. Code will be released at link.

title: Decoding What iOS Location Services Send to Apple: An LLM Is an Unreliable Analyst but a Useful Toolmaker
abstract: Reverse engineering the data formats used by mobile software is skilled and slow, and using AI to assist with it is attractive. We evaluate this for the protobuf messages that an iPhone sends to Apple's location services. Working from Apple's binaries, we use two frontier models (Claude Opus 4.8, Codex GPT Sol 5.6) to reconstruct the schemas of protobufs observed in network traffic. The great majority of the schemas contain substantial errors, and these are hard to detect because the schemas are internally consistent. Direct AI use is therefore unsuitable for forensic and privacy analysis. AI can, however, write reliable analysis tools when their output can be validated. We use Claude to write a Python tool, Extractor, that reliably recovers protobuf schemas from Apple binaries. We validate it against binaries compiled from schemas with known answers, previously published schemas, and network measurements. We demonstrate the use of Extractor to decode and analyse the location services network traffic of a jailbroken iPhone 8 (iOS 16.7.11).

title: Hierarchical Graph Convolutional Network Approach for Detecting Low-Quality Documents
abstract: Consistency within a document is a crucial feature indicative of its quality. Recently, within the vast amount of information produced across various media, there exists a significant number of low-quality documents that either lack internal consistency or contain content utterly unrelated to their headlines. Such low-quality documents induce fatigue in readers and undermine the credibility of the media source that provided them. Consequently, research to automatically detect these low-quality documents based on natural language processing is imperative. In this study, we introduce a hierarchical graph convolutional network (HGCN) that can detect internal inconsistencies within a document and incongruences between the title and body. Moreover, we constructed the Inconsistency Dataset, leveraging published news data and its meta-data, to train our model to detect document inconsistencies. Experimental results demonstrated that the HGCN achieved superior performance with an accuracy of 91.20% on our constructedInconsistency Dataset, outperforming other comparative models. Additionally, on the publicly available incongruent-related dataset, the proposed methodology demonstrated a performance of 92.00%, validating its general applicability. Finally, an ablation study further confirmed the significant impact of meta-data utilization on performance enhancement. We anticipate that our model can be universally applied to detect and filter low-quality documents in the real world.

title: Simple grammar bisimilarity, with an application to session type equivalence
abstract: We provide an algorithm for deciding simple grammar bisimilarity whose complexity is polynomial in the valuation of the grammar (maximum seminorm among production rules). Since the valuation is at most exponential in the size of the grammar, this gives rise to a (single) exponential running time. Previously only a double-exponential algorithm was known. As an application, we provide a conversion from context-free session types to simple grammars whose valuation is linear in the size of the type. In this way, we provide the first polynomial-time algorithm for deciding context-free session type equivalence.

title: Performance Evaluation of Chatbot Based on LLM and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Retrieving Tajweed Knowledge Information
abstract: The development of artificial intelligence technology, especially Large Language Models (LLM), has driven innovation in chatbot-based learning systems. However, pure LLM still has limitations in producing accurate information in specific domains, such as Tajweed science, due to the phenomenon of hallucination. This study evaluates the performance of a chatbot based on LLM and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to address these limitations. The proposed methodology involves developing a RAG system using the Zephyr-7B-Beta model combined with BGE embedding (BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5). The system was tested using the Tajweed dataset with 21 question iterations to ensure consistency of results in Indonesian and English. The evaluation was conducted based on key metrics: Accuracy, Relevance, and Consistency assessed by experts. The results show that the RAG-based chatbot outperforms pure LLM with a 20% increase in accuracy, and exhibits higher stability in maintaining the correspondence of answers to knowledge sources and cross-language consistency. This research contributes to the development of a reliable AI-based learning system for the religious domain through a knowledge-grounded system.

title: Typological Challenges in Treebank Construction: Morphosyntactic Mapping of the Kubeo Language in the UD Standard
abstract: The inclusion of Amazonian indigenous languages in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) is hindered by the lack of treebanks and structured resources. This paper describes the initial phase of morphosyntactic modeling of the Kubeo language (Eastern Tukanoan family) under the Universal Dependencies (UD) guidelines. Kubeo exhibits high typological complexity, characterized by agglutinative processes, pervasive nominal classifiers, and pragmatic markers that challenge the static grammatical categories of the UD standard. The scope of this stage focuses on the extraction and tagging of native sentences, with a methodological emphasis on measuring the structural distance between the explicit nominal subject and the core verb. Based on data from the Pamiene Mama Buei-Tukubo primer, the study proposes token mapping solutions, utilizing the morphological features layer FEATS to preserve the language's morphosyntactic richness without excessively fragmenting the dependency trees. This pioneering corpus aims to establish a reproducible annotation protocol for future Kubeo computational tools.

title: Validating Semantic Content in Sentence Simplification using OpenIE and Relational Graphs
abstract: A simplificação de sentenças frequentemente altera a estrutura textual enquanto preserva o significado, tornando a fidelidade semântica difícil de avaliar. Neste trabalho, investigamos se representações baseadas em grafos derivadas de Extração Aberta de Informação (Open IE) podem capturar a preservação semântica em diferentes níveis de simplificação. Utilizando o corpus PorSimplesSent, extraímos triplas relacionais de sentenças originais e simplificadas para construir grafos semânticos comparáveis. Os resultados fornecem indícios exploratórios de que a análise baseada em grafos pode capturar diferenças semânticas relevantes e fornece sinais complementares além da sobreposição lexical superficial para avaliar a qualidade da simplificação.

title: Exploring Hybrid Pre-training for Automatic Essay Scoring
abstract: Alternatives to Large Language Models have been proposed to develop smaller models that require substantially less training data. In this paper, we propose a monolingual (Portuguese) Hybrid Transformer model trained with only 260M words, whose size is comparable to that of small Encoder-based models. After pre-training, we fine-tune our model and compare it against 11 existing models on the AES-ENEM dataset — an Automatic Essay Scoring benchmark in which models are required to evaluate five distinct textual dimensions. Our experiments demonstrate that our model is always competitive with the (bigger) best available model, despite its smaller scale.
