title: QUANTUM ENHANCED NEURAL BIOSENSING CLOSED LOOP Quantum Biosensing x Neural-State Estimation x Classical Adjudication STARLI Research Works | Institute XXIII | Flagship Research Monograph 04 Research Edition v1.0 | October 2026 Feng Cheng-en 33 x STARLI DESCRIPTION Quantum sensing has opened powerful new routes for measuring weak magnetic and thermal signals, including experiments using nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. Yet superior device sensitivity does not automatically establish superior neural-state inference, and it certainly does not establish clinical efficacy or permission to intervene. This research monograph develops a falsifiable, nonclinical scientific architecture for comparing quantum biosensing with the strongest feasible classical alternatives on equal experimental terms. The central question is deliberately adversarial: does a quantum readout provide neural information that is genuinely absent from an independently calibrated electrical, optically pumped magnetic, SQUID, or hybrid reference? A credible answer must survive matching of bandwidth, integration time, optical and microwave exposure, biological burden, calibration lineage, sensor footprint, operational cost, and estimator uncertainty. The objective is not to guarantee a quantum advantage, but to reveal precisely when one exists, when it disappears, and which physical assumptions make either outcome meaningful. The book begins with research positioning, scientific boundaries, a five-layer architecture, and a reader's guide. Thirty linked mathematical derivations introduce magnetic forward operators, spin-dependent readout, filter functions, photon statistics, Fisher information, inverse-problem identifiability, uncertainty decomposition, conditional neural information, domain-shift risk, instrument transfer, and authorization constraints. Each derivation connects to later chapters and experimental gates rather than remaining an isolated display of mathematics. Eighty-two research chapters, each with five independent section pages, examine source biophysics, quantum sensing mechanisms, classical comparators, neural-state models, calibration and epistemic uncertainty, adversarial artifacts, blind experimental designs, closed-loop governance, and scientific continuity. Two hundred Research Gates then offer successor researchers specific nonclinical questions with experimental tests, required evidence, competing explanations, failure criteria, and possible next steps. References to published studies are accompanied by DOI identifiers for independent source inspection. Distinctive research proposals include a resource-normalized neural-information criterion, hidden-source magnetic phantom challenges, nuisance-randomization tests, cross-laboratory reference lineage auditing, principled abstention under unidentifiable conditions, and a rigorous separation between inference accuracy and intervention rights. The framework treats negative results and successful classical counterexamples as valuable knowledge. This is a hypothesis-generating research monograph, not a report of original laboratory trials, an approved clinical protocol, a claim of autonomous intracranial quantum sensors, or a demonstration of treatment benefit. Some equations are conditional applications of established theory; others are explicit proposed measurement criteria that remain to be experimentally validated. The guiding principle is simple: a measurement becomes scientifically valuable when an independent observer can distinguish the signal from the instrument, challenge the model, and preserve the evidence needed to correct it.

title: Feeling or thinking? User aversion to AI customer service in online education
abstract: Introduction AI customer service is increasingly integrated into online education, yet users may not always respond favorably to AI-assisted service interactions. Drawing on robotic role theory, this study examines how thinking and feeling AI customer service influence user aversion in online educational service encounters. Methods Three experiments were conducted to examine the effect of AI customer service type on user aversion (Study 1, N = 120), the mediating role of perceived intelligence (Study 2, N = 120), and the moderating role of AI identity disclosure timing (Study 3, N = 120). Across the three between-subjects experiments, thinking AI was operationalized through analytical, information-processing, and task-oriented communication, whereas feeling AI emphasized emotional recognition and relational support. Results The results show that feeling AI generates greater user aversion than thinking AI. Perceived intelligence mediated this effect, such that feeling AI is perceived as less intelligent, which in turn increases user aversion. Further, AI identity disclosure timing moderates the indirect effect through perceived intelligence. Early disclosure of AI identity attenuates the negative effect of feeling AI. Discussion These findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of different AI customer service types depends on the service context and highlight the importance of aligning AI communication with users’ task-oriented service needs.

title: Multi-environment evaluation and decision-level analysis of clinical prediction models under dataset shift
abstract: Clinical machine-learning models are often evaluated within a single dataset, although deployment occurs across heterogeneous institutions and measurement processes. We evaluated Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting for ICU hospital-mortality prediction across MIMIC-III Demo and eICU using a 24-h landmark design, explicit feature mappings, and predictors retained only when sufficiently observed in both domains. A decision-level diagnostic analysis examined how predicted-probability distributions interact with a fixed 0.5 threshold. The primary cohort contained 110 MIMIC and 1,324 eICU ICU episodes. In eICU-to-MIMIC transfer, AUC-ROC was 0.598 for Logistic Regression, 0.642 for Random Forest, and 0.613 for Gradient Boosting. Random Forest generated no positive predictions, a threshold failure already visible during internal eICU validation. Logistic Regression retained partial sensitivity with substantial false-positive burden, whereas Gradient Boosting detected only two deaths. These findings show that clinical model evaluation should examine calibration, threshold behavior, feature harmonization, and source-to-target operating-point stability, not only aggregate discrimination.

title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
abstract: Robot learning has advanced by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. The resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration), an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration: enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by +37.4% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform in which new robot embodiments are integrated through their APIs alone, without teleoperated data collection or policy training.

title: GNN-Guided Local Refinement for Efficient Layout Decomposition with DSA-MP
abstract: Multiple patterning lithography (MPL) has been widely used to improve lithography resolution in advanced nodes, but it faces cost limits as feature sizes shrink. Directed self-assembly (DSA) offers a cost-effective complement, extending the resolution of optical lithography to sub-10 nm and beyond. Integrating DSA into MPL (DSA-MP) further enhances the resolution of contact/via patterning. Nevertheless, growing design complexity exposes the limits of existing decomposition methods, which struggle to balance solution quality and runtime, and neglect edge-to-edge spacing constraints of DSA templates, compromising manufacturability. To address these issues, we introduce a new conflict graph model capturing the previously overlooked constraints and develop a local refinement strategy powered by the graph neural network, enabling efficient and scalable layout decomposition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves higher solution quality with faster convergence than state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining robustness across layout scales, design styles, technology nodes, and varying mask counts.

title: Connectivity Bounds for GHZ Graphs
abstract: Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states are multipartite entangled quantum states that play a central role in quantum information theory, with applications in quantum communication, cryptography, and distributed quantum computing. A major experimental goal is to create high-dimensional GHZ states using multiple entangled parties. Krenn, Gu and Zeilinger discovered a surprising bridge between these quantum-optical experiments and graph theory: certain photonic experiments can be represented by edge-coloured, edge-weighted graphs, and the dimension of the produced GHZ state equals the number of feasible monochromatic inherited vertex colourings. This led Krenn and Gu to conjecture that every GHZ graph with more than four vertices has dimension at most $2$. A counterexample would give a new high-dimensional multipartite GHZ construction, while a proof would clarify fundamental resource limitations in quantum optics. It is known that the conjecture holds for graphs of vertex connectivity at most $2$ [MFCS 2024], and that simple GHZ graphs with $n>4$ vertices have dimension less than $n/\sqrt{2}$ [Quantum 2024]. However, no general upper bound depending only on vertex connectivity was known. We prove that every simple connected GHZ graph $G$ with at least four vertices has dimension at most $2^{κ(G)-1}+\binom{κ(G)}{2}$, where $κ(G)$ is the vertex connectivity of $G$. We also prove new bounds in terms of edge connectivity and maximum degree.

title: Predicting Live Birth After Fresh Embryo Transfer in IVF/ICSI: Differential ICM/Trophectoderm Morphology Encoding and a Hybrid Attention--Logistic Regression Ensemble
abstract: Predicting live birth before fresh embryo transfer could support shared decision-making in IVF/ICSI, but routine clinical data are small, heterogeneous, and contain pathway-dependent variables prone to outcome leakage. We aimed to construct a curated single-centre IVF/ICSI dataset and develop a prediction model suited to small tabular clinical data. \textit{Materials and Methods:} We assembled 616 fresh embryo-transfer cycles (251 live birth, 365 non-live birth) with clinical, laboratory, and embryological predictors, and embryo morphology encoded with a novel differential weighting of the inner cell mass and trophectoderm. After KNN imputation, robust scaling, and selection of 50 features, we developed a Hybrid Attention Network (HAN), a learnable feature-attention gate followed by a compact multilayer perceptron, and a HAN + logistic-regression (LR) ensemble with a validation-tuned weight. title: Novo CorPop Saúde: Data Collection for Simplified Health Communication in a Brazilian Patient Information Leaflet Corpus
abstract: This paper presents exploratory results from the "Novo CorPop Saúde" project, evaluating whether validation by expert linguists improves readability levels compared to AI-generated simplifications. We analyzed original, AI-generated, and human-validated versions of thirty Patient Information leaflets. Using the Flesch Reading Ease Index, two adapted Dale-Chall metrics, and lexicometric analysis, we assessed automatic simplification against human strategies. Results indicate that while AI improves readability scores primarily through text compression, expert linguists prioritize elaborative strategies, maintaining key terminology while providing didactic explanations to fill semantic gaps. This suggests that human intervention plays a key role in balancing terminological precision with communicative accessibility, a nuance that purely reductive AI strategies might overlook. This study provided evidence on the use of the complex and simplified lexical repertoire of medicine leaflets for the "Novo CorPop Saúde".

title: Prompt Engineering for Small Language Models: Evaluating ICL for Portuguese Sentiment Analysis
abstract: The In-Context Learning (ICL) paradigm enables adapting LLMs without parameter tuning. This work evaluates the impact of prompt engineering on 9B models for Brazilian Portuguese sentiment classification, comparing six prompting formats (fewand zero-shot) across three linguistically diverse models (Gemma2-9B-it, Boto-9B-IT, Qwen3.5-9B) and four public datasets, anchored by a fine-tuned encoder (MSA-DistilBERT, ∼0.1B) and a 685B MoE model (DeepSeek-V3.2) under a unified protocol. Results show that all 9B models outperform the encoder and recover 71–101% of the weak-to-strong gap, with Qwen3.5-9B achieving the highest mean coverage (94.5%). Statistical tests indicate that well-defined instructions are the main driver of ICL performance, capturing most of the achievable accuracy even in zero-shot settings, while elaborate formats (roleplay, JSON schema, meta-prompting) add no consistent gain over a minimal instruction-plus-demonstrations prompt, offering practical guidance for deploying SLMs in resource-constrained PT-BR NLP scenarios.

title: Beyond Retrieval: Bidirectional Neuro-Symbolic Validation for Reliable Graph-RAG
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and its graph-based extensions improve factual grounding in LLMs but do not guarantee logical consistency when responses must satisfy explicit domain constraints. We propose a bidirectional neuro-symbolic validation framework for Graph-RAG that combines First-Order Logic reasoning over a domain knowledge graph with an Annotated Datalog engine built on PyReason, propagating confidence bounds across inferred facts. A bidirectional mechanism supports symbolic enrichment, post-hoc validation with corrective rewriting, and direct symbolic execution. In a Brazilian public university advisory benchmark, the framework achieves strict accuracy of 84.2% and weighted accuracy of 87.7% (with partial-credit weighting), an 87% reduction in factual errors relative to LLM-only; a backend-sensitivity study with gemma4:12b preserves the baseline ordering with no answer labeled incorrect (0/57).

title: QSMEF: Quantum Software Engineering Module Evaluation Framework — Software v1.1.0
abstract: QSMEF — Quantum Software Engineering Module Evaluation Framework (v1.1.0) QSMEF is a computational framework for evaluating the functional contributions of quantum circuit components using cooperative game theory and Shapley values. The implementation provides a modular architecture that separates case-study construction from a general applicability validation procedure. Each case is represented through a common computational specification, including the initial quantum state, functional blocks, execution schedule, Hermitian observable, functional constraints, and executable semantic contract. The framework supports coalition evaluation through identity neutralization of absent functional blocks while preserving the original execution order. It evaluates technical conditions, functional constraints, and declared semantic invariants before determining whether functional attribution is applicable. For applicable configurations, QSMEF computes Shapley values and numerically verifies the efficiency property. The implementation also includes an optional granularity assistant for evaluating alternative functional block groupings. The software includes five computational case studies: SKW quantum walk search, QAOA-MaxCut, TwoLocal-H₂, QPE/Shor, and Minimum Bisection. Semantic validation is limited to the declared executable criteria and does not independently establish complete semantic comparability across coalitions. This release supports the computational implementation and reproducibility of the QSMEF journal article.

title: AI powered education system
abstract: Online learning platforms can make educational resources easier to access, but learners may still need immediate explanations when they encounter difficult concepts, especially in programming. This paper presents an AI Powered Education System that brings coding courses, learning materials, quizzes, learner progress, and AI-assisted concept support into a single webbased platform. Its central feature, Gopu AI Tutor, is designed to help students ask questions and receive conversational guidance when a human teacher is not available. The tutor interface includes controls for text, voice, camera, and file upload, allowing learners to interact in different ways. The platform also provides course discovery, learner-facing dashboards, and access to learning and career-related information. This paper describes the system's design, workflow, interface modules, and proposed evaluation approach. Screenshots are used to document the implemented user-facing features. Since controlled learning- outcome measurements were not provided, the paper does not claim statistically verified improvements. Further evaluation should assess usability, response quality, learner task completion, and changes in assessment performance.

title: SUPN: Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks
abstract: The SUPN (Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks) tool implements a single-layer neural network that transforms inputs using Chebyshev polynomials to create efficient surrogate models. This approach delivers accuracy comparable to deep neural networks and other advanced methods while using fewer parameters. The tool offers a complete, easy-to-install package with tutorials and automated testing. It supports researchers and practitioners in applying SUPNs for modeling complex, nonsmooth problems with strong theoretical convergence guarantees. title: Star Light, Star Bright: Can Multimodal Models Parse an Astronomy Visual Question Answering Dataset Right?
abstract: Figures are essential for scientific communication, and the field of Visual Question Answering (VQA) aims to test the figure understanding capabilities of large multimodal models (LMMs). Here, we investigate the accuracy of several low-cost LMMs on domain-specific VQA tasks for astronomical images of the sky. As instrument for this task we build a domain-specific VQA dataset comprising 2001 partially-synthetic figures divided evenly between contour plots, real telescope images drawn from NASA's SkyView, and "fake" sky images which share the axes and angular scales of the real images but draw their colors from a gaussian mixture model, alongside 47357 questions. Each figure is released as pristine and with realistic page-aging degradations mimicking the historical astronomical corpus. Testing three low-cost proprietary LMMs, we find models frequently fail to answer domain-specific questions at high accuracy. An initial comparison with 104 human-verified, astrometrically tagged figures from historical journal publications shows similar median errors in angular extent. All code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/jnaiman/SkyImagesWASP2026 and dataset is available on HuggingFace: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/astro_sky_image_vqa.

title: BridgeAfford: Bridging Query-Target Gap for Generalizable 3D Affordance Grounding
abstract: Language-guided 3D affordance grounding aims to localize functional regions on 3D objects according to interaction intents. However, existing methods exhibit poor generalization to unseen objects. One challenge is the query-target gap: a semantic discrepancy between query features encoding interaction intents and target-region features, leading to inaccurate grounding. End-to-end training favors query representations tailored to seen objects, limiting their compatibility with shifted target-region features on unseen objects. To address this issue, we propose BridgeAfford, a framework that reduces the query-target semantic gap from two complementary perspectives. First, Interaction Region Alignment (IRA) promotes cross-object alignment among geometrically similar interaction regions during training. This enables structures on unseen objects that resemble previously observed ones to produce representations similar to those learned during training, facilitating target-region recognition. Second, Visual Evidence Aggregation (VEA) leverages a 2D affordance model to refine the attention distribution and guide the query toward the correct region, yielding more target-aware queries. Extensive experiments on the LASO and PIAD datasets demonstrate that BridgeAfford outperforms existing methods, particularly on unseen objects, highlighting its robust generalization ability.

title: LOADBench: A Large Open Analog Dataset and Benchmark for Machine Learning in IC Design
abstract: Machine learning (ML) for analog IC design is constrained by limited open data and the absence of standardized evaluation: results reported in different papers are typically obtained on bespoke, often closed, datasets and with ad-hoc metrics, leaving comparisons across methods unreliable. We address both gaps with a large opensource dataset and a suite of standardized benchmarks. The dataset contains more than 100 operational amplifier (opamp) topologies (1-, 2-, and 3-stage) in the SkyWater130 PDK, each shipped with structural and functional annotations, topology-specific sizing constraints (symmetry and sizing rules), an Ngspice testbench, and a multi-objective NSGA-II sizing run producing around 103 Pareto-optimal and 106 intermediate sizing-performance pairs per topology. On top of this data we define six benchmark tasks with precise protocols: inverse sizing, topology selection, sub-circuit classification, structural circuit generation, Pareto-membership prediction, and multi-objective optimization. Thus, the data presented here constitutes the most comprehensive dataset for ML development in over four decades of analog IC design automation. The dataset, ground-truth annotations, and reference implementations of the metric-defining routines are released under an open license, enabling reproducible and directly comparable evaluation across heterogeneous analog design automation methods.

title: Trajectory Prediction Method for person under WSN with Hierarchical Envelope Adversarial Domain Adaptation
abstract: Pedestrian trajectory prediction holds significant applications across autonomous driving, intelligent surveillance, and smart cities. However, the complexity and unpredictability of pedestrian interactions make this task a persistent challenge. Current models face two common limitations: 1) Consider only a single type of social coupling. This introduces redundant interactions. More critically, it fails to account for the varying nature of trajectory coupled across different scenarios and between different pedestrians. Consequently, models cannot deeply adapt to diverse scenes. 2) Inadequate domain shift handling. Although very few methods address domain shift, they rely on statistical criterion-based domain distribution alignment. Such approaches exhibit strong dependency on predefined statistical metrics. This leads to significant limitations in complex and dynamic environments. To address these problems, a Hierarchical Envelope Adversarial Domain Adaptation with Loosely-Tightly coupled model (HEADA-LTCTPM) is proposed. First, an envelope sample construction mechanism was proposed. It constructs envelope samples and extends them into graph structures. Secondly, an adversarial domain adaptation module was proposed. This integrates both local and global domain adaptation strategies. It dynamically adapts to diverse coupled relationships across scenarios. These innovations collectively enhance prediction accuracy and robustness. In the experimental section, two representative public datasets were employed for validation and comprehensive comparisons with six relevant baseline algorithms were conducted. Results demonstrate that our model achieves significantly higher accuracy compared to existing methods, with the ADE and FDE metrics reduced by 17.6% and 19.1% respectively. The time overhead meets practical requirements, which verifies the effectiveness of our key innovations.

title: Emergent play anonymous survey dataset
abstract: This dataset contains 15 anonymous survey responses collected in 2026 as part of the Emergent Play study. It includes 26 variables combining structured survey items and open-ended responses. The quantitative questions examine five main dimensions of the experience: exploration, readability, player agency, uncanniness, and map legibility. The dataset also includes qualitative comments in which participants describe their navigation experience, their interpretation of the environment, and their perception of how the AI system generated or modified elements of the game space. The dataset is designed to capture both how participants experienced and understood the procedurally generated environment and how they perceived the role of AI in shaping that experience.

title: ESMAS-ES+ — French Ontological Paths: Interactive Reference Resource
abstract: This dataset provides the French version of the ontological paths developed within the ESMAS-ES+ project (Automatic and sustainable multilingual semantic tagger). The resource contains 260 hierarchical ontological paths organised into seven top-level conceptual domains: Animé, Matériel, Intellectuel, Situations dynamiques, Situations statiques, Lieu and Unité. Each path is associated with illustrative French lexical examples intended to facilitate the interpretation and application of the semantic categories. The dataset is distributed in three complementary formats: an interactive HTML interface for human consultation, and JSON and XML files for machine-readable reuse and processing. The package also includes documentation describing the ontological structure and the methodology followed in the preparation, terminological normalisation and human revision of the French version. The French resource derives from the Spanish ESMAS-ES+ ontological-path resource: Domínguez Vázquez, M. J., Valcárcel Riveiro, C., & Arias-Arias, I. (2026). Itinerario de rutas - ESMAS-ES+. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20348314 The resource is intended for use in semantic annotation, lexical semantics, lexicography, linguistic analysis, multilingual language-resource development, and related research and teaching activities. This resource was developed within the framework of the research project ESMAS-ES+ — Automatic and sustainable multilingual semantic tagger (PID2022-137170OB-I00), funded by MICIU/AEI/10.13039/501100011033 and by ERDF/EU.

title: Adaptive Self–Mutual Model Framework: A General Architecture for Autonomous and Interacting Computation Across Parallel Worlds and Heterogeneous Computational Processes
abstract: Computational systems increasingly rely on multiple reasoning processes, alternative solution trajectories, interacting agents, and adaptive allocation of computational resources. However, autonomous computation and interactive computation are often implemented as separate mechanisms, fixed workflows, or task-specific coordination strategies. This paper proposes the Adaptive Self–Mutual Model Framework (ASMMF), a general conceptual and algorithmic framework for organizing autonomous and mutual computational processes through state-dependent adaptation. The framework is built around a proposed Self–Mutual Model, which treats autonomous processing and mutual interaction as complementary operational modes rather than mutually exclusive architectures. It introduces three interconnected computational levels: intra-process self–mutual adaptation, parallel-world self–mutual adaptation, and heterogeneous cross-computation self–mutual interaction. Parallel worlds are alternative computational trajectories originating from a shared computational problem or state but potentially pursuing different assumptions, representations, strategies, or objectives. Heterogeneous computations, by contrast, may have different origins, structures, tasks, or computational purposes. A supervisory controller estimates the expected utility of autonomous execution, internal interaction, parallel-trajectory interaction, and cross-computation collaboration. It selects or combines these modes according to task progress, uncertainty, disagreement, reliability, computational cost, and interaction overhead. The proposed framework is independent of any particular learning architecture and may be instantiated in large language models, optimization algorithms, scientific computing, autonomous agents, simulation systems, and heterogeneous computational pipelines. This paper formalizes the framework, specifies an adaptive control mechanism, presents a reference algorithm, establishes testable propositions, and proposes an empirical evaluation protocol. It does not claim that self-refinement, multi-agent interaction, parallel search, or adaptive routing are individually new. Instead, its principal research hypothesis is that these mechanisms can be organized within a common, hierarchical control architecture that dynamically determines when computation should proceed autonomously and when interaction is expected to provide sufficient additional value to justify its cost.

title: QVIC-Global™ — Cryptographic Migration Governance and Prioritization Framework: Commercial Intellectual Property Asset, Licensing Technology, and Enterprise Governance Platform
abstract: QVIC-Global™ — Cryptographic Migration Governance and Prioritization Framework GLOBAL ECOSYSTEM RELEASE v1.1.2 TECHNICAL DOCUMENTATION | MIGRATION ASSESSMENT MODEL | ADVISORY PLANNING DEMONSTRATOR | SOFTWARE VERIFICATION | RELEASE INTEGRITY AUTHORSHIP AND RELEASE IDENTIFICATION Author: Bidyut Mazumdar Research Profile: Independent Researcher–Scholar ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5615-3558 Project Designation: QVIC-Global™ Release: Global Ecosystem Release v1.1.2 Release Date: 15 October 2026 Resource Type: Software Technical Domains: Post-Quantum Cryptography, Cryptographic Migration Planning, Cybersecurity Governance, Digital Infrastructure Resilience, and Technology Risk Assessment Implementation Classification: Research-Stage Framework and Python-Based Advisory Planning Demonstrator Operational Classification: Advisory Only Production Deployment: Not Established Independent Security Certification: Not Established Independent Empirical Validation: Not Established Persistent Identifier: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18378901 1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY QVIC-Global™ is a research-stage framework for structuring cryptographic migration assessments, generating preliminary prioritization estimates, and supporting governance-oriented planning for organizations preparing for the transition toward post-quantum cryptography (PQC). Cryptographic migration is not limited to replacing one algorithm with another. It can involve interconnected applications, authentication services, cryptographic libraries, digital certificates, communication protocols, key-management systems, legacy components, third-party dependencies, and information assets requiring long-term confidentiality. Changes to cryptographic components may affect interoperability, system dependencies, operational availability, implementation assurance, configuration integrity, and established security assumptions. Consequently, migration planning benefits from an explicit distinction between observed technical facts, manually supplied assessment values, model-generated estimates, and formally authorized engineering decisions. QVIC-Global™ addresses a defined subset of this problem through a Migration Assessment Template (MAT), a weighted linear prioritization model, structured JSON assessment records, JSON Schema-related validation assets, a Python-based planning demonstrator, automated tests, technical documentation, and release-integrity evidence. The v1.1.2 implementation provides a limited advisory workflow. It processes manually supplied assessment factors and calculates preliminary numerical priority estimates. Where required assessment information is missing or invalid, the implementation may prevent a complete score from being generated. The central design objective is to make selected migration-prioritization assumptions explicit, computationally inspectable, and suitable for structured human review. The current release must not be interpreted as an autonomous cryptographic discovery platform, a production migration controller, a cryptographic algorithm implementation, or an independently validated security-assurance system. QVIC-Global™ is therefore presented as a research-stage planning framework and software demonstrator. Its outputs are preliminary decision-support information, not verified security findings, mandatory migration instructions, or substitutes for qualified cryptographic engineering. 2. RESEARCH PROBLEM AND DESIGN RATIONALE 2.1. The Cryptographic Migration Challenge The transition toward post-quantum cryptography introduces technical and organizational planning requirements for systems that depend on cryptographic mechanisms to protect information, authenticate identities, establish secure communications, and maintain digital trust. Migration programmes may need to consider: • Cryptographic inventory: Identifying the algorithms, protocols, certificates, libraries, keys, and cryptographic services used by relevant systems. • Dependency analysis: Understanding relationships between applications, infrastructure components, external services, and cryptographic implementations. • Exposure assessment: Examining relevant exposure conditions and the consequences of cryptographic compromise. • Data-lifetime considerations: Evaluating how long information may require confidentiality or integrity protection. • Migration sequencing: Considering dependencies, interoperability requirements, implementation constraints, and operational change windows. • Uncertainty management: Distinguishing verified facts from incomplete information, estimates, and assumptions. • Rollback planning: Assessing whether a proposed change can be reversed safely and what constraints may complicate recovery. • Governance and accountability: Recording the rationale for prioritization and ensuring that consequential decisions remain subject to authorized human review. These considerations are related but are not interchangeable. A scoring model cannot independently establish the vulnerability of a system, verify the security of an implementation, determine regulatory compliance, or prove that a migration sequence is technically safe. 2.2. Defined Research Scope QVIC-Global™ addresses the narrower problem of representing selected migration-assessment considerations in a structured format and combining supplied factor values through an explicit weighted calculation. Its purpose is to support preliminary planning discussions and make the calculation process inspectable. The framework does not claim to resolve cryptographic discovery, dependency mapping, migration engineering, algorithm selection, security assurance, or enterprise-wide risk management in their entirety. 2.3. Design Principles The framework is organized around the following principles: Explicit Assumptions: Assessment inputs and configured weights should be identifiable and reviewable. Structured Representation: Assessment records should follow a defined data structure. Computational Transparency: The calculation should be expressible as an inspectable mathematical model. Input Discipline: Missing, malformed, or out-of-range values should not silently be treated as valid assessments. Bounded Interpretation: Numerical outputs should not be presented as more authoritative than the underlying model and evidence justify. Human Accountability: Consequential operational decisions should remain with appropriately qualified and authorized decision-makers. Reproducibility: The release should provide sufficient implementation and verification information to support inspection of the checks actually performed. These are design objectives. Their implementation and effectiveness remain subject to the capabilities and evidence available in the specific release. 3. TECHNICAL SCOPE AND RELEASE ARCHITECTURE The v1.1.2 release contains five principal functional and documentary components. 3.1. Migration Assessment Template The Migration Assessment Template (MAT) provides a structured representation of selected attributes associated with cryptographic migration work items. Its purpose is to make assessment inputs explicit, consistently represented, and available for review. The MAT is a proposed design component of this framework. Independent field validation, comprehensive coverage, and universal applicability have not been established. It is not presented as an independently recognized industry standard. 3.2. Weighted Advisory Prioritization Model The demonstrator combines seven configured assessment factors using a weighted linear scoring formula. The model exposes the configured weights and calculation structure, enabling reviewers to inspect how supplied values contribute to the resulting numerical estimate. The weights are implementation-specific configuration choices. They have not been established as universally applicable or empirically calibrated coefficients of cryptographic risk. 3.3. Structured Assessment Data The release includes JSON-based assessment examples and schema-related assets intended to support consistent data representation. Structural validation can identify certain data-format, type, and schema-conformance problems. It cannot independently establish that supplied information is accurate, complete, current, or supported by reliable technical evidence. 3.4. Python-Based Planning Demonstrator The Python implementation processes assessment records, applies the configured scoring model, handles selected invalid or incomplete input conditions, and generates machine-readable output. The demonstrated workflow is advisory. It does not establish automated cryptographic discovery, production-network inspection, autonomous configuration changes, cryptographic algorithm deployment, or operational change authorization. 3.5. Documentation and Verification Assets The release includes project documentation, execution instructions, example assessment records, schema-related files, automated tests, build-test documentation, and package-integrity information. These materials support inspection of the distributed implementation and reproduction of the documented local checks, subject to the availability of the relevant files and a compatible execution environment. 4. title: Learning with Communication in Multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Communication enables cooperating agents to coordinate their behavior and to access information about the environment. In multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL), communication protocols can be learned rather than predefined, alongside agents' value functions and policies. However, learning effective communication remains challenging in environments that are stochastic, continuous, or multi-task. This thesis addresses these challenges with the aim of improving learning stability, learning efficiency, and task performance through learnable and adaptive communication. First, we survey the literature on MADRL with communication and propose a classification framework of nine dimensions that capture key aspects of communication design and learning. The framework provides a structured basis for analyzing, comparing, and developing communication methods. Second, we study the Communicating Critics and Decentralized Actors (CCDA) setting, in which critics exchange messages during training while actors act without communication at execution. Under stated assumptions on ideal and noisy communication, we show that the variance of policy gradients under communicating critics is equal to or greater than that obtained with a centralized critic that has access to the complete joint information. To mitigate this variance, we derive a message-dependent baseline, characterize its variance-minimizing form, and propose a complementary regularization technique. Experiments show reduced gradient variance and improved learning performance. Third, we propose Communication with Factorized Policy Gradients (CFPG) for continuous control. CFPG uses centralized but factorized value functions to distinguish the contribution of each communicating agent, and propagates gradients through both policies and message encoders so that communication and action selection are learned jointly. Experiments in continuous-control benchmarks show improved performance and faster learning relative to the evaluated baselines. Finally, we introduce Multi-task Communication Skills (MCS), a Transformer-based method that enables agents to learn and perform multiple tasks with a single shared communication protocol. The protocol accommodates varying numbers of agents as well as heterogeneous observation and action spaces by encoding task-specific observations into a shared message space, limiting unnecessary communication, and aggregating received messages. An additional learning objective encourages messages to carry information about the senders' actions. Together, these contributions provide theoretical insights and practical methods for learning communication in cooperative MADRL. Evaluations on simulated benchmarks demonstrate improvements in learning stability, efficiency, or task performance relative to the evaluated baselines, with the magnitude of improvement varying across tasks.

title: FROM PIXELS TO PROMPTS: A STRUCTURED NARRATIVE REVIEW OF SECURITY, PRIVACY, AND ADVERSARIAL ROBUSTNESS IN HEALTHCARE AI
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare, where evaluations usually ask whether a system is accurate on ordinary clinical data. This review asks instead what can happen when someone deliberately changes the data, instructions, or training to make a system fail, behave in hidden ways, or reveal confidential information, a field known as adversarial machine learning. We reviewed 113 publications (2018–2026) and grouped the reported threats into six categories: altering an input after training; corrupting the training examples; teaching a hidden rule triggered later; using the model to learn private information; placing malicious instructions in language or image-and-language models; and attacking models trained jointly across hospitals or devices. Laboratory studies showed that small deliberate changes to medical images could alter a diagnosis or a model's outline, corrupted training data could change what a model learned, and malicious prompts could produce unsafe medical responses. Effect sizes varied greatly across models, datasets, attacks, and test conditions. Several defenses helped in individual experiments, but no single defense was shown to work across all threats and settings; in one imaging study, attacks tailored to the tested defenses bypassed all five. The studies do not show how often these attacks occur in practice or harm patients; their value is to demonstrate possible failure modes under controlled conditions. Medical AI should therefore be evaluated both on ordinary clinical data and in clearly described, clinically plausible attack scenarios.

title: Federated learning with adaptive reliability aware aggregation for privacy preserving healthcare IoT systems
abstract: Abstract Healthcare Internet of Things (IoT) devices generate vast amounts of sensitive patient data, creating significant privacy risks and regulatory challenges when processed through centralized architectures. Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising solution by enabling decentralized model training without sharing raw data. However, real-world deployment faces critical challenges including device heterogeneity, intermittent connectivity, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, and unreliable node participation. This paper proposes a Reliability-Aware Adaptive Aggregation (RAAA) framework that dynamically evaluates client trustworthiness through three dimensions: update quality (local accuracy and gradient alignment), participation consistency (historical engagement patterns), and communication latency. These metrics are integrated into a composite reliability score using weighted aggregation, which adaptively prioritizes contributions from trustworthy nodes during global model updates. The framework was validated using PhysioNet electrocardiogram (ECG) datasets (MIT-BIH and PTB) with 20 simulated healthcare IoT clients under conditions of node dropout and data heterogeneity. Experimental results demonstrate that RAAA achieved 91.7% classification accuracy on arrhythmia detection, outperforming Federated Averaging (FedAvg) (85.2%), Federated Proximal (FedProx) (86.4%), and Q-FedAvg (87.1%) by 6.5%, 5.3%, and 4.6%, respectively. The proposed method converged 17% faster (43 versus 52 rounds) and maintained an 85.6% client participation rate. Cross-dataset validation on the PTB database confirmed consistent improvements across different physiological signals. The RAAA framework provides a robust, privacy-preserving FL solution for healthcare IoT environments with superior accuracy, faster convergence, and resilience to unreliable nodes. All evaluations are conducted in a simulated environment; while theoretical energy and complexity analyses suggest suitability for resource-constrained edge devices, real-hardware validation remains an important direction for future work.

title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., π0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

evidence.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
evidence.abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., π0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. title: Hear, Localize, and Reason: Spatially Aware Scene Understanding for Audio-Visual LLMs
abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) have made strong progress in multimodal understanding, yet most treat audio as monaural semantic content, limiting their ability to reason about where sounds originate and how they relate to the visual scene. Recent spatial audio-visual studies address parts of this problem, but often focus on specific abilities, such as spatial correspondence or direction and distance reasoning. In this work, we introduce HLR-AVSceneQA, a comprehensive benchmark with a hear-localize-reason hierarchy that evaluates whether models can recognize what is heard, localize sound sources in egocentric and allocentric views, and use these localized sources to reason about how they relate to the visual scene. We further introduce HLR-LLM, which augments a strong audio-visual foundation model with a binaural spatial audio branch alongside its monaural semantic audio pathway. We train HLR-LLM with a curriculum that incorporates final-stage chain-of-thought supervision for multi-step spatial reasoning. Experiments show that existing AV-LLMs remain limited in spatial grounding and relational reasoning, while HLR-LLM substantially improves spatial audio-visual scene understanding without compromising semantic audio-visual perception.

title: Sparse Attention for Video Generation Acceleration via Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search
abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.

title: Rare Event Simulation of Quantum Error-Correcting Circuits
abstract: We describe a practical approach for accessing the logical failure rates of quantum error-correcting (QEC) circuits under low physical (component) failure rate regimes. Standard Monte Carlo is often the de facto approach for studying the failure rates of quantum circuits. However, in the study of fault-tolerant error-correcting circuits, the ability to extend this approach to low physical failure rates is limited. In particular, the use of Monte Carlo to access circuits that are relatively large or have high correcting power becomes more difficult as we lower the input failure rates of the individual components (gates) in the circuit. For these reasons, many simulations studying the circuit model go no lower than end-to-end logical failure rates in the 10 − 6 regime.In this report, we outline an approach that borrows from earlier work by Bravyi and Vargo \cite{bv13} to the more complex circuit noise model. Earlier works studied both the capacity and phenomenological noise models \cite{bv13,Beverland2019,bonilla2021xzzx}, but the work is insufficient for generating similar simulations in the circuit-noise model. To the best of our knowledge, our team is the first to develop a full prescription of the rare event simulation by splitting technique for the circuit-based noise model. We have also generated promising results that are confirmed by standard Monte Carlo simulation under an accessible regime. This work shows that we can access noise in the circuit-model prescription of quantum error-correcting code to failure rates below 10 − 20 regime.

title: Constraining Tool Authority in AI Agents: A Risk-Tiered Framework for Mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection
abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents read untrusted content, such as emails, web pages, and documents, and act through tools. Instructions hidden in that content can steer the agent, and the agent's permissions can turn that influence into unauthorized actions. This paper proposes a risk-based authorization architecture that reduces the consequences of indirect prompt injection without assuming the model resists it. The architecture separates model-generated action proposals from execution authority and combines task-scoped capabilities, a deterministic authorization gateway, risk-tiered approval bound to the exact proposed action, constrained tool interfaces, and security audit records. We state a threat model, six security objectives, and a control flow; position the design against recent architectural defenses (CaMeL, design patterns for prompt-injection-resistant agents, Progent, AgentSpec, and ClawGuard); and specify a reproducible evaluation protocol using instrumented mock tools and synthetic data. No prototype, benchmark run, or empirical result is reported. The contribution is a design and an evaluation protocol, not a validated defense, and the design is not claimed to be novel in its individual principles.

title: Adaptive Self-Search and Collaborative Search in World-Level Self–Mutual Models: A Unified Framework for Autonomous and Cooperative Search
abstract: Search is a fundamental operation in intelligent systems because it enables the discovery of states, solutions, relationships, strategies, and possible futures. Conventional search mechanisms often follow a predetermined search policy, while collaborative search systems rely on interactions among multiple agents, models, or computational processes. Although these approaches can be effective, autonomous search and collaborative search have different computational costs, information requirements, and problem-solving capabilities. A system that always searches independently may fail to exploit useful external knowledge, whereas a system that always collaborates may incur unnecessary communication, coordination, and evaluation costs. This paper proposes the Adaptive Self–Mutual World Search (ASMW-Search) framework, a conceptual architecture that integrates self-models, mutual-models, and world models to support adaptive transitions between self-search and collaborative search. The framework is not designed as a large language model or as a language-model-based multi-agent system. Instead, it treats the world model as a structured representation of environmental states, transitions, constraints, relationships, uncertainties, and potential outcomes. The self-model maintains an internal representation of the system's own knowledge, capabilities, search history, limitations, and predictions. The mutual-model represents relationships between the self-model and other models, including differences in knowledge, complementary capabilities, dependencies, and potential contributions to a search task. The proposed architecture selects among autonomous search, collaborative search, and intermediate forms of interaction according to estimated uncertainty, expected information gain, predicted search progress, computational cost, and the value of coordination. It further incorporates search-result integration, model updating, switching control, and feedback-driven adaptation. A formal decision objective is introduced to balance solution quality, search efficiency, communication overhead, and robustness. The paper defines research questions, testable hypotheses, an experimental design, evaluation metrics, limitations, and potential applications. As a conceptual proposal, the framework does not claim demonstrated performance or established superiority. Its central contribution is a unified research formulation in which autonomous and collaborative search are treated as dynamically selectable operating modes of a world-level self–mutual modeling system.

title: World Self–Mutual Models: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Planning and Collaborative Planning
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, transition dynamics, and possible future outcomes, enabling agents to plan actions before executing them. However, planning systems may face a fundamental architectural trade-off: independent planning can reduce communication and coordination costs but may lack complementary information, whereas collaborative planning can improve information coverage and resolve conflicting predictions but introduces additional computational and communication overhead. This paper proposes the World Self–Mutual Planning Framework (WSMPF), a conceptual architecture that integrates world models with two complementary planning modes: self-planning and collaborative planning. Self-planning enables an individual model to construct, evaluate, and revise its own action sequences using its internal world model. Collaborative planning enables multiple interacting models to exchange selected state representations, predictions, constraints, and candidate plans to construct or refine a coordinated plan. A meta-planning controller adaptively selects between these modes according to uncertainty, predicted task difficulty, plan disagreement, expected coordination benefit, communication cost, and execution risk. The framework is model-agnostic and does not require large language models. Its central hypothesis is that planning architecture should be selected dynamically rather than fixed permanently to either independent or collaborative operation. The paper formalizes the planning problem, defines a switching mechanism, presents an implementable algorithm, and proposes an experimental protocol for evaluating task success, planning quality, computational cost, communication overhead, robustness, and switching stability. The framework is presented as a research proposal; its empirical effectiveness and novelty relative to the complete existing literature remain to be established.

title: World Self-and-Mutual Models: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Diagnosis and Mutual Diagnosis for World-State Understanding and Model Reliability
abstract: World models provide computational representations of environmental states, transitions, and potential outcomes. However, a world model may contain internal inconsistencies, inaccurate state estimates, incorrect transition predictions, or assumptions that no longer correspond to the environment. Diagnosing these problems is therefore essential for maintaining reliable world representations. Existing research has investigated model-based diagnosis, multi-agent fault diagnosis, self-correction, and collaborative reasoning, but these research directions do not, by themselves, establish a unified framework in which self-diagnosis and mutual diagnosis are adaptively selected as complementary operating modes within a world-model architecture. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Models (WSMM) framework, a conceptual architecture that combines world-model-based state representation with a higher-level self-and-mutual modeling principle. WSMM distinguishes two diagnostic modes. In self-diagnosis, an individual world model examines its own state estimates, transition predictions, internal constraints, and accumulated discrepancies. In mutual diagnosis, multiple world models examine one another's predictions, compare their representations, and investigate inconsistencies that cannot be adequately resolved through isolated analysis. A diagnostic controller dynamically selects between these modes according to uncertainty, prediction error, disagreement, diagnostic confidence, task risk, computational cost, and the expected value of additional evidence. The framework formalizes world-state estimation, diagnostic discrepancy, mode selection, cross-model evidence integration, and model updating. It also introduces a distinction between diagnosing the state of the external world and diagnosing the internal reliability of the model representing that world. This distinction is important because an apparent environmental anomaly may originate from a faulty model, incomplete observations, an incorrect transition assumption, or a genuine change in the environment. The proposed framework is independent of any particular model architecture and does not require large language models. It can be implemented using predictive state-space models, robotics models, simulation systems, scientific models, or heterogeneous computational representations. Finally, the paper develops research questions, testable hypotheses, evaluation metrics, baseline comparisons, and a reproducible experimental design. The proposed framework is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated; its principal contribution is a formal research direction for adaptive switching between individual and cross-model diagnosis in world-model systems.

title: Doctrinal Problems of Applying Copyright to Literary Works Created by Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The article analyses five doctrinal problems in applying copyright to literary works created by artificial intelligence (AI). First, it shows that the classical theories (Locke’s labour theory, Hegel’s personality theory, the utilitarian theory and the fair remuneration theory) come into conflict when applied to AI activity. Second, it examines the concept of “author” under the legislation of Uzbekistan, Russia and the United States and under the Berne Convention, together with the question of AI subjecthood. Third, it addresses the originality requirement, fourth, moral rights, and fifth, the idea–expression dichotomy. The author concludes that all these problems share a single cause: classical doctrines rest on human consciousness, will and personality. Accordingly, AI should be treated as a tool rather than a subject. The article also proposes the “objective control criterion doctrine”, which ties the emergence of copyright to objective, verifiable criteria: purposeful direction of AI activity, creative selection among outputs, and determination of the work’s final content and form.

title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
abstract: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. evidence.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
evidence.abstract: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. Moreover, validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting. These results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research.

title: TRACE: Topology-Aware Reconnection via Prediction-Adaptive Connectivity Enforcement for Thin-Structure Segmentation
abstract: Thin, elongated structures are particularly sensitive to connectivity errors, as even a few local segmentation mistakes can disrupt otherwise continuous paths. Existing skeleton-based objectives typically supervise fixed centerline locations and do not account for alternative local routes that may restore connectivity. We propose TRACE, a topology-aware, prediction-adaptive objective that uses a target skeleton to define required local connections. For each connection, TRACE identifies the easiest valid reconnection under the current prediction and jointly supervises its bottleneck with the corresponding skeleton point. The supervision thus adapts to the evolving prediction rather than remaining fixed to the centerline. We further introduce a topology-aware skeleton carrier that preserves both foreground and class-specific topology, enabling reliable definition of these connections. Extensive experiments across six 2D and 3D benchmarks show that TRACE improves connectivity and topology while maintaining strong segmentation accuracy with low training overhead. Code will be released upon acceptance.

title: AVALON: Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation with Human-Seeded Topological Memory
abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.

title: Auxiliary modalities add no detectable discrimination or calibration over structured EHR for 30-day COPD readmission: evidence from a leakage-audited MIMIC-IV cohort
abstract: Background: Hospital readmission is a common and costly outcome in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Multimodal deep learning models combining structured electronic health record (EHR) data with physiological, imaging, and textual data have been proposed to improve its prediction, but whether such fusion outperforms EHR data alone, once temporal-leakage safeguards are applied, remains unclear. Methods: Using a stratified MIMIC-IV cohort of COPD patients enriched to about 50% readmission (natural prevalence 18.1%; n=1,279; 895/192/192 training/validation/test), we predicted 30-day, all-cause readmission from four frozen, pre-trained encoders (electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, clinical notes, structured EHR). We audited and corrected temporal leakage in the admission-linkage pipeline of each modality, then compared three fusion architectures (naive concatenation, scalar gated fusion, EHR-anchored residual fusion) against unimodal baselines and an EHR-alone reference, using bootstrap significance testing, a missingness stress test, and calibration analysis with and without post-hoc recalibration. Results: The audit corrected three previously undetected temporal-alignment issues, affecting 5-9% of patients for clinical notes, 29-43% for chest radiographs, and 53-58% for ECG. After correction, every modality except EHR showed near-chance discrimination alone (ROC-AUC 0.46-0.53), confirmed with a non-linear adapter probe. No fusion architecture significantly outperformed the EHR-alone baseline (ROC-AUC 0.63); removing auxiliary modalities improved rather than degraded fusion performance under stress testing. The raw Brier score was lower for all three fusion architectures than for EHR-alone (about 0.24 versus 0.32), but this reflected overconfidence of the EHR-alone probe (calibration slope 0.12); after logistic recalibration fitted on the validation set, Brier scores were indistinguishable (EHR-alone 0.239; fusion 0.240-0.244; all paired bootstrap 95% CIs included zero). Conclusions: Structured EHR data alone matched the discrimination and, after recalibration, the calibration of more complex multimodal fusion for 30-day COPD readmission prediction. These findings highlight the importance of rigorous temporal-leakage auditing in multimodal clinical prediction research and suggest that reformulating this task around temporal proximity to the outcome, rather than refining the fusion mechanism further, may be more productive for future work.

title: Compile What the Environment Decides: Read-Only Speculation and Compiled Procedures for LLM Agents
abstract: An LLM agent pays a model turn for every decision, yet many of its decisions are fixed by what its tools returned, not by what the user said. We make this precise and use it in two regimes. While a user is present, a program learned from traces can take over only reads, speculatively. Because reads leave the state unchanged until the next write, the decision to speculate separates over reads: make each read whose probability of use before the next write exceeds $\delta/(\beta+\delta)$, for a detour's cost $\delta$ and a saved turn's value $\beta$. That probability, not the next-step probability speculative-action systems rank by, is the one to estimate, and counting estimates it with a calibration error of 0.01–0.08 (against 0.06–0.16). In replay across nine frontier agents it never saw, the speculator takes 86% of retail's read-only ceiling, 10 points more than the next-step speculator. Live on τ²-bench, with no model of its own, it cut GLM-5.3's LLM turns by 28% (95% CI 19–36%) and, in a pre-registered run of three trials, Claude Sonnet 5's by 21% (17–24%) and Claude Haiku 4.5's by 22% (16–29%), with passes no lower. Run live in AgentDojo's own environment with GLM-5.3 and Claude Haiku 4.5, it cut LLM turns by 10% (6–14%) in the suites where the replay found reads to take, with passes unchanged. Where no user speaks, a whole procedure, writes included, can be compiled once: on τ²-bench's solo telecom tasks, a cascade that hands a model only what the procedure's outcome check cannot confirm passes 39 of 40 held-out tasks at 0.48 LLM turns per ticket, against 15.9 for the model alone. Both run in Hoist, an open-source MCP proxy and procedure runtime that serves any agent and any MCP server.
