title: QEC Invariant Compendium: Baseline Equivalence, Trace-Indexed Reuse, Decoder Pipelines, and Dark-State Observables
abstract: This compendium presents four revised studies of deterministic computation, reusable intermediate results, and transformation invariants in belief-propagation diagnostics and quantum error-correction software. It connects earlier QSOL-IMC preprints with commit-pinned QEC source snapshots, reproducible experiments, and machine-checked mathematical models. The four studies examine baseline equivalence between min-sum decoding and unit-weight uniformly reweighted belief propagation; trace-indexed reuse of sign vectors and CRC32 values; the interaction of clipping, damping, freezing, and ternary projection in decoder transformation pipelines; and the interpretation of local “dark-state” observables in belief-propagation traces. The deposit contains four revised papers, editable manuscript sources, a dependency-free Lean 4 project, source snapshots, validation scripts, measured results, proof logs, provenance records, and integrity manifests. The formalization comprises 43 compiled theorem declarations. Empirical validation includes 576 paired decoder cases, 80 cached-versus-inline diagnostic comparisons, a reproduced reduction from 81 to 20 sign computations, 204 selected historical tests, and 18 synthetic dark-state scenario runs. The analysis also documents counterexamples and boundary conditions involving CRC32 collisions, cache provenance, source mutation, damping, NaN handling, transformation order, and the distinction between observed local stability and safe computational reuse. The Lean proofs establish properties of the stated exact mathematical models. They do not constitute a complete refinement proof for the Python/NumPy implementations or IEEE-754 arithmetic, nor do they establish physical quantum-hardware correctness or justify skipping live-decoder updates. Historical runtime improvements are identified as previously reported results, separate from the measurements reproduced in this deposit.

title: Deep Learning-Based Japanese Speech Recognition for Robust Organizational Knowledge Capture
abstract: Online Japanese teaching and organizational knowledge management depend on reliable Japanese automatic speech recognition, while existing conformer models perform poorly amid regional dialects, complex phonetics, and background noise. This paper proposes an improved conformer connectionist temporal classification framework with multi-scale acoustic feature enhancement, dialect adaptation layers, bidirectional acoustic-language model fusion, and multi-task training. Tests on 800 hours of standard, mixed-dialect, and noisy speech data and three months of real-scene deployment show the model improves dialect recognition accuracy by nearly 15% and reduces word error rate by 12% under heavy noise, with only 5 milliseconds longer inference latency than the baseline. Separate module tests show each design strengthens noise resistance, dialect adaptability, and long-sentence modeling. The framework balances accuracy and efficiency, supporting real-time oral teaching feedback and structured extraction of implicit enterprise knowledge from voice recordings.

title: ENSEMBLES DE DEEP LEARNING NO DIAGNÓSTICO DE LESÕES ENDOSCÓPICAS
abstract: Lesões gastrointestinais representam um relevante problema de saúde pública, cuja detecção precoce reduz a mortalidade, apesar da subjetividade da análise manual de imagens endoscópicas. Este trabalho propõe o DeepEnsemble-Endo, um ensemble de weighted soft voting com pesos otimizados via grid search. Após avaliar 11 CNNs pré-treinadas por transfer learning e selecionar as cinco melhores (DenseNet121, ResNet50, InceptionV3, MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB2), os pesos foram sistematicamente otimizados, alcançando 96,63% de acurácia e 97,25% de F1-score - superandos ensembles simples da literatura e evidenciando o potencial da abordagem como suporte automatizado à decisão clínica.

title: From Diagnosis to Decision‐Making: AI ‐Driven Triage of Oral Mucosal Lesions Detected on Intraoral Photographs
abstract: BACKGROUND: Managing oral mucosal lesions in general dental practice is challenging, as visually similar conditions may require very different treatments. We developed an AI-based triage system connecting intraoral image analysis with guideline-based treatment recommendations, tested it externally, and compared its performance with clinicians' recommendations. METHODS: YOLOv8 and YOLOv11 were trained on 4079 intraoral photographs to classify 11 oral mucosal lesion types. These were mapped into five treatment tiers defined by urgency and management aim: T1 specialist referral for malignant and high-risk lesions, T2 interdisciplinary referral for specialist-led non-cancer management, T3 risk-adapted surveillance, T4 dental treatment with reassessment, and T5 no treatment. Model performance was compared with two general dentists and four specialists on an internal test set. YOLOv11 was additionally tested on an external dataset. RESULTS: YOLOv11 outperformed YOLOv8 in macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 score, achieving 0.72, 0.74, and 0.73 respectively. However, 25% of T1 high-risk cases were under-triaged. YOLOv11 significantly outperformed all clinicians, whose F1 scores ranged from 0.33 to 0.69. External performance decreased markedly (F1 score: 0.58), consistent with domain shift. CONCLUSION: Guideline-oriented AI triage is feasible but requires multicentre training for improved generalizability, as well as safety-focused optimization, and prospective user evaluation before clinical use.

title: Lean4AgenticRL: Advancing Agentic RL with Verifiable Multi-level Process Rewards
abstract: Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards, with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose **Lean4AgenticRL**, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. **Lean4AgenticRL** first builds a *problem-specific workflow* system that balances the agent's own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using **Lean4AgenticRL**, we train **LAR-9B/27B**, a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of similar size. **LAR-27B** achieves **77.3%** on TerminalBench-2.1. On average, our models outperform the base model by **9.89%** and surpass the second-best model of comparable size we know by **5.07%**. These results indicate the potential of integrating formal methods in enhancing open-ended agentic RL.

title: Jianmu-Q: Bridging Quantum Field Theory and Quantum Hardware with AI Agents
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to non-perturbative simulations of quantum field theories, particularly for real-time dynamics and systems affected by the sign problem. Yet translating continuum field theories into quantum computations remains a challenging interdisciplinary task. Here we introduce \texttt{Jianmu-Q}, a multi-agent framework that transforms natural-language descriptions of quantum field theories into quantum simulation workflows. Specialized agents handle theoretical formulation, lattice discretization, qubit mapping, and circuit design, while physical consistency checks and independent numerical calculations provide validation throughout the workflow. We benchmark the framework on three field theories of increasing complexity: the $(1+1)$-dimensional Nambu--Jona-Lasinio and Schwinger models, and a $(2+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory. Across these systems, noiseless quantum-circuit simulations converge toward independent exact-diagonalization and tensor-network results, while selected circuits are executed on IBM quantum hardware, demonstrating an end-to-end, validation-guided approach to quantum simulation of field theories.

title: Transfer Learning in Bandits from Unknown Adaptive Policies: Problem-Dependent Lower and Upper Bounds
abstract: Transfer learning in stochastic multi-armed bandits is typically studied assuming that prior data forms a fixed offline dataset or is generated by a known source. In practice, historical observations come from a previous adaptive decision process whose policy is unknown. We study this setting for bounded rewards in $[0,1]$. Before the online game starts, the learner receives, for each arm $k$, $N'_k$ observations drawn i.i.d.\ from an unknown distribution $ν'_k$, collected by an arbitrary and possibly data-dependent strategy, so the sample sizes $N'_k$ may be random. Source and target means satisfy $|μ_k-μ'_k|<L_k$ for known constants $(L_k)_k$. We derive an asymptotic problem-dependent lower bound and propose KL-UCB-Transfer, which combines online and historical data and achieves logarithmic regret with an improved leading constant whenever $μ'_a<μ_1-L_a$, and recovers the classical KL-UCB guarantee otherwise. evidence.abstract: Transfer learning in stochastic multi-armed bandits is typically studied assuming that prior data forms a fixed offline dataset or is generated by a known source. In practice, historical observations come from a previous adaptive decision process whose policy is unknown. We study this setting for bounded rewards in $[0,1]$. Before the online game starts, the learner receives, for each arm $k$, $N'_k$ observations drawn i.i.d.\ from an unknown distribution $ν'_k$, collected by an arbitrary and possibly data-dependent strategy, so the sample sizes $N'_k$ may be random. title: Quantum Versus Classical Machine Learning for Neuropsychiatric Disorders: A Feature-Matched Multi-Cohort Evaluation
abstract: Resting-state functional connectivity is widely used in machine learning-based classification of neuropsychiatric disorders. Quantum machine learning models have been proposed for functional connectivity data, but few studies have evaluated them under leave-site-out validation or against matched classical models. We compared six quantum model families with classical ones using identical correlation-derived features across four public cohorts (4,308 subjects). Leave-site-out validation was used for the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE I), ADHD-200 (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), and REST-meta-MDD (major depressive disorder) cohorts, while the UCLA Consortium for Neuropsychiatric Phenomics (UCLA-CNP) was evaluated using stratified 10-fold cross-validation. The quantum kernel was statistically indistinguishable from a matched classical kernel across all four cohorts, with the average accuracy difference within 1.4 percentage points at 95% confidence. On ABIDE I, a hybrid quantum convolutional network achieved similar accuracy to its classical counterpart (0.645 vs. 0.641), while a trainable quantum kernel exceeded its classical counterpart by 0.064 in area under the curve (AUC). Quantum convolutional networks also achieved higher AUC than their matched classical networks on this cohort and showed smaller train-test gaps on all four cohorts, without an accuracy gain. Overall, most quantum models matched their classical counterparts, but none consistently outperformed them. This study, among the first quantum evaluations of ABIDE I under leave-site-out validation, provides a feature-matched benchmark of quantum and classical models comprising 284 matched comparisons. We further analyse fidelity-based graph construction and account for the observed quantum-classical parity through effective-dimension and eigenspectrum analyses.

title: Magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires a universal gate set, but the necessary non-Clifford gates represent a significant resource cost for most quantum error correction architectures. Magic state cultivation offers an efficient alternative to resource-intensive distillation protocols; however, testing the proposal's assumptions represents a challenging departure from quantum memory experiments. We present an experimental study of magic state cultivation on a superconducting quantum processor. We implement cultivation, including code-switching into a surface code, and develop a fault-tolerant measurement protocol to bound the magic state fidelity. Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40, with a state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1) (retaining 8% of attempts). Our results experimentally establish magic state cultivation as a viable solution to one of quantum computing's most important challenges.

title: Reproducibility package: An experimental comparison of hyperparameter optimization methods for healthcare machine learning
abstract: Code, data and results for the article “An experimental comparison of hyperparameter optimization methods for healthcare machine learning: From grid search to swarm intelligence” (submitted to PLOS ONE). The package compares six hyperparameter optimization strategies (library defaults, grid search, random search, Bayesian optimization with TPE, the Grey Wolf Optimizer and Particle Swarm Optimization) for Random Forest, Support Vector Machine and Logistic Regression on four public clinical datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, with ten paired seeds (720 runs) and a matched-budget experiment. Contents: the benchmark code and experiment notebook; the exact data arrays with SHA-256 checksums and all train/validation/test split indices; all per-seed results; the optimizer traces; scripts that regenerate every table and figure; and check_paper.py, which recomputes all statistics from the raw results and verifies the tables and the numbers stated in the manuscript (run: python check_paper.py; needs Python 3.9+ with numpy and pandas). Code is released under the MIT licence. The four datasets keep the terms of their original sources.

title: Project Pushkalāvatī / Nirgundi: the Sanskrit parser, its data-driven rule compiler and the Sūtram rule-rewrite language (BUILD-0024 to BUILD-0027)
abstract: The integrated research repository for the Sanskrit source inventory (all 3,983 sūtras as data), a data-driven rule compiler, the observed-form bootstrap, the Sūtram rule-rewrite language, the Sanskrit analysis pipeline, Hindawi ports and Romenagri transliteration tooling. This deposit preserves BUILD-0024, BUILD-0025, BUILD-0026 and BUILD-0027 exactly as delivered: each original archive is included byte for byte, the repository history carries one commit per build, and the final tree is BUILD-0026 with the BUILD-0027 results and correction applied. Twenty files that BUILD-0025 and BUILD-0026 dropped in packaging, including the Pages workflow, are restored from BUILD-0024, and the shell scripts are executable again; SEED-NOTE.md records each. Third-party components keep their own licences.

title: Building Trust in AI-Driven Marketing
abstract: This study investigates the mediating role of Green Knowledge Management (GKM) in the relationship between responsible AI marketing practices and customer trust within the Iraqi digital market. Drawing on the Knowledge-Based View (KBV) and sustainability perspectives, the study proposes that organizations can enhance customer trust by integrating environmentally and ethically oriented knowledge processes, including knowledge acquisition, sharing, and application, into their AI-driven marketing practices. A quantitative research design to be employed using a cross-sectional survey targeting digital platform users in Iraq. Data will be analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) to test both direct and indirect relationships.

title: Variational quantum principal component analysis for Hilbert space Gaussian process regression
abstract: Abstract Gaussian processes are widely used probabilistic models for regression and classification tasks. Their flexibility and ability to quantify uncertainties make them well-suited for many applications. However, their applicability to large datasets is limited by the cubic computational time complexity. While reduced-rank methods such as Hilbert space approximations reduce this complexity, scaling to very large datasets remains challenging. Quantum algorithms are promising candidates to further accelerate such computations. Quantum principal component analysis has previously been applied to Hilbert space Gaussian process regression to address this scaling limitation. However, its applicability is limited by the requirement for fault-tolerant quantum hardware. In this work, we present a hybrid quantum-classical model for reduced-rank Gaussian process regression, where we apply a quantum principal component analysis algorithm based on parameterized quantum circuits to Hilbert space Gaussian process regression. In noiseless simulations on a one-dimensional test function, the resulting model reaches a regression accuracy comparable to that of the exact Gaussian process and the classical Hilbert space Gaussian process. The framework uses shallow parameterized circuits and does not require fault-tolerant quantum hardware, which makes it a candidate for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

title: Leveraging Large Language Model Token Probabilities for Literature Review Abstract Filtering
abstract: Grasping the latest knowledge in any field has become increasingly challenging given the rapid pace of modern publishing. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly embedding models and large language models (LLMs), provide promising tools to aid researchers in the filtration and identification of the most relevant literature. However, there is little practical guidance on how to incorporate LLMs into literature reviews, and there are not yet direct comparisons of embedding models versus generative approaches. In this work, we compare these methods using small local LLMs for literature screening on both a simple dataset containing distinct categories and a more complex example with abstracts obtained from the Web of Science. We find that embedding models perform strongly for simple, well-separated queries due to their robustness and computational efficiency. For more complex filtering tasks, generative approaches based on token probabilities can achieve competitive or superior performance, but only when properly calibrated and when token-level outputs are interpreted as continuous scores rather than binary decisions. However, we show these methods are highly sensitive to prompt formulation, token conventions, and threshold selection.

title: Event-STVG: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding for Long-Form Event Reasoning
abstract: Spatio-Temporal Video Grounding (STVG) aims to jointly localize a target in space and time given a natural-language query. Despite continued advances, existing STVG benchmarks remain largely centered on localizing targets through instance-specific descriptions, leaving them largely decoupled from long-form reasoning increasingly emphasized in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). In this paper, we introduce Event-STVG, a task that shifts STVG from locating what is described toward event-level reasoning by unifying long-form context, repeated-event reasoning, event localization, role inference, and multi-target grounding. To facilitate research on Event-STVG, we construct a large-scale benchmark comprising 4,016 annotated event occurrences across soccer and seven additional domains. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs reveal substantial difficulty, with the strongest model achieving only 5.4% m-vIoU at the 10-minute horizon. Across domains, we consistently observe confusion among repeated same-type events, spatial grounding bottlenecks, and rare success in jointly grounding all required roles. Event-STVG establishes a new challenge for visual understanding in MLLMs, calling for future models that can jointly reason about complex events across space and time. Code and annotations are available at https://github.com/THU-KEG/EventSTVG

title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
abstract: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.

title: The Tilted Sampling Problem: Optimism, Posterior Sampling, and Logarithmic Regret
abstract: Many modern learning systems are used not to select a single best action, but to sample diverse high-quality outputs. Examples include entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, RLHF, and reward-guided generative modeling. Motivated by these settings, we study tilted sampling: an online learning problem in which the goal is to sample from the Gibbs distribution induced by an unknown reward function. We define sampling regret as the temperature-normalized cumulative KL divergence between the learner's distribution and the Gibbs target, corresponding to the suboptimality gap in entropy-regularized reward maximization. Our framework generalizes recent sampling-based and KL-regularized formulations in bandits and reinforcement learning. Our main contribution is a general regret framework that captures the different uncertainty structure of tilted sampling and classical regret minimization. While standard regret scales as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ due to first-order uncertainty, sampling regret is governed by squared confidence widths, yielding logarithmic-in-$T$ regret in standard settings at fixed temperature. We develop sampling analogues of UCB and Thompson sampling (UCS and TS$^2$) and provide unified regret decompositions that explain and extend recent logarithmic guarantees, including the first Bayesian sampling-regret decomposition based on new bounds for posterior-random Gibbs distributions. Our results show that learning to sample from a soft-optimal distribution is statistically distinct from learning to identify a hard optimum.

title: Descending Everest with First-Order Oracles: Oracle Complexity of Convex Optimization under $(L_0,L_1)$-Smoothness
abstract: For convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth functions, the curvature may grow together with the gradient norm. Therefore, even when $\|x^0-x^*\|\le R$, the gradient and the optimality gap at the starting point may be exponentially large in $L_1R$, and the bound $\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}$, known for the accelerated method on functions with Lipschitz gradient, no longer describes the complexity of the problem. We determine the oracle complexity of this class for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods: for $L_0R^2/\varepsilon\ge1$, the optimal number of oracle calls $N$ satisfies $1+N=\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+L_1R)$. The upper bound reads $O(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(1+L_1R)\log(2+L_1R))$: the method first passes through the large-gradient regime in $O(1+L_1R)$ iterations with an inexact line search, and then the standard accelerated method with a constant stepsize takes over. The lower bound is obtained by means of chains and the orthogonal invariance principle on functions conjugate to strongly convex functions on a polytope. If the initial optimality gap is at most $4\varepsilon$, the optimal bound becomes $1+N=\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{L_0R^2/\varepsilon}+(L_1R)^{2/3})$.

title: Online Quantile Omniprediction for Proper Losses
abstract: The task of constructing a predictor that is simultaneously accurate under multiple evaluation metrics has been popularized recently under the name omniprediction. Prior work in this area has largely focused on binary prediction tasks, and existing results for multiclass and continuous outcomes typically suffer from slow error rates. In this paper, we consider forecasts expressed as a set of quantiles over a discrete but otherwise arbitrary set of probability levels. We develop sample-efficient algorithms for constructing forecasts that are accurate simultaneously across all proper losses that satisfy mild regularity conditions, where proper losses are those minimized by predicting the true quantiles. Our algorithms are online and can operate in a dynamic environment, while simultaneously taking multiple losses into account, and their forecasts offer the potential to provide diverse end-users with rich information for evaluating risk and informing a range of practical decision-making tasks. As an example, we demonstrate how our procedure can be used to ensemble quantile forecasts of COVID-19 hospitalizations made by experts during the pandemic.

title: Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

title: Compression-Based Linguistic Complexity Metrics in Automatic Essay Scoring
abstract: Compression-based linguistic complexity metrics enable cross-linguistic comparison without prior annotation. Their sensitivity to variation across languages and Portuguese registers highlights their applicability in NLP tasks. This study investigates their use as readability proxies and complementary features in Automatic Essay Scoring. We analyze how these metrics capture variation in essay quality across traits, genres, and educational levels in Brazilian Portuguese. In addition, we evaluate their sensitivity to differences between humanand AI-generated essays. Our results suggest that complexity metrics are effective (i) in differentiating educational levels, (ii) in detecting whether they were written by humans and (iii) as predictors of essay quality.

title: Symmetric weighing matrices SW(25,16), SW(27,16) and SW(29,16)
abstract: We exhibit symmetric weighing matrices SW(25,16), SW(27,16) and SW(29,16), i.e. symmetric n×n matrices W with entries in {0,±1} and WWT = 16I for n = 25, 27, 29. These three orders were listed as the remaining open instances for weight 16 in recent literature (Rosin, arXiv:2505.23881; arXiv:2501.17725, Table 2). Each matrix was found by a SAT search in which a signed-permutation automorphism of a chosen cycle type was prescribed. Existence is established by the explicit certificates, which are printed in the appendix of the note and supplied as plain-text files (a second, different SW(27,16) is included); each was checked by two independently written exact-integer programs. To verify any matrix in seconds: python3 check_sw_int.py SW_27_16.txt 27 16 (pure Python, no dependencies; prints VALID and exits 0). Provenance: the searches were planned and run by an AI agent (agent-afk) under the author's supervision.

title: Phaneia Evaluation Methodology for AI Agents
abstract: This document defines how Phaneia GmbH evaluates whether an AI agent or agentic system does something it must not when an adversary controls part of its inputs: content it reads, its configuration, or messages from other agents. Every trial is scored deterministically against evidence the agent did not produce: what the systems it acts on actually recorded, compared with obligations defined outside the agent. No language model sits in the scoring path. The methodology covers: access tiers and environment fidelity; scenario families and trial design, with attack and baseline arms of at least 30 trials; two complementary checks (obligation-detection and claim-verification), and statistical reporting with Fisher exact tests and Wilson intervals; instrument validation; the content and validity of the evaluation letter; re-evaluations and repeat runs; independence rules, versioning and limitations. It builds on Schwyzer (2026), Adversarial Assessment of Agentic Systems (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23043956). Payloads, attack chains and the scenario library are not part of this public document. Reports and evaluation letters cite the version DOI of the methodology they were produced under.

title: VTutor Pro VZona v10.6.5 STABLE: AI-Assisted Conversational Tutoring with Institutional Mini-RAG for Moodle
abstract: VTutor Pro VZona v10.6.5 STABLE — Institutional Mini-RAG for Moodle VTutor Pro VZona es un componente de software educativo para Moodle 4.5+, desarrollado para apoyar procesos de tutoría conversacional mediante inteligencia artificial generativa y recuperación documental contextualizada. La versión 10.6.5 STABLE (build 2026082406) integra un Mini-RAG institucional con recuperación semántica, mecanismos de respaldo léxico, aislamiento contextual por curso y permisos de usuario, trazabilidad documental y herramientas de diagnóstico READ-ONLY. El proceso de desarrollo se documenta desde la perspectiva de Design Science Research (DSR), mediante iteraciones de construcción, revisión técnica, pruebas funcionales y decisiones de estabilización. La versión publicada corresponde a la promoción de FINAL QA6 (build 2026082405) a STABLE (build 2026082406). La comparación estática de ambos paquetes identificó modificaciones de metadatos, documentación y actualización, sin cambios en la lógica principal de recuperación y enrutamiento. Alcance de la evidencia: Las verificaciones documentadas respaldan la integridad y características técnicas examinadas. No constituyen evidencia experimental de mejoras en el aprendizaje, eficacia pedagógica ni validación independiente de seguridad o rendimiento. title: Adversarial Robustness of Deep Learning–Based Network Intrusion Detection Under Encrypted Traffic
abstract: The deployment of encryption protocols, such as TLS 1.3, QUIC, Encrypted Client Hello and DNS-over-HTTPS, has compelled deep learning-based network intrusion detection systems (DL-NIDS) to rely on metadata for classification. This chapter explores adversarial robustness issues and challenges of DL-NIDS on encrypted traffic. Contrary to adversarial machine learning that assumes a common feature space to which attacks are defined, encrypted metadata has heterogenous, protocol-constrained features: packet sizes constrained by transmission unit sizes, timing features constrained by latency budgets, and nominal handshake features constrained by candidate lists. This chapter defines metadata-specific adversarial models, identifies protocol-valid evasion and poisoning attacks, studies countermeasures in constrained feature spaces, and proposes protocol-aligned evaluation for DL-NIDS. By developing perturbation models for encrypted and non-encrypted traffic, this chapter lays the groundwork for developing secure DL-NIDS in an encrypted future.

title: Event Log Behavioral Privacy Protection Method Based on Relaxed Behavioral Profiles
abstract: Privacy preservation techniques for event logs prevent sensitive information leakage by injecting noise into log data, thus mitigating privacy risks in business process management. While ensuring privacy, this approach often reduces data utility and impacts subsequent analysis accuracy. Current research mainly optimizes noise injection based on data attributes to preserve utility, but overlooks how behavioral relationship changes affect data quality. To address this, this paper proposes a privacy protection method for event logs based on relaxed behavioral profiles. First, a behavioral privacy attack model is formalized to reveal how behavioral relationships can lead to privacy leakage. Building on this, data attributes are utilized to extend behavioral profiles, and a behavioral profile extension algorithm is proposed to analyze implicit behavioral relationships between activities. This allows building a multi-perspective perturbation set combining behavioral and data attributes. Finally, perturbations are injected using differential privacy methods. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the event logs generated by this method are behavior-unchanged at the level of the modeled relations, effectively mitigating the utility loss caused by log anonymization and attaining F1-scores of up to 0.874 on synthetic data, comparable to those of the baselines.

title: DEEP LEARNING ENSEMBLES FOR THE DIAGNOSIS OF ENDOSCOPIC LESIONS
authors: Luiz Otávio de Oliveira Souza Júnior
abstract: Gastrointestinal lesions represent a significant public health concern, where early detection reduces mortality despite the subjectivity of manual endoscopic image analysis. This work proposes DeepEnsemble-Endo, a weighted soft voting ensemble with weights optimized via grid search. After evaluating 11 pre-trained CNNs via transfer learning and selecting the top-5 (DenseNet121, ResNet50, InceptionV3, MobileNetV2, EfficientNetB2), weights were systematically optimized, achieving 96.63% accuracy and 97.25% F1-score - outperforming simple ensembles from the literature and demonstrating potential as automated clinical decision support.

title: Quantisation Costs More in Greek than in English, Cybersecurity Knowledge of Small Local Language Models
abstract: Small open language models that run on an ordinary office computer are an attractive basis for a security awareness assistant, and platforms such as SentinelSphere ship one in a compressed quantised form, that stores the numbers inside the model with fewer bits. This study asks how much cybersecurity knowledge this compression costs, and whether the cost is larger in Greek than in English. A sample of questions from the CyberMetric benchmark was translated into Greek with an open translation model that was not itself tested, the translation was checked by translating it back, and the same questions were put in both languages to Phi-4-mini at three levels of compression, to the general model Qwen2.5-3B and to the Greek adapted model Krikri-8B, all on a two core processor. Phi-4-mini answers Greek questions clearly worse than English ones even with light compression. The four bit compression that platforms ship costs almost nothing in English but a clear share of accuracy in Greek, and the strongest compression brings Greek close to guessing while English stays usable. The general model is the most accurate in English but among the weakest in Greek, where it needs about four times as many text pieces per question, while the Greek adapted model keeps the gap smallest at the price of a larger and slower file. Files made without the calibration step that relies on mostly English text, including the file the platform publishes, lose the same Greek accuracy at four bits. A compression level found acceptable in English should therefore not be assumed acceptable in Greek.

title: Embeddings Are Overpriced? A Frozen 16 MB Vocabulary for Small and Ternary Language Models
abstract: In a small language model the vocabulary is the single largest part. In Gemma 3 270M the embedding table holds 168M of 268M parameters, and because quantisation methods leave the embedding in 16-bit, it is also most of the file once the rest of the model is compressed. We ask what that table actually buys. We replace it with one frozen table of 512-bit codes, 16 MB, with no trainable parameters, derived once from a pretrained embedding by principal-component projection and sign binarisation, and we train the same Gemma-shaped body from scratch on the same 2.05B tokens with and without it. The learned table buys 0.20 nats of validation loss for 2.6 times the trainable parameters, but on LAMBADA, HellaSwag and PIQA the frozen-table model is better or tied; only ARC-Easy favours the learned table. With a ternary BitNet b1.58 body the whole model is a 46 MB file, still ties the float model on LAMBADA and PIQA, and on a laptop CPU generates 615 to 740 tokens per second in 62 MB of memory, five to six times the speed of the float model's 8-bit GGUF in llama.cpp at a seventh of the memory. The frozen table wins by 1.7 to 2.3 nats on rare words, accepts 10,000 new words after training with a 3% cost where the learned table collapses by 43%, and all of it is released with the weights, the data and every evaluation answer.

title: Gradient-Hessian Query Tradeoffs: Matching Lower Bounds in Logarithmic Dimension
abstract: We establish matching lower bounds for the tradeoff between gradient and Hessian queries in nonconvex optimization with Lipschitz Hessian. In normalized units, the initial objective gap is at most $T$, the Hessian Lipschitz constant is at most one, and the target gradient norm is one. For sufficiently large $T$, dimension $d \ge C\log(2+T)$, and a prescribed Hessian budget $h \ge 1$ with $h+1 \le aT$, every randomized algorithm requires $Ω(\min\{Td^{1/3}, T^{3/2}/\sqrt{h+1}\})$ ordinary queries. An ordinary query returns the value and gradient; a Hessian query returns the complete second jet and is charged only to its own budget. Both budgets are worst-case caps. Queries and outputs may be arbitrary real points, and no Hessian-norm bound is imposed. The hard input law consists of fixed, globally $C^3$, coercive functions. The construction combines sequential readouts of a continuous random matrix with localized completion blocks and reliability dimensions that vary across hierarchy levels. Premature disclosures are charged by their expected task cost, while every oracle reply remains the exact jet of the presampled objective. This yields a logarithmic dimension threshold and a depth-independent third-derivative bound. Together with a translation of the NALEN upper bound of Chen, Liu, Luo, and Zhang, the result determines the query tradeoff up to absolute constants throughout the stated range.

title: Seeing is Believing: Benchmarking and Mitigating the Interference of Language Priors on Visual Perception in MLLMs
abstract: Language priors in MLLMs can override visual evidence, impairing visual perception. Existing benchmarks assume shared priors across models and rely solely on accuracy. However, cross-model prior agreement falls below 80%, and over 15% of items can be answered correctly without any image, causing accuracy to overestimate prior resistance. To address these limitations, we introduce ViSiP-Bench, a benchmark grounded in rare-but-real scenarios across six prior categories, with a model-aware dynamic prior induction protocol and three metrics that more precisely and continuously measure prior resistance than accuracy alone. Evaluating 24 models reveals that prior adherence is pervasive, does not improve with scale, and larger models tend to either strongly override their priors or firmly adhere to them. We therefore propose MAPS, which identifies each model's strongest priors and fine-tunes on factually grounded knowledge to soften excessive prior reliance without disrupting general capabilities.

title: Learning to Search for Executable Patternmaking from Certified Programs
abstract: Recent models generate sewing patterns from images or text, and program-based representations make these patterns executable. These systems produce a finished pattern and do not model how a patternmaker turns one pattern into another. In practice a new style is made by editing an existing pattern: lengthening the bodice, moving a dart, swapping a sleeve. Pattern archives record the results of such edits and none of the steps. We observe that the steps can be recovered by searching over editing actions until one pattern becomes the other. A deterministic compiler makes the recovered steps checkable. To this end, we present SemDraft, the first framework that learns to search for executable patternmaking programs from paired before-and-after sewing patterns without recorded editing steps. Specifically, a bounded search recovers a program of editing actions and certifies it only after three checks: it recompiles from scratch, every pair of its actions is classified as ordered or interchangeable, and an independent replay reaches the same pattern. The certified programs then train a model that ranks candidate actions inside the same search. On two frozen draws of 80 order-sensitive cases, with every other search component fixed, the learned ranker certifies 63 and 64 cases within 1,000 search executions, against at most 53 and 52 for non-learned rankers.

title: DST-Net: Decomposed Spatio-Temporal Network for Time Series Forecasting
abstract: Series decomposition has emerged as a widely acknowledged paradigm in deep time series forecasting models. However, existing approaches predominantly employ a homogeneous modeling strategy for all subsequences, thereby overlooking the distinct inductive biases inherent in different components. We identify that the trend component exhibits dominant spatial coupling across channels but carries significant temporal redundancy, whereas the seasonal component is characterized by local temporal evolution but remains susceptible to attention distraction. To address this, we propose a novel disentangled architecture that tailors specific modeling strategies to align with the intrinsic properties of each component. For the trend branch, we design a Latent Graph Block, employing latent graph modeling to capture global topological dependencies and system-wide co-movements. Conversely, for the seasonal branch, we introduce a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism to mitigate attention distraction. By injecting learnable Gaussian priors, we impose structural constraints that compel the model to focus on multi-granular local contexts, effectively filtering out global noise and accurately capturing local evolutionary phases. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

Conversely, for the seasonal branch, we introduce a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism to mitigate attention distraction. By injecting learnable Gaussian priors, we impose structural constraints that compel the model to focus on multi-granular local contexts, effectively filtering out global noise and accurately capturing local evolutionary phases. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

title: Interpolation of unitaries with time-dependent Hamiltonians via Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Quantum systems governed by time-dependent Hamiltonians pose significant challenges for the accurate computation of unitary time-evolution operators, which are essential for predicting quantum state dynamics. In this work, we introduce a physics-informed deep learning approach based on Physics-Informed Neural Networks to estimate these operators over the full time domain. By incorporating physical constraints such as unitarity and leveraging the second-order Magnus expansion or Trotterization on the evolution operator, the proposed framework enables the estimation of unitary matrices at different time intervals. The model is trained using simulated unitary operators and evaluated on quantum systems ranging from 2 to 6 qubits, governed by a fully non-zero Pauli Hamiltonian. For larger many-body systems, specifically those with 7 and 8 qubits, the same methodology is employed to reconstruct an effective time-dependent Hamiltonian, restricted to nearest-neighbor Ising and XYZ Heisenberg models, from which the corresponding time-evolution operator is computed over the entire temporal domain. Across all system sizes, the framework achieves high gate fidelities using a limited number of unitary samples, with a statistical analysis over independent Hamiltonian realizations confirming mean fidelities close to 0.99 and low variability. Furthermore, once trained, the model interpolates the evolution operator with inference times substantially lower than those of a numerical interpolation baseline, indicating a potential reduction in measurement and data acquisition costs. These results highlight the effectiveness of the approach for data-driven simulation and identification of quantum dynamical systems, with direct relevance to quantum computing and quantum simulation applications.

title: Evaluating Portuguese Tokenizers as Morpheme Sequence in Relation to LLM Downstream Performance
abstract: Sub-word tokenizers allow us to handle open vocabulary problems using a relatively small set of tokens. Despite its ease of use, it usually relies on a data-driven approach that does not directly employ linguistic or morphologic features for text tokenization. [Bostrom and Durrett 2020] and [Hofmann et al. 2021] demonstrate that morphemes improve LLM performance on English texts. In this work, we explore the hypothesis that tokenizers that are capable of producing a token sequence better aligned with a morpheme sequence can improve LLMs performance on Brazilian Portuguese. To evaluate how the presence of morphemes can impact LLMs for Brazilian Portuguese, we propose MorphEval-PT, a new evaluation procedure based on the psycholinguistic concept of morphological models of word processing. We build new BPE and Unigram vocabularies that are evaluated on MorphEval-PT and, in order to validate the impact of morphemes on LLMs performance, train new LLMs from scratch and evaluate its performance on downstream tasks. Consistently, BPE demonstrates a higher precision score than Unigram in its ability to represent morphemes, as well as better performance on every downstream task. These promising results indicate that accessing the ability of tokenizers to represent morphemes is an important feature in the development of LLMs for Brazilian Portuguese and that MorphEval-PT is a good and lightweight method to improve LLM performance before any pre-training.

title: Garbage Collecting the External Effects of AI Agents
abstract: AI agents open pull requests, allocate cloud resources, charge cards, and post status updates to team channels. They increasingly delegate their work to trees of sub-agents and helper processes that the model shapes at runtime. When these computations end before their work is done, for example because the user cancels them, their token budget runs out, or they crash, their processes stop, but their effects remain. We argue that managing these effects is a garbage collection problem over external services. Remove an effect too early, and something that depends on it breaks. Never remove it, and it leaks. Unlike memory, this heap belongs to other services, the code that creates effects is chosen at runtime and cannot be instrumented, other people start depending on effects without telling anyone, and every part of the system can crash. We present effect recovery, an abstraction for disposing of the external effects a computation leaves behind when it ends. It guarantees that a computation leaves no dangling effects and no silent leaks. It records every effect before it happens and decides what happens to each one after the computation ends. Requests leave the computation only through a monitor, which records each one before forwarding it. Because the computation can stop at any point, a controller that outlives it works from this record. It removes an effect only when removal is known to be safe, and otherwise keeps it or escalates it to a human. Effects that no later step needs, such as the final pull request, wait until the user completes the task, so an aborted task never creates them. Our evaluation shows that our implementation of effect recovery mediates real agent workloads without meaningfully reducing their task success or adding noticeable latency, and that its guarantee holds when computations fail at any point.

title: Beyond Pairwise Accuracy: Testing Synthetic Manufacturing Data
abstract: This Jupyter Notebook investigates whether synthetic quality-control records preserve a manufacturing relationship defined by XOR. Using two fictional datasets with identical one-way and two-way distributions but different three-way structures, it compares pairwise and full-joint OpenDP measurements fitted with Private-PGM, alongside an MST demonstration. Repeated experiments measure marginal accuracy, defect prevalence, XOR agreement and synthetic sampling error. Tables, plots and a data-driven interpretation explain the findings, privacy accounting and implications for sharing manufacturing data.

title: From "Computational Problem-Solving" to "Question Emergence": On the Intrinsic Boundary of Al Mathematical Research and the Ultimate Defense of Human Cognition
abstract: Recently, Al has concentrated on solving a large number of unsolved problems in mathematics with its powerful computational capacity, sparking widespread attention in both academia and industry. Some views hold that Al will rapidly replace mathematicians, and by extension, gradually replace physicists and all engineering professionals. This paper dissects this "computational replacement theory" through logical reductio ad absurdum. It points out that machine-style problem-solving can produce correct "results, " yet it cannot "emerge new disciplines and fields in the process of solving major problems as humans do. Current Al technology is essentially confined to three closed technical paths: "brute-force enumeration, internal optimization within closed systems, and probability theory." It lacks the "conceptual isolation" and "practicality" core that are crucial to human cognition. Therefore, Al cannot truly replace the subject position of humanity in scientific exploration. Keywords: Computational problem-solving; Question emergence; Conceptual isolation; Practicality; Intrinsic boundary;Human originality

title: Orb GraphRAG pipeline study: raw results and model-call cache (September-October 2026)
abstract: Every run, log and recorded model call from a four-week study (18 September to 14 October 2026) of the local question-answering pipeline of Orb, a desktop notes app that builds a knowledge graph from your notes. Ten rounds on HotpotQA and MuSiQue tested extraction models (Gemma 4, Qwen 3.5, Phi-4, Granite 4.2), retrieval strategies (raw passages, keyword search, PageRank expansion, evidence ordering), answering models, and a reranker scoring fix. Contents: llm-cache/ holds 76,023 recorded model calls, content-addressed, which replay every run without a GPU. machines/ holds each GPU machine's per-question results with full traces, run configurations, index-build records and logs. The README maps folders to rounds. Code, reports and the lab notebook: branch orb-testing of github.com/josetseph/Orb (commit b4e51c0). Notes are passages from HotpotQA (CC BY-SA 4.0) and MuSiQue (CC BY 4.0), derived from Wikipedia. The bundle is one tar.gz split into six parts. Rebuild with cat orb-research-data.tar.gz.part-* > orb-research-data.tar.gz (md5 5526e60e3817f3fabd46f8e9d78bd243). The same data is browsable at https://huggingface.co/datasets/josetseph/orb-graphrag-study.

title: Special issue on trustworthy and safe AI: Interpretability, robustness, and security
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly in large language models (LLMs) and physical robotics, have rapidly reshaped daily life and industrial applications.As these systems become more capable and autonomous, ensuring their safety, trustworthiness, robustness, and alignment with human values has become increasingly important.In response to these challenges, this special issue on "Trustworthy and Safe AI: Interpretability, Robustness, and Security" brings together recent research that advances the safety and trustworthiness of AI across diverse models, systems, and real-world applications.This special issue received 50 submissions, reflecting the growing research interest in trustworthy and safe AI.Following a rigorous peer-review process, 11 papers were selected for publication.Together, these studies span several interconnected dimensions of the field, ranging from emerging security threats in LLMs and multiagent systems to robustness, autonomous system safety, and explainability for practical deployment.The following five papers focus on emerging security and safety threats across modern AI systems.These studies examine how vulnerabilities arise from adversarial attacks, multi-agent interactions, social context, multilingual settings, and hidden information while exploring the corresponding mechanisms for detection and defense.In [1], the authors investigate a more evasive mixed clean/dirty-label X-to-X backdoor attack and propose an ensemble defense that combines complementary detectors such as Neural Cleanse, PT-RED, CEPA, and MMBD.This work is significant because it addresses both robustness and interpretability, and the ensemble improves resilience across diverse backdoor mechanisms while also supporting trigger inversion to help explain the nature of the detected attack.By jointly considering stronger adversarial attacks, generalized defense, and interpretable backdoor analysis, this study aligns well with the themes of Trustworthy and Safe AI: Interpretability, Robustness, and Security.In [2], the authors study how a single malicious agent can compromise the collective decision-making of otherwise well-aligned LLM agents in a collaborative financial multi-agent environment and proposes a datalineage-based systemic defense.Its main contribution is to show that the interaction dynamics themselves can become a security vulnerability, extending AI safety concerns beyond isolated models to multi-agent societies.By analyzing poisoning, social conformity, and system-level verification across multiple models and network settings, this study offers timely insights into the robustness, safety, and trustworthy coordination of emerging autonomous multi-agent AI systems.The paper [3] titled "Lost in the comments: Social context as a single-pass jailbreak and defense on agentic platforms" by Jeongsu Park and colleagues investigates how comments, reactions, and engagement signals surrounding harmful content influence the safety behavior of LLMs in agentic social platforms.The study demonstrates that the ambient social context, even without explicit malicious instructions, can substantially alter attack success rates, whereas ethically framed comments can reinforce safe behavior through the same contextual channel.Through controlled experiments that varied the valence, volume, and engagement of social signals, this study shows that the nature of the surrounding commentary is more important than its quantity in determining whether model safety is weakened or strengthened.This work is particularly valuable because it extends indirect prompt-injection research to the emerging setting of multi-agent platforms and provides evidence that social context can function as both an attack mechanism and a potential defensive control.Supported by comparisons with PAIR, independent rescoring with WildGuard, human adjudication, and signal-separation ablation

title: When the Image Lies
abstract: Generative systems can now synthesize moving images that are indistinguishable from footage captured by a camera. In doing so, they quietly dismantle two assumptions on which law has long depended: that a video is recorded by someone, and that it shows something that actually occurred. This chapter examines the consequences of that dismantling along three fault lines. The first is authorship, where the requirement of human creativity leaves fully machine-generated video in an uneasy ownership vacuum. The second is accountability, where responsibility for a harmful fabrication is spread thinly across model developers, platforms, deployers, and end users. The third is legal uncertainty, expressed in a fast-growing but fragmented body of statutes, transparency mandates. The chapter argues that the core problem is not a single doctrinal gap but a mismatch between an evidentiary culture inherited from photography and a technology that severs the image from its origin. It proposes a governance response on content provenance, graduated liability, evidentiary reform, and media literacy.

title: ResStreamGS: Residual-Sensitive Dual-Stream Gaussian Splatting for Mobile Volumetric Video Streaming
abstract: Real-time mobile volumetric video enables immersive free-viewpoint experiences, but delivering high-quality 3D content under constrained bandwidth and computation remains challenging. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) systems, such as V$^3$, enable efficient mobile streaming by encoding time-varying Gaussian attributes with commodity video codecs and hardware decoding. However, existing pipelines treat all Gaussians as frame-varying signals, which is poorly suited to full-scene content where large portions remain temporally stable. Our empirical study shows that frame-wise adaptation and video coding of all Gaussians cause quality degradation in complex full-scene content, particularly in temporally stable regions. To address this issue, we propose ResStreamGS, a residual-sensitive dual-stream framework that processes Gaussians according to their temporal behavior. ResStreamGS identifies residual-sensitive primitives through lightweight probe adaptation and reuses stable Gaussians within each Group of Pictures (GOP). Stable Gaussians are transmitted once per GOP, while only residual-sensitive Gaussians remain in the frame-wise hardware-decodable video stream. Experiments on complex full-scene volumetric videos show that ResStreamGS improves post-codec PSNR by 7.51--8.35~dB over a controlled V$^3$-style all-Gaussians baseline, reduces amortized payload by up to 56.5%, and achieves 30.883~FPS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 778G platform.

title: Construction and decoding of convolutional codes with optimal column distances
abstract: The construction of Maximum Distance Profile (MDP) convolutional codes in general requires the use of very large finite fields. In contrast, convolutional codes with optimal column distances maximize the column distances for given code parameters $ (n, k, \delta) $ and a given arbitrary finite field. In this paper, we present a construction of such convolutional codes. In addition, we prove that for the considered parameters the codes that we constructed are the only ones achieving optimal column distances. The structure of the presented convolutional codes with optimal column distances is strongly related to first order Reed-Muller block codes and we leverage this fact to develop a reduced complexity version of the Viterbi algorithm for these codes.

title: Demonstration of RDF and SPARQL 1.2 Interoperability through Query Rewriting
abstract: With the finalization of rdf 1.2 and sparql 1.2, the new triple-term construct brings native reification to rdf. native support, however, does not imply uniform adoption: existing datasets continue to model statement-level metadata through established reification patterns, so federated queries must mediate between these patterns and the new syntax. we address this by rewriting queries written against triple terms into queries over the reification pattern actually used by each source, expressing the relationship as a sparql construct query that is unfolded into the user’s query. this paper demonstrates the approach through a web interface in which users author their own mappings, select sources, and observe how their queries are rewritten and executed across federated endpoints. reification translation is one application of a more general framework for sparql query answering under declarative rdf-to-rdf mappings, which we plan to formalize and optimize. the language gaps it exposes also give us concrete input for the upcoming sparql maintenance-mode standardization.

title: Site adaptation of CAMS without a local station in West Africa: transfer cost and bias structure
abstract: Ground measurements of solar irradiance are scarce in West Africa, and most sites have no station with which to adapt satellite estimates. A CAMS site adaptation learned at existing stations can instead be transferred to such a site. The cost of this transfer is evaluated at 31 West African stations, with corrections learned on one year of data and tested on the following year. For global horizontal irradiance (GHI), having no local measurement adds about one percentage point to the mean absolute error of the annual total. The north–south trend in the bias transfers, but each station retains an offset of its own. Part of the observed excess error comes from the sensors. With independent calibration errors of 0.95 %, the excess of the trend corrections is no longer detectable with this network. Assuming a centred error, their one-sided 90 % bound on the annual error is 2.6–2.7 %, compared with 2.2 % for one year on site. Measured against the true irradiance, only the two transfers based on the nearest stations remain worse than on-site adaptation across the whole network (permutation test with Holm correction). On the Tier 1 stations alone, no transfer is worse. A bias–latitude line with prediction intervals is provided for sites within the study domain. For direct normal irradiance (DNI), no transfer cost is established after correction for multiple comparisons. One year of measurement is not enough to pin down its bias.

title: A SMOTE enhanced multi stream deep learning ensemble for credit card fraud detection
abstract: Credit card fraud detection is highly imbalanced, making minority-class metrics and deployment efficiency more informative than accuracy alone. This study proposes SMOTE-EnsembleNet (SENet), combining CNN, BiLSTM, and Transformer streams through learnable cross-attention fusion. Among 100%, 200%, and 500% SMOTE ratios with focal loss, 200% SMOTE achieved the best overall balance. SENet obtained AUC-ROC values of 0.9967 (95% CI 0.9955–0.9979), 0.9567 (95% CI 0.9542–0.9592), and 0.9923 (95% CI 0.9911–0.9935) on ULB, IEEE-CIS, and PaySim, respectively. Compared with no SMOTE, AUC-ROC improved by 1.55, 1.55, and 1.34 percentage points, while cross-attention improved AUC-ROC by 0.22 percentage points over concatenation. Fold-level significance testing ((p < 0.05)) was conducted against all tuned baselines. SENet achieved 12.4 ms inference latency per transaction on an NVIDIA A100 GPU while supporting interpretable error and feature-importance analyses. AUC-ROC and AUC-PR are threshold-independent, whereas precision, recall, and F1-score are reported separately in the experiments. The 12.4 ms latency applies only to the stated NVIDIA A100 configuration. Cross-attention additionally improved AUC-PR by 1.3 percentage points over concatenation, and the small differences between 200% and 500% SMOTE are interpreted together with fold-level statistical tests.

title: New results on hypercube coloring problem from linear codes over Z2k
abstract: This paper is concerned with the hypercube coloring problem. Let 𝜒 ℓ ⁡ ( 𝑚 ) be the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices of a hypercube with 2 𝑚 vertices such that every two vertices with Hamming distance ≤ ℓ have different colors. Using linear codes over ℤ 2 𝑘 (the ring of integers modulo 2 𝑘 ) and the generalized Gray map, we establish a connection between the parameters of linear codes over ℤ 2 𝑘 and 𝜒 ℓ ⁡ ( 𝑚 ) . Furthermore, we obtain some new upper bounds on 𝜒 ℓ ⁡ ( 𝑚 ) . In some cases, the new upper bounds are tighter than the previously best known results. In particular, we determine the exact values 𝜒 5 ⁡ ( 1 4 ) = 2 8 and 𝜒 4 ⁡ ( 1 3 ) = 2 7 .

title: Reflective Compositional Grounding for Natural-Language-to-SPARQL
abstract: Natural-language query generation over large knowledge graphs embodies the classical vocabulary problem in human-systems communication. Questions express concepts through wording and compositions that can differ substantially from the target schema, while limited model context requires selective access to schema information. We present an NL2SPARQL framework that places conceptual compositionality at the center of query interpretation and connects it to the relational composition required for binding and query construction. A fixed concept encoder represents compound expressions jointly, and schema candidates are ranked using semantic similarity, type compatibility, and hierarchy proximity. Reflective refinement critically examines how the grounded meanings are realized through argument bindings, joins, and operator scope. Diagnosed semantic discrepancies guide revisions to the responsible stage. We formalise a monotone refinement discipline that accumulates scoped interpretation requirements and establish conditions under which changes to the composed process preserve previously validated interpretations. Across five benchmark/knowledge-graph targets, mean schema recall@10 increases from 0.712 to 0.837. With retrieval held fixed, reflective prompt rewriting adds 2.27-3.33 answer-F1 points. These experiments evaluate the grounding and refinement mechanisms, while the formal analysis specifies the stronger requirements for conservative adaptation across queries.

title: Clause Linkage in Brazilian Portuguese Narratives: Evidence from Enhanced Dependency Annotation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of Enhanced and Extended Enhanced Universal Dependencies for narrative analysis in Brazilian Portuguese, focusing on how enhanced dependency relations contribute to clause linkage. The study examines narrative sentences annotated in CoNLL-U format and compares basic and enhanced dependency layers. The results show that enhanced dependencies are particularly useful for recovering implicit subject relations in Portuguese and for enriching clause relations through information from prepositions and conjunctions. These enhancements enable a more explicit representation of participant continuity and event relations in narratives, supporting the transition from syntactic dependency analysis to richer semantic annotation.

title: Vocabulary-constrained rewriting and translation for dictionary-based sign language avatars, code
abstract: Code of a study that measures how much a dictionary-based International Sign (IS) avatar with several hundred signs fingerspells in English meeting transcripts (AMI Meeting Corpus) and written sentences (FLORES-200), and whether rewording the text, or translating text from Greek, French, Spanish and German, into words that the avatar can sign avoids the fingerspelling without changing the meaning. The code replaces words without a sign by WordNet synonyms or by similar words judged by word vectors, rewrites and translates text with EuroLLM-1.7B-Instruct, with and without a llama.cpp grammar that restricts the output to words with a sign, translates with NLLB-200-distilled-600M, estimates the fingerspelling and signing time of a dictionary avatar, scores the meaning kept with COMET, chrF, sentence embeddings and mutual entailment, analyses the failures of restricted rewriting and writes the tables and figures of the article. Every model runs on an ordinary processor. The system outputs, scores and analyses are in the data deposit https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23396571.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Correction and Mutual Correction in Multi-Agent Systems: A Feedback-Driven Framework for Dynamic Error Repair
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve the reliability of intelligent problem-solving through error detection, iterative refinement, and information exchange. However, two fundamental correction mechanisms present different advantages and limitations. Self-correction allows an agent to identify and repair errors within its own reasoning or behavior, whereas mutual correction enables agents to inspect, challenge, and improve one another's outputs. Continuous reliance on either mechanism may introduce undesirable behavior, including persistent individual reasoning errors, redundant refinement, uncritical acceptance of peer feedback, and unnecessary communication costs. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Correction (ASMC), a feedback-driven framework that dynamically switches between self-correction and mutual correction according to observed correction outcomes, estimated residual errors, agent disagreement, confidence calibration, and computational costs. Rather than assuming that independent correction or collaborative correction is universally superior, ASMC treats the selection of a correction mechanism as a dynamic decision problem. The framework includes independent error diagnosis, peer-based verification, correction-quality estimation, adaptive mode selection, and outcome-based evaluation. A formal optimization objective is introduced to balance task accuracy, correction effectiveness, computational efficiency, and the preservation of valid solutions. The framework is designed to support heterogeneous or homogeneous intelligent agents, including software agents, robotic agents, planning systems, and language-model-based agents. A theoretical analysis identifies conditions under which adaptive selection can outperform fixed correction policies, while also clarifying the assumptions required for such guarantees. An experimental protocol is proposed to evaluate the framework against self-correction-only, mutual-correction-only, fixed alternating, and other adaptive baselines. The proposed approach provides a general research direction for dynamically coordinating individual error repair and collaborative error repair in multi-agent intelligence.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Reflection and Mutual Reflection in Multi-Agent Systems: A Unified Framework for Dynamic Reflective Intelligence
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve problem-solving through iterative reflection, error detection, information exchange, and collaborative decision-making. However, existing reflective processes often rely on fixed interaction patterns, such as allowing each agent to revise its own output independently or requiring multiple agents to critique one another throughout a predefined sequence. These static patterns may be inefficient when independent reflection is sufficient, yet inadequate when an agent's reasoning is constrained by its own assumptions or incomplete information. This paper proposes Adaptive Switching between Self-Reflection and Mutual Reflection (ASSMR), a unified framework that dynamically selects between two complementary reflective mechanisms according to the evolving state of a multi-agent system. Self-reflection enables an agent to examine and revise its own reasoning, decisions, or actions without requiring external reflective input. Mutual reflection enables agents to evaluate, challenge, and refine one another's outputs through structured interactions. The proposed framework estimates the relative utility of these mechanisms using indicators such as uncertainty, unresolved errors, disagreement, information diversity, reflection progress, communication cost, and observed task performance. A switching controller then selects an appropriate reflective mode, determines the participating agents, and evaluates whether further reflection is beneficial. The framework also incorporates adaptive switching thresholds, bounded reflection cycles, historical feedback, and safeguards against premature consensus and repetitive reasoning. Unlike approaches that simply combine individual reasoning with multi-agent debate, ASSMR treats the selection and transition between reflective modes as an explicit system-level decision problem. This paper formalizes the framework, presents a reference algorithm, develops research propositions, and outlines an experimental protocol for evaluating effectiveness, efficiency, robustness, and reflective diversity across heterogeneous multi-agent environments. The framework is a methodological proposal; its comparative advantages and empirical performance remain to be established through experiments.

title: A Geospatial Operational Event Knowledge Graph for Traceable Air–Ground Robotic Inspection in Grain-Reserve Warehouses
abstract: Intelligent monitoring in grain-reserve warehouses increasingly combines fixed sensors, UAVs, quadruped robots, human review, and site information systems, yet the resulting operational records are typically stored separately. This fragmentation makes it difficult to reconstruct how a detected problem evolves from observation to execution, evidence, and review, and limits traceable data-driven decision support. To address this issue, this study proposes a Geospatial Operational Event Knowledge Graph (GOEKG) that uses a stable managed-event identity to organize geographic anchors, source provenance, air–ground tasks, evidence, review, and lifecycle states within a property graph. The framework combines source-record normalization and graph mapping with competency queries and operational-semantic constraints for temporal order, spatial continuity, review reachability, lifecycle transitions, and provenance-aware reconciliation. A Panqiao warehouse case is used to instantiate and evaluate the graph. The case instantiated 11 reference-case nodes and 15 typed relations; six competency queries recovered the corresponding paths with temporal and spatial continuity across both robot branches. Controlled mutations of a source-derived record fixture returned UNKNOWN for missing temporal anchors, resolved spatial conflicts by explicit rules, and rejected temporal-order, spatial-linkage, and unauthorized-closure violations. A Neo4j benchmark on synthetic fixtures scaled from 1000 to 50,000 events. Secondary evaluations measured chronological alert-type relation completion and strict temporal fixed-snapshot follow-up candidate ranking. Under the latter protocol, Context-only achieved Macro-F1 0.783 and balanced accuracy 0.836, while Full context achieved average precision 0.952 and prioritized Pending Verification records in the limited-budget queue. The fixed-snapshot analysis supports context-assisted review prioritization under a retrospective event-time protocol. GOEKG therefore provides a traceable event-centered integration layer for intelligent monitoring and review-oriented operational decision support.

title: Self-Calibrated Subspace Robust PCA for Parameter-Free Removal of Mixed Noise and Line Stripes in Hyperspectral Images
abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSIs) are often corrupted by Gaussian noise, impulses and stripes whose intensities vary across bands. The representative coefficient correlated total variation (RCCTV) model restores HSIs efficiently, but it lacks Gaussian and stripe terms, and its noise-aware extensions require the noise level and a stripe budget to be specified in advance. This article proposes a self-calibrated RCCTV (SC-RCCTV) model, in which the noise parameters are estimated adaptively during the iterations. A band-wise dense term and line-constant column and row stripe terms are introduced into RCCTV. The noise level of each band is initialized by a stripe-invariant median absolute deviation estimator and refined online from the residual, which turns the separation of sparse and dense noise into a band-adaptive Huber loss, and the stripe thresholds follow from a significance test whose false-alarm rate can be predicted analytically. No parameter is tuned for a specific image, and every subproblem of the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) solver is solved in closed form. Under line stripes, SC-RCCTV outperforms the parameter-free FastHyMix by 8.17 dB on native-size cubes, and, without any noise information, it exceeds S3TTV, which is given the true noise parameters, by 1.52 dB while running more than 1,900 times faster. On average, it stays within 0.01 dB of the same model given the true noise levels, and its online calibration improves on a two-stage estimate-then-denoise scheme. Experiments on real Indian Pines and Urban data further delineate its scope for stripes that do not span entire lines.
